Vector: "exposes content of non-allowed files using ?inline&import or ?raw?import. Only apps explicitly exposing the Vite dev server to the network (using --host or server.host config option) are affected." attack_vector adds that a remote attacker can read files including source and environment secrets outside the served root. patch_available true, live_patch_available false, live_patch_notes: "No live-patch tool registered for this entry at bulk-import time. Vendor patch typically requires service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction."

CVE-2025-54313.name: Prettier eslint-config-prettier Embedded Malicious Code Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: embedded malicious code (CWE-506) published in compromised versions of the eslint-config-prettier npm package (maintainer-account compromise), executing on developer and CI machines that installed the tainted versions. CISA KEV-listed 2026-01-22 with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (the malicious code is delivered through a trusted update channel or package; no authentication to the victim is required)
attack_vector.complexity: low — KEV-listed, actively exploited; treat as weaponized
attack_vector.ai_factor: No AI involvement documented in discovery or weaponization.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Enforce cryptographic integrity and provenance verification on all installed/updated code (code signing with verification, Sigstore/in-toto, SLSA provenance), pin dependencies to verified versions, and require multi-factor and review gates on package-publishing/maintainer accounts.
prevention.adequacy: Signature and provenance verification is the definitive control; the compromise succeeded precisely because the trusted channel was trusted without independent verification.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Monitoring for unexpected install/post-install script execution and outbound connections during npm install on developer/CI machines, and version-pinning alerts on dependency changes.
detection.adequacy: Necessary because supply-chain compromise runs in a trusted context — the anomaly is the unexpected code execution alongside the legitimate tool.

response.what_would_have_worked: Pin and upgrade to a clean eslint-config-prettier version, delete node_modules and reinstall from a verified lockfile, rotate any credentials reachable from developer/CI machines that installed the tainted version, and verify build artifacts produced during the exposure window.
response.adequacy: Mandatory; supply-chain compromise propagates through every host that installed the tainted code, so response is environment-wide and includes build-artifact verification.

NIST-800-53-SR-11.gap: Component authenticity / anti-counterfeit is named, but verification is not enforced at install/update time — the tainted code shipped through a trusted channel without consumer-side signature/provenance verification, so the control is paper unless signed-artifact verification (Sigstore/in-toto) is mandated.

NIST-SSDF-800-218-PS.2.gap: The SSDF calls for protecting release integrity and providing provenance, but downstream consumers had no enforced way to verify it; without signed releases plus provenance a consumer cannot detect maliciously-published or substituted code.

SLSA-build-provenance.gap: SLSA build provenance and signed releases would let a consumer detect a maliciously-published version; absent enforced verification at the install/update step, a compromised maintainer account or update channel propagates the malicious code unchecked.

EU-CRA-secure-update.gap: The EU Cyber Resilience Act requires secure update mechanisms and shipping without known exploitable defects; an update channel or package registry that ships embedded malicious code violates the secure-update and integrity expectations.

compliance_exposure_score.basis: eslint-config-prettier (npm) is trusted by default; audited organizations that install vendor updates or npm dependencies without enforcing signature/provenance verification or pinning are exposed to maliciously-published code, and the compromise reaches every host that installed it.

new_control_requirements.name: NPM-CI-IGNORE-SCRIPTS-DEFAULT
new_control_requirements.description: CI and developer installs that resolve eslint-config-prettier must run with lifecycle scripts disabled (npm/pnpm/yarn install --ignore-scripts), because the payload in the tainted releases is an install.js that the package manager executes automatically the moment the tarball is unpacked — no import, no build step, no developer action required. eslint-config-prettier is a lint-configuration package with no legitimate native build, so it belongs in the deny-by-default set with no postinstall allowlist entry; a formatting/lint dependency that suddenly requires an install hook is itself the detection signal. With scripts off, the tainted tarball can land in node_modules without ever launching the Windows node-gyp.dll payload, which converts a code-execution event on every build machine into an inert file on disk.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The packet records the exploitation path as "Installing an affected package executes an install.js file that launches the node-gyp.dll malware on Windows," running on developer and CI machines that installed the tainted versions. CWE-506 (embedded malicious code), CVSS 8.8, RWEP 77, PoC available, CISA KEV-listed 2026-01-22 with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation.

new_control_requirements.name: LOCKFILE-INTEGRITY-VERIFIED-AT-CI-BOOT
new_control_requirements.description: The compromise arrives as new versions of a package the build already trusts, so the only consumer-side control that stops the tainted eslint-config-prettier tarball being fetched at all is a strict-lockfile install: npm ci / --frozen-lockfile / --immutable refuses to resolve any version not already pinned, so a CI run that starts after the malicious publish still installs the pre-compromise pinned release and never touches install.js. Pair it with a tarball integrity-hash check against a known-good cache snapshot at CI boot — for a lint config whose declared purpose has not changed, an integrity hash that moved without a deliberate version bump is the signal. Remediation here is dependency-side: a clean release exists, so move off the tainted versions and re-pin the lockfile; there is no live-patch path to buy time.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet attack_vector: "embedded malicious code (CWE-506) published in compromised versions of the eslint-config-prettier npm package (maintainer-account compromise), executing on developer and CI machines that installed the tainted versions." patch_available is true and live_patch_available is false. KEV-listed 2026-01-22, confirmed in-the-wild exploitation, RWEP 77.

new_control_requirements.name: NPM-MAINTAINER-MFA-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: The root cause the packet records is maintainer-account compromise, not a coding defect in eslint-config-prettier — the attacker published under the legitimate maintainer identity, so every publisher-identity and signature check on the release passes and no vulnerability scanner has anything to flag. For a lint config with reach across essentially every JavaScript build, consuming organizations should make MFA-on-publish attestation from critical-path maintainers a precondition of accepting a version bump, and refuse to upgrade where the attestation is absent; upstream, registry-side MFA enforcement on publish-enabled accounts at this download volume is the structural fix. This is the control that addresses the compromise itself rather than its blast radius.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet attack_vector attributes the tainted releases to "(maintainer-account compromise)" of the eslint-config-prettier npm package. CWE-506, CVSS 8.8, RWEP 77, PoC available, KEV-listed 2026-01-22 with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation.

attack_vector.complexity: low — KEV-listed, actively exploited; treat as weaponized

detection.adequacy: Necessary to catch exploitation of instances not yet patched within the compressed window.

response.what_would_have_worked: Patch immediately under the KEV SLA, then investigate for post-exploitation persistence and rotate credentials reachable from the Unified Communications management surface.
response.adequacy: Mandatory for a KEV-listed unauthenticated flaw; patch-in-place without compromise assessment can leave attacker persistence.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The 30-day flaw-remediation SLA is far longer than the observed exploitation window for a KEV-listed unauthenticated network flaw; CISA KEV due dates are days, not a month.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: 'Appropriate timescales' is undefined; the standard 30-day reading is unsafe for an unauthenticated, actively-exploited flaw on an internet-facing service.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: The packet names five separately shipped products — Cisco Unified Communications Manager, Unified CM Session Management Edition, Unified CM IM & Presence Service, Unity Connection, and Webex Calling Dedicated Instance — each carrying its own version and its own upgrade, so a remediation record showing Unified CM at the fixed version says nothing about the IM & Presence Service or Unity Connection instances standing beside it. For this CVE the control's clock therefore has to be tracked per named product and per instance, running from the 2026-01-21 KEV listing. The mitigation the clock demands here is the vendor update and nothing else: the packet records patch_available true, live_patch_available false, and a note that the vendor patch typically requires a service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction — so there is no in-place mitigation to deploy while the update waits, and an instance that has taken the update but not restarted still runs the vulnerable code and must be counted as exposed rather than as met. Keep the sweep to the five products the packet names: it ties the CWE-94 sink to those and provides no mapping into other Cisco software, so treating every Cisco system in the estate as an instance of this CVE manufactures findings and upgrade work against products no evidence implicates. Priority follows the packet rather than the CVSS band on its own — confirmed in-the-wild exploitation, a public PoC, and an outcome the packet describes as user-level access to the underlying operating system followed by elevation to root, which means the end state is control of the platform, not degradation of a service. Distinguishing test: produce, per named product and per instance, the running version and the restart timestamp against the vendor's fixed version — a vulnerability-management attestation that records the estate as compliant because the change tickets closed inside the window passes cleanly while an unrestarted instance keeps serving.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: 'Cisco Unified Communications Manager (Unified CM), Cisco Unified Communications Manager Session Management Edition (Unified CM SME), Cisco Unified Communications Manager IM & Presence Service (Unified CM IM&P), Cisco Unity Connection, and Cisco Webex Calling Dedicated Instance contain a code injection vulnerability that could allow the attacker to obtain user-level access to the underlying operating system and then elevate privileges to root.' CWE-94. cisa_kev true, kev_date 2026-01-21, active_exploitation confirmed, poc_available true, CVSS 9.8, RWEP 77. patch_available true; live_patch_available false; live_patch_notes: 'No live-patch tool registered for this entry at bulk-import time. Vendor patch typically requires service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction.' Citing gaps closed here: AU-Essential-8-Patch, ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8, NIS2-Art21-patch-management, NIST-800-53-SI-2.

new_control_requirements.name: CONTROL-PANEL-PLUGIN-USER-SURFACE-MUST-NOT-REACH-ROOT-OPERATIONS
new_control_requirements.description: The packet's escalation has two stages, and the second is the one this control governs: code injection gives the attacker user-level access to the underlying operating system of the Unified Communications product, and from that user-level context privileges are elevated to root. A constrained context reaching root operations on the platform beneath it is exactly the pattern the control forbids. Bound to these five products, it means the platform's privileged operations sit behind their own authorization boundary that the application tier can only reach through a constrained, validated interface, so that a defect in the application's input handling does not leave an attacker one step from root on the call-control and messaging platform. This is why the least-privilege gap cited on this entry cannot close the path: the escalation happens inside the product, between an operating-system user context the attacker obtained through injection and root — there is no operator-assignable account whose privileges could be narrowed to prevent it, so an attestation covering administrator accounts on these products passes while the path stays open. Preconditions, stated rather than implied: the boundary is a property the vendor update establishes, so this control names what to verify and does not implement it, and the packet records no live-patch path, meaning each instance carries the service restart or system reboot the fix requires before it is remediated. Until that lands, the operator-side lever is restricting which segments can reach the affected products' interfaces — that bounds who can attempt the injection but leaves the path fully exploitable to anything inside a permitted segment, and it is simply unavailable where the interface must stay reachable for the products to carry calls, voicemail and presence. And because active_exploitation is confirmed with a public PoC, any instance reachable during the exposure window needs forensic triage and credential rotation: an update applied to a system that already granted root does not remove what the attacker left behind.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: CWE-94 code injection in Cisco Unified CM, Unified CM SME, Unified CM IM&P, Cisco Unity Connection and Cisco Webex Calling Dedicated Instance; vector states the flaw 'could allow the attacker to obtain user-level access to the underlying operating system and then elevate privileges to root'. active_exploitation confirmed; cisa_kev true, kev_date 2026-01-21; poc_available true; CVSS 9.8; RWEP 77. patch_available true; live_patch_available false; live_patch_notes: 'No live-patch tool registered for this entry at bulk-import time. Vendor patch typically requires service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction.' Citing gaps closed here: NIST-800-53-AC-6 (Least Privilege), UK-CAF-B4 (System security).

attack_vector.description: an information-disclosure flaw (CWE-200) in a Windows component, used as a primitive in a privilege-escalation chain (kernel-address leaks defeat KASLR for follow-on exploits). CISA KEV-listed 2026-01-13 with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation; LPEs of this class are routinely paired with an initial-access flaw by ransomware operators.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low (any local foothold — an unprivileged process, RDP session, or commodity malware on the endpoint)
attack_vector.complexity: low — KEV-listed, actively exploited; treat as weaponized
attack_vector.ai_factor: No AI involvement documented in discovery or weaponization.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the Microsoft security update; enforce hypervisor-protected code integrity (HVCI) / Virtualization-Based Security (VBS), and enable the Microsoft Vulnerable Driver Blocklist to shrink kernel-LPE attack surface on the long tail.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The 30-day flaw-remediation SLA is far longer than the observed exploitation window for a KEV-listed Windows kernel/driver LPE; ransomware operators typically pair these with an initial-access flaw and elevate to SYSTEM within hours of a foothold.

new_control_requirements.name: SCANNER-PAPER-COMPLIANCE-TEST
new_control_requirements.description: The packet records no live-patch path for this CVE and states the vendor fix typically requires a service restart or system reboot, which creates a specific paper-compliance state on Windows estates: the update is installed, the inventory or scanner reports the host as remediated, and the machine has not restarted — so the vulnerable Desktop Window Manager code is still the code in memory. Long-uptime workstations, session hosts and VDI golden-image children sit in exactly that state for weeks. The operational test for this CVE is therefore not 'is the update present' but 'is the host's last-boot time later than the update's install time'; any host failing that comparison must be counted as unremediated against the KEV clock rather than as patched. A scan that reports compliance from installed-package state alone certifies an estate that is still exploitable through the pending-reboot population.

compliance_exposure_score.basis: Internet-facing Gogs is run by audited organizations on a standard patch SLA and is mass-exploited within days; the required secret rotation / web-shell hunt is rarely part of the documented patch procedure, and dev-tool/CI exposure adds software-supply-chain blast radius.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: The Gogs Git server must be moved to the fixed build on the KEV clock, not on the informal cadence self-hosted developer tooling usually gets. A Git service is treated as internal infrastructure and patched when someone has time, but this flaw is confirmed exploited in the wild and lets an attacker write outside the intended directory on the Git server through the PutContents API and reach code execution. No live-patch path exists for this entry, so the SLA must budget for the service restart or system reboot the KEV requiredAction calls for -- a self-hosted Git server frequently has no standing restart window at all, which is precisely how a KEV-listed build survives in production past its due date.

Vendor patch typically requires service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction.' CVE-2009-0556.name: Microsoft Office PowerPoint Code Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: a code-injection / memory-corruption flaw (CWE-94) in Microsoft Office PowerPoint document parsing, exploitable by an attacker-controlled presentation for code execution in the PowerPoint process. CISA KEV-listed 2026-01-07 with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation; the legacy re-listing exists because long-tail unpatched estates remain exposed.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (the victim opens the attacker's document or visits the attacker's content)
attack_vector.complexity: low — KEV-listed, actively exploited; treat as weaponized
attack_vector.ai_factor: No AI involvement documented in discovery or weaponization (predates the AI-discovered-zeroday era).

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the Microsoft security update for Microsoft Office PowerPoint; enforce centralized patch management on the long tail; harden Office (Protected View, ASR rules) and disable legacy ActiveX/IE components where unused.
prevention.adequacy: Patch is definitive on a managed estate; legacy KEV re-listings exist because patch hygiene on the long tail is the failure mode.

detection.what_would_have_worked: EDR signatures for child-process execution from PowerPoint after attacker-content open, document-exploit telemetry, and inbound-content filtering (mail/web).
detection.adequacy: Backstops endpoints not yet patched on the long tail; necessary for unmanaged or legacy estates that cannot be patched promptly.

response.what_would_have_worked: Force the patch across the estate, isolate exploited endpoints, hunt for follow-on payloads (document-exploit chains often drop loaders), and review for credential theft.
response.adequacy: Mandatory; document/browser RCE typically leads to credential harvest and lateral movement, which a bare patch does not remediate.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The 30-day flaw-remediation SLA is far longer than the observed exploitation window for a KEV-listed, actively-exploited client-side document/browser RCE; legacy KEV re-listings document organizations still running unpatched builds.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: 'Appropriate timescales' is undefined; the standard reading is unsafe for an actively-exploited client RCE, and the legacy KEV re-listing exists because organizations still run vulnerable Office/IE/Windows builds.

AU-ISM-1546.gap: Essential 8 patch-applications (48h at ML3) is closer to the reality for a client RCE than 30 days, but legacy KEV re-listings show that long-tail unpatched estates persist; centralized update management and Office hardening are the load-bearing controls.

compliance_exposure_score.basis: Microsoft Office PowerPoint is ubiquitous on endpoints; audited organizations that maintain long-tail legacy estates (older Windows, Office, IE) are exposed even after newer estates are patched, which is why CISA re-lists these older KEV entries.

new_control_requirements.name: DOWNLOAD-PROVENANCE-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Exploitation here requires a victim to open an attacker-supplied presentation: the packet's vector is a PowerPoint file whose OutlineTextRefAtom carries an invalid index value, triggering memory corruption and code execution inside the PowerPoint process at the user's own privilege. On the unpatched long-tail installs the packet says the re-listing exists for, the delivery path is the only enforceable control. Require Mark-of-the-Web on every presentation arriving by mail, web download, or untrusted file share, and require MOTW-tagged presentations to open in Protected View — an isolated, reduced-privilege render — rather than the full parsing path that reaches the vulnerable record handling. Provenance has to survive the container: a presentation extracted from an archive, mounted from an ISO or VHD, or renamed must inherit the tag rather than lose it, and 'Enable Editing' on externally sourced presentations must be blocked by policy rather than left to the user, because parsing the file is the whole exploit. Distinguishing test: mail a presentation nested inside a ZIP to a managed workstation, extract it, and confirm the extracted file still opens in Protected View — an application-hardening attestation covering only macro and ActiveX/OLE settings passes cleanly while a provenance-stripped presentation reaches the parser with full user privileges. Preconditions: Protected View bounds the render, it does not repair the parser. A user who clicks through to editing, or a file arriving on an ingress path that never applies the tag, is back on the vulnerable path with nothing in between — so the tagging must be enforced at each ingress rather than assumed. This is a holding measure for hosts that have not yet taken the vendor fix, not a substitute for it.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet vector: a PowerPoint file with an OutlineTextRefAtom containing an invalid index value that triggers memory corruption, allowing remote attackers to execute arbitrary code; the packet's attack_vector places execution in the PowerPoint process. CWE-94. CISA KEV-listed 2026-01-07 with confirmed active exploitation; poc_available true; CVSS 9.8; RWEP 77. Citing gaps include AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening (User application hardening) and NIST-800-53-AC-6 (Least Privilege).

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: The vendor fix for this defect is not new; what the 2026-01-07 KEV listing changes is that the installs which never took it are now on a KEV clock. The packet states the reason for the re-listing outright — long-tail unpatched estates remain exposed — so for this CVE the control is not 'apply the update' but 'enumerate what never received it'. Run the clock from the listing against a census of every PowerPoint install actually in service, and measure completion by the build each install reports rather than by a 'no updates pending' state in a management console: the hosts that keep a defect of this vintage reachable are precisely the hosts that fell out of the managed update path, so the console's silence is an absence of visibility rather than evidence of remediation. The packet records no live-patch path and states the vendor patch typically requires a service restart or system reboot, so an install updated but not restarted is still exposed. Distinguishing test: pull the reported PowerPoint build from every host carrying the product — including machines restored from backup images and rebuilt from older media, which is where a pre-fix build silently returns — and confirm none is pre-fix; a patch-management attestation scoped to the currently supported Office channel reports clean while the long-tail installs the packet names stay exploitable. Precondition: this closes the exposure only where the inventory can see the install. A copy no console enumerates is remediated by removing it or bringing it under management, never by recording it as compliant.
new_control_requirements.evidence: patch_available true; live_patch_available false, with the packet noting no live-patch tool registered and that the vendor patch typically requires service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction. CISA KEV-listed 2026-01-07 with confirmed active exploitation; poc_available true; CVSS 9.8; RWEP 77. The packet's attack_vector states the legacy re-listing exists because long-tail unpatched estates remain exposed. Citing gaps include NIST-800-53-SI-2 (Flaw Remediation), ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8 (Management of technical vulnerabilities) and NIS2-Art21-patch-management (Vulnerability handling and disclosure).

CVE-2025-37164.name: Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) OneView Code Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: a code-injection flaw (CWE-94) enabling unauthenticated remote code execution on the HPE OneView infrastructure-management appliance. CISA KEV-listed 2026-01-07 with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (the device/appliance is reachable by an unauthenticated attacker on its network interface)
attack_vector.complexity: low — KEV-listed, actively exploited; treat as weaponized
attack_vector.ai_factor: No AI involvement documented in discovery or weaponization.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the vendor update; treat an exploited appliance as fully compromised — rebuild it from a known-good image and rotate every credential, key, and session secret it held, since the appliance terminates trust for the network behind it.
prevention.adequacy: Patch is necessary but an exploited appliance must be rebuilt and its secrets rotated — a patch in place does not evict a resident attacker from a device that fronts the network.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Monitoring of the HPE OneView: exploit-shaped requests, web shells, new processes, credential/config changes, and crashes.
detection.adequacy: Necessary because device/appliance compromise is often silent and persists across reboots in firmware/config.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rebuild the appliance from a known-good image, rotate all credentials and secrets it held, and review the network behind it for lateral movement; assume the device's trust is fully compromised.
response.adequacy: Mandatory; network-device/appliance compromise gives an attacker a durable, trusted position that patching alone does not remove.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The 30-day flaw-remediation SLA is far longer than the observed exploitation window for a KEV-listed unauthenticated flaw on an internet-facing network device/appliance; consumer/embedded devices are mass-exploited into botnets within days (some end-of-life with no fix), and enterprise appliances are change-window-gated and exposed past the KEV due date.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: 'Appropriate timescales' is undefined; the standard reading is unsafe for an actively-exploited internet-facing device, and unmanaged/EOL devices fall outside most patch programs entirely.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Treats network devices/appliances as essential-function infrastructure but lacks a CISA-KEV-style compressed remediation SLA and does not address end-of-life devices that can only be replaced, or appliance compromise that requires rebuild rather than patch-in-place.

PCI-DSS-4.0-6.3.3.gap: The 30-day critical-patch window is exploitation acceptance for an internet-facing network device or edge appliance fronting or bridging the CDE.

compliance_exposure_score.basis: Internet-facing HPE OneView is a load-bearing edge/management appliance run on change-controlled patch windows; the required rebuild and secret rotation is rarely part of the documented patch procedure.

new_control_requirements.name: DEVICE-MANAGEMENT-GATEWAY-CONFIG-ENDPOINT-AUTH-INPUT-NEUTRALIZATION
new_control_requirements.description: HPE OneView is the management plane for the server infrastructure it administers, and the packet places the defect on a path a remote unauthenticated user can reach: code injection (CWE-94) ending in remote code execution on the appliance itself. Bound to this product, the control means every endpoint the OneView appliance exposes authorizes its caller before the request reaches anything that evaluates content, and that caller-supplied content is neutralized rather than passed into an interpreter — and that no OneView instance is left answering from a segment with no operational need to manage infrastructure. This is also why the least-privilege gap cited on this entry does not close the path: the attacker never holds a OneView operator account, so per-account privilege scoping is never consulted and an access-review attestation passes cleanly while the injection path stays open. Distinguishing test: from a segment with no operational need to reach the management plane, send unauthenticated requests to each endpoint on a staging OneView appliance and confirm each is refused before any supplied content is evaluated. Precondition: the endpoint-side authorization and input neutralization are properties the vendor update establishes — this control states what to verify, it does not implement it. Until that update and its restart land, restricting which segments can reach the appliance bounds who can send the request but leaves it fully exploitable from anything inside the permitted segment, and that lever is unavailable for the management network the appliance must keep answering in order to administer the hardware it exists to manage.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: HPE OneView contains a code injection vulnerability (CWE-94) that allows a remote unauthenticated user to perform remote code execution on the infrastructure-management appliance; CVSS 9.8, RWEP 77; poc_available true; CISA KEV-listed 2026-01-07 with active_exploitation confirmed; NIST-800-53-AC-6 (Least Privilege) is one of the framework controls this entry cites as insufficient; patch_available true with live_patch_available false and live_patch_notes recording that the vendor patch typically requires a service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction.

new_control_requirements.name: FLEET-COMPROMISE-IR-PLAYBOOK
new_control_requirements.description: OneView is a fleet control plane for server infrastructure, and the packet gives a pre-auth RCE with a public PoC and confirmed in-the-wild exploitation — so an appliance that was reachable between the 2026-01-07 KEV listing and its restart has to be triaged as possibly already compromised, because the vendor update closes the injection path and removes nothing an attacker executed, placed or read through it beforehand. For this CVE the playbook means: rotating every credential the appliance holds or brokers for the hardware it manages and every account that authenticated through it during that window; auditing the appliance's configuration and profile changes across the window; and having stated quarantine criteria for managed hardware whose configuration OneView could have altered while under attacker control. Precondition: this is a response control, not a preventive one — it does not lower the chance of exploitation, it bounds what an already-executed compromise retains, and it is only worth running where the exposure window can be established. Since the flaw yields code execution on the appliance, an attacker is above the appliance's own logging, so the window has to be reconstructed from network-side and collector-side records rather than trusted from the appliance's local logs.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: remote unauthenticated code execution (CWE-94) on the HPE OneView infrastructure-management appliance; CISA KEV-listed 2026-01-07 with active_exploitation confirmed; poc_available true; CVSS 9.8, RWEP 77; patch_available true, live_patch_available false, with live_patch_notes recording that the vendor patch typically requires a service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: An infrastructure-management appliance is usually inventoried as the tool an estate patches its servers with rather than as an asset carrying its own patch clock, which is exactly how a KEV-listed pre-auth RCE on OneView ends up riding the next infrastructure maintenance window while the operating-system patching attestation reads clean. For this CVE the control means the appliance's own update runs on the KEV clock that opened 2026-01-07, not on the cadence of the fleet updates OneView distributes, with completion measured by the version the appliance is actually running rather than by a staged or downloaded update. The packet records no live-patch path and a fix that typically requires a service restart or system reboot, so an appliance that has taken the update but not restarted still carries the vulnerable code and must be counted as exposed — and on a management appliance that restart is the step most likely to be deferred, because it interrupts the console the estate's operators depend on. Priority follows the packet: unauthenticated remote code execution with a public PoC and confirmed exploitation, on the plane that administers the hardware underneath it.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: CISA KEV-listed 2026-01-07 with active_exploitation confirmed; poc_available true; CVSS 9.8, RWEP 77; unauthenticated remote code execution (CWE-94) on the HPE OneView management appliance; patch_available true, live_patch_available false, live_patch_notes stating the vendor patch typically requires a service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction; the entry cites AU-Essential-8-Patch (Patch operating systems), ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8 and NIST-800-53-SI-2 as insufficient.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: Applied here the control's real work is dragging a network video recorder inside the same remediation clock as a server. The packet records a vendor fix as available, so the required action from the 2025-12-22 KEV listing is the vendor firmware update — and because no live-patch path exists for this class and the update lands only across a device restart, the SLA has to include a scheduled recorder restart, not just a firmware file staged on a management console. new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-DEVICE-ZERODAY-SLA-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: The Firebox is the trust boundary, and the packet places the defect in the Fireware OS iked process — the IKEv2 daemon that has to answer unauthenticated packets for mobile-user VPN and for branch-office VPN with a dynamic gateway peer to work at all. That is what makes the standard appliance-patch window the wrong tier here: the vulnerable listener cannot be firewalled off without taking remote access down, and the dynamic-gateway-peer configuration the packet names does not pin a source address, so peer-address restriction is not available as a stopgap for those tunnels. The requirement is the fixed Fireware build within hours of KEV listing, with the reboot budgeted inside that clock, or the IKEv2 remote-access interface disabled until the upgrade lands — there is no live-patch path for this entry, so there is no third option that keeps the tunnel up on a vulnerable build.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet vector: 'WatchGuard Fireware OS iked process contains an out of bounds write vulnerability in the OS iked process. This vulnerability may allow a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code and affects both the mobile user VPN with IKEv2 and the branch office VPN using IKEv2 when configured with a dynamic gateway peer.' new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Exploitation of this one is confirmed in the wild and needs no credentials, so any Firebox that ran an affected Fireware build with its IKEv2 listener reachable has to be triaged as possibly-compromised rather than merely unpatched. The default response is to export and diff the configuration against a known-good baseline, rebuild onto the fixed Fireware release, and rotate what the appliance held — VPN pre-shared keys, IKEv2 credentials and certificates, firewall admin accounts, and any RADIUS or directory service account bound to the device — before the tunnels come back up. Upgrading in place closes the out-of-bounds write in iked and nothing else: an admin account, tunnel definition, or policy change an attacker added pre-upgrade survives the new firmware, and the upgrade ticket closes green.

new_control_requirements.name: FIREWALL-EGRESS-TELEMETRY-SEPARATE-TRUST-ZONE

Firebox logging must therefore already be streaming to a SIEM in a different trust zone, under credentials the firewall itself cannot use to delete history, so the VPN negotiation and admin-account records survive an attacker who owns the device. new_control_requirements.evidence: The packet places the flaw in the Fireware OS iked process, exploitable by 'a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code' (CWE-787), CISA KEV-listed 2025-12-19 with active_exploitation 'confirmed' and poc_available true — the attacker's code runs on the same device that produces the firewall's own logs.

CVE-2025-59374.name: ASUS Live Update Embedded Malicious Code Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: embedded malicious code (CWE-506) in the ASUS Live Update software/update channel, executing on the ASUS endpoint in the trusted context of the vendor update utility. CISA KEV-listed 2025-12-17 with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (the malicious code is delivered through a trusted update channel or package; no authentication to the victim is required)
attack_vector.complexity: low — KEV-listed, actively exploited; treat as weaponized
attack_vector.ai_factor: No AI involvement documented in discovery or weaponization.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Enforce cryptographic integrity and provenance verification on all installed/updated code (code signing with verification, Sigstore/in-toto, SLSA provenance), pin dependencies to verified versions, and require multi-factor and review gates on package-publishing/maintainer accounts.
prevention.adequacy: Signature and provenance verification is the definitive control; the compromise succeeded precisely because the trusted channel was trusted without independent verification.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Monitoring for the update utility fetching/executing unsigned payloads and behaving anomalously, and version-pinning alerts on dependency changes.
detection.adequacy: Necessary because supply-chain compromise runs in a trusted context — the anomaly is the unexpected code execution alongside the legitimate tool.

response.what_would_have_worked: Remove or upgrade ASUS Live Update to a known-good signed version, verify the update-channel integrity, and audit ASUS endpoints that ran the tainted updater for follow-on payloads and credential theft.
response.adequacy: Mandatory; supply-chain compromise propagates through every host that installed the tainted code, so response is environment-wide and includes build-artifact verification.

NIST-800-53-SR-11.gap: Component authenticity / anti-counterfeit is named, but verification is not enforced at install/update time — the tainted code shipped through a trusted channel without consumer-side signature/provenance verification, so the control is paper unless signed-artifact verification (Sigstore/in-toto) is mandated.

NIST-SSDF-800-218-PS.2.gap: The SSDF calls for protecting release integrity and providing provenance, but downstream consumers had no enforced way to verify it; without signed releases plus provenance a consumer cannot detect maliciously-published or substituted code.

SLSA-build-provenance.gap: SLSA build provenance and signed releases would let a consumer detect a maliciously-published version; absent enforced verification at the install/update step, a compromised maintainer account or update channel propagates the malicious code unchecked.

EU-CRA-secure-update.gap: The EU Cyber Resilience Act requires secure update mechanisms and shipping without known exploitable defects; an update channel or package registry that ships embedded malicious code violates the secure-update and integrity expectations.

compliance_exposure_score.basis: ASUS Live Update is trusted by default; audited organizations that install vendor updates or npm dependencies without enforcing signature/provenance verification or pinning are exposed to maliciously-published code, and the compromise reaches every host that installed it.

new_control_requirements.name: INDEPENDENT-INTEGRITY-VERIFICATION-OF-SIGNED-VENDOR-INSTALLERS
new_control_requirements.description: This is the sharpest form of the control's premise: the packet does not describe a coding defect that a vendor build fixes, it describes ASUS Live Update clients that were themselves distributed with unauthorized modifications introduced through a supply chain compromise, executing on the endpoint in the trusted context of the vendor update utility. Every downstream check that resolves to 'it arrived through ASUS Live Update' therefore fails open, and so does an update-hygiene posture whose whole content is keeping the utility current. On managed ASUS hardware the in-app updater must stop being the trust decision: pull Live Update builds through managed software distribution, verify each build against an integrity reference obtained independently of the download itself — vendor-published per-release integrity values fetched over a separate channel, or a behavioural baseline of the installed binaries — and only then push it to endpoints. The packet's targeting detail makes one shortcut unusable: because only devices meeting specific conditions perform the unintended actions, a build that behaves benignly on a test bench is not evidence of a clean build, so verification has to be against a per-release integrity reference rather than against observed behaviour on one machine. The distinguishing test: take the build the endpoint's own updater would install and confirm it can be matched to an integrity value obtained over a channel other than that updater — a build whose only validation is that the updater fetched it is precisely the case this CVE describes.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CWE-506 embedded malicious code. The packet states ASUS Live Update clients 'were distributed with unauthorized modifications introduced through a supply chain compromise' and that 'the modified builds could cause devices meeting specific targeting conditions to perform unintended actions'; the attack vector places execution on the ASUS endpoint in the trusted context of the vendor update utility. CISA KEV-listed 2025-12-17, active_exploitation confirmed, poc_available true, CVSS 8.8, RWEP 77.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: The KEV clock here does not buy a code fix, it buys removal of a tampered build. The packet records the defect as embedded malicious code introduced through a supply chain compromise rather than a flaw in the software's logic, so remediating an affected endpoint means getting the modified ASUS Live Update client off it and a known-good build — or nothing — in its place, and the packet's live-patch note puts that behind a service restart or system reboot per the KEV required action rather than anything applied in place. Scope the clock to the ASUS endpoint population rather than to a server: the packet places execution on the endpoint in the trusted context of the update utility, so the first task inside the SLA is enumerating which endpoints carry the affected Live Update client at all, and an estate that cannot answer that question has not started the clock regardless of what its patch dashboard reports. The packet also records the product statement that the impacted build could be end-of-life or end-of-service, with users directed to discontinue product utilization — so for any endpoint where no clean build applies, removing the utility is the action this SLA covers, recorded as a documented compensating control rather than as a deferral.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA KEV-listed 2025-12-17 with active_exploitation confirmed and poc_available true. patch_available true; live_patch_available false, with the packet stating no live-patch tool was registered for this entry and that the vendor patch typically requires service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction. The packet's product statement records that the impacted product could be end-of-life (EoL) and/or end-of-service (EoS) and that users should discontinue product utilization.

attack_vector.description: a missing-authorization flaw (CWE-862/CWE-250) on the SonicWall SMA1000 secure-access appliance, letting an attacker reach functionality with unnecessary privileges without proper authorization. CISA KEV-listed 2025-12-17 with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation.

attack_vector.complexity: low — KEV-listed, actively exploited; treat as weaponized
attack_vector.ai_factor: No AI involvement documented in discovery or weaponization.

prevention.adequacy: Patch is necessary; restricting the management plane to a trusted network is the compensating control when the access-control enforcement is itself bypassed.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The 30-day flaw-remediation SLA is far longer than the observed exploitation window for a KEV-listed access-control/security-control bypass on an internet-facing system; these grant unauthorized access to protected functionality and are mass-exploited within days.

The flaw here is missing authorization on the AMC yielding privilege escalation rather than a pre-auth RCE, but the tier logic is unchanged: deploy the vendor fix on a KEV-tied clock, accepting the service restart or reboot it requires, and where that restart genuinely cannot be scheduled inside the clock, isolate the AMC interface to an operator-only management segment so the unauthorized-privilege path is unreachable in the interim. Inventory must name every SMA1000 whose AMC is reachable from anything wider than that segment.

Vendor patch typically requires service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction.'

new_control_requirements.name: FLEET-CONTROL-PLANE-ADMIN-PRIVILEGE-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: The SMA1000's appliance management console governs remote access for everyone who enters the network through the appliance, which makes AMC administration a control-plane tier rather than an application-admin tier. That distinction is load-bearing for this CVE specifically: the defect is a missing-authorization check inside AMC — the console invokes privileged functionality without confirming the caller is entitled to it — so no amount of role definition inside the console is reliable, and the residual control is reducing who can reach the console at all. Require PAM-jumphost-only reachability for AMC, step-up authentication per session, just-in-time elevation with approval, an AMC identity distinct from every other admin role, and dedicated privileged-access-workstation hardware. A framework that collapses 'appliance admin' into general admin leaves a wide population of accounts positioned on the escalation path.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: CWE-862 (missing authorization) plus CWE-250; the packet's attack_vector describes 'a missing-authorization flaw (CWE-862/CWE-250) on the SonicWall SMA1000 secure-access appliance, letting an attacker reach functionality with unnecessary privileges without proper authorization', and the vector locates it in the appliance management console (AMC). new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-DEVICE-ZERODAY-SLA-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: Cisco Secure Email Gateway, Secure Email, AsyncOS Software and Web Manager appliances sit on the mail-flow trust boundary, and this input-validation flaw hands an unauthenticated attacker arbitrary command execution with root privileges on the appliance's underlying operating system. new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Because this flaw yields root on the appliance's own operating system and exploitation is confirmed in the wild, any Cisco Secure Email Gateway or Web Manager that was reachable and unpatched during the exposure window has to be treated as compromised, not merely vulnerable. The IR default for these appliances must therefore be: export and review the running configuration, rebuild from vendor media at the fixed release, and rotate every credential the appliance stored or presented (directory bind, mail-relay, and management/API credentials) - patch-in-place is the wrong response and a flaw-remediation attestation recording it as resolved is exactly the paper outcome to avoid.

new_control_requirements.name: PEN-TEST-SCOPE-INCLUDES-SECURITY-PRODUCTS

new_control_requirements.name: FRAMEWORK-DEFAULT-SECRET-DETECTION
new_control_requirements.description: Because CentreStack and Triofox ship the same AES key material in every install, the constant an attacker needs to forge trusted material is obtainable from the product itself rather than from the target — which means no amount of credential hygiene on the operator's side reduces the exposure. Re-run the check after any restore-from-image, template clone or appliance rebuild, since those are the operations that quietly reintroduce the shipped key on a host that was previously remediated. The packet ties the weakness specifically to publicly exposed endpoints, so this gate belongs on every internet-facing CentreStack/Triofox node before it is returned to service.

Applying the update alone does not retire key material an attacker could already have taken from the product, so an SLA that closes on package version alone closes on the wrong condition for a hardcoded-key flaw.

The control this CVE demands is a mitigation clock that starts at the KEV listing date regardless of CVE age: on 2025-12-12 every ALEOS unit in the fleet needed a verified mitigation — the vendor firmware update, which the packet records as available with no live-patch path and therefore a reboot-bearing field change, or removal of the device's web administration surface from any reachable network — inside the KEV response window, not at the next scheduled site visit.
