Bound to this product the requirement is that any SimpleHelp server which was reachable by untrusted callers while running 5.5.7 or earlier is handled as a configuration-exfiltration event rather than a patching item: rotate every secret the server's configuration held and every credential it stored, and treat the technician accounts and the downstream machines that server could reach as in scope, because that reach into customer networks is exactly what the ransomware affiliates were acquiring. Scope note, stated rather than glossed: this control is written around pre-authentication remote code execution on a boundary system, and the primitive the packet records here is an unauthenticated read, not execution — so the rebuild half applies to hosts where follow-on access or execution is evidenced, while the configuration-exfiltration-and-rotation half is what the packet documents directly and applies to every exposed instance. Precondition: rotation is only complete if it covers material that is not obviously credential-shaped, because the packet says 'various secrets' rather than naming them, so anything the server used to authenticate outward is in scope; and hashed passwords remain usable for offline cracking and for replay wherever those accounts reused them, so rotation has to follow those accounts onto their other systems rather than stopping at SimpleHelp's own login.
new_control_requirements.evidence: vector: 'These files include server configuration files containing various secrets and hashed user passwords.' active_exploitation_notes: 'Actively exploited since January 2025 by ransomware affiliates (DragonForce) as an initial-access vector against unpatched SimpleHelp servers, most notably a utility billing software provider per CISA advisory AA25-163A; CISA KEV flags confirmed ransomware use.' The packet's UK-CAF-B2 gap: 'Identity and access management control assumes credentials in config files stay secret; path traversal defeats that assumption entirely regardless of IAM posture.' patch_available true with affected_versions 'SimpleHelp <= 5.5.7'.

CVE-2025-24200.name: Apple iOS and iPadOS Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An attacker with physical possession of a locked iOS/iPadOS device uses specialized forensic-extraction hardware to exploit a state-management flaw and disable USB Restricted Mode, restoring full USB data access to a device that should only permit charging when locked.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none in the software sense, but requires physical possession of the target device plus specialized hardware/tooling
attack_vector.complexity: high — requires physical access, purpose-built forensic hardware, and precise timing/state manipulation; Apple describes the observed use as 'extremely sophisticated'
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — reported by Bill Marczak of The Citizen Lab. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Patch to iOS 18.3.1/iPadOS 18.3.1 (or the corresponding fix for older-branch devices); enable auto-update and minimize the window a device sits unpatched
prevention.adequacy: Patching is necessary but not sufficient for high-risk individuals whose devices may be physically seized before an update cycle completes

detection.what_would_have_worked: MDM/EMM monitoring for unexpected USB Restricted Mode state changes or device-lock-state anomalies on managed devices
detection.adequacy: Personal devices belonging to high-risk individuals are frequently unmanaged, so this detection surface doesn't exist for the population most targeted

response.what_would_have_worked: Forensic re-imaging and credential/session revocation for any device suspected of physical tampering, plus threat-intel engagement (e.g., Citizen Lab, Amnesty Security Lab) for suspected targeted-surveillance cases
response.adequacy: Effective response requires specialist digital-forensics capability most individuals and even most enterprises lack in-house

NIST-800-53-AC-3.gap: Access enforcement for a locked device assumed the USB Restricted Mode state machine was sound; the authorization flaw let a physical attacker force the device back into an accessible state without credentials.

new_control_requirements.name: MOBILE-ENDPOINT-MDM-ENFORCED-KEV-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: Every enrolled iPhone and iPad must be driven to the fixed build for its own OS line by declarative device management on a KEV-tied clock, with user deferral removed. USB Restricted Mode is the only thing standing between a locked handset in someone else's hands and its data over a port that is supposed to be delivering charge only; because the attack needs physical possession rather than network reach, no perimeter rule, no VPN posture check and no conditional-access policy compensates while the device is still on a vulnerable build, and a user who postpones the update for a week is carrying an extractable device for that week. The campaign has to target four separate fixed builds (iOS/iPadOS 15.8.4, iOS/iPadOS 16.7.11, iPadOS 17.7.5, iOS/iPadOS 18.3.1) rather than a single 'update to latest', because the older lines exist precisely for hardware that cannot take the newest release.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: CISA KEV-listed 2025-02-12 with active_exploitation confirmed. patch_available is true and the vendor text names the fixed builds — 'This issue is fixed in iOS 15.8.4 and iPadOS 15.8.4, iOS 16.7.11 and iPadOS 16.7.11, iOS 18.3.1 and iPadOS 18.3.1, iPadOS 17.7.5.' The recorded exploitation path is an attacker with physical possession of a locked iOS/iPadOS device using specialized forensic-extraction hardware to disable USB Restricted Mode; Apple 'is aware of a report that this issue may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals.' poc_available is false and CVSS is 6.1 (RWEP 49), so a severity-threshold patch queue leaves this below the cut line even though exploitation is confirmed — which is exactly why the SLA has to key off the KEV listing, not the score.

new_control_requirements.name: MOBILE-OS-MINIMUM-PATCH-LEVEL-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Access to organizational mail, documents and internal services from an iOS/iPadOS device must be conditioned on the device actually running at or above the fixed build for its OS line — enforced as a gate, not recorded as a compliance datapoint. The packet enumerates fixes across four OS lines, which means the estate contains hardware that will never reach the newest release; for those devices the gate is 15.8.4 / 16.7.11 / 17.7.5, and a device that cannot reach its line's fixed build should lose access to organizational data rather than appear as a stale row on a dashboard. The gate matters more than usual for this flaw because the exploitation state is a locked, powered-on device in an attacker's hands — the exact condition of a lost, stolen or seized corporate handset, where the MDM has no further influence and only the installed build decides whether the USB data path opens.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: CWE-863 incorrect authorization; 'A physical attack may disable USB Restricted Mode on a locked device', restoring full USB data access to a device that should only permit charging when locked. patch_available is true with the fixed builds enumerated per OS line, and live_patch_available is false — there is no mitigation that can be applied to a device short of installing the fixed OS build, so the build level is the whole of the device's defensive state. KEV-listed 2025-02-12, active_exploitation confirmed.

CVE-2024-41710.name: Mitel SIP Phones Argument Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An attacker who already holds administrative access to a Mitel SIP phone's management interface injects shell metacharacters into a boot-process parameter, escaping the intended parameter context to execute arbitrary commands in the phone's underlying OS.
attack_vector.privileges_required: high (authenticated administrator on the phone's management interface)
attack_vector.complexity: low — a public PoC documents the exact injection point in the boot process
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — reported through Mitel's own coordinated disclosure program. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Patch to the fixed firmware release and restrict/rotate SIP phone admin credentials so a compromised admin account can't reach the injection point
prevention.adequacy: Patching removes the injection flaw, but doesn't address weak/shared VoIP admin credential hygiene that made the precondition reachable in the first place

detection.what_would_have_worked: Log and alert on SIP phone provisioning/boot-parameter changes containing shell metacharacters
detection.adequacy: VoIP endpoint management traffic is rarely captured by enterprise SIEM pipelines, so this detection is largely absent in practice

response.what_would_have_worked: Isolate and re-image affected phones, rotate the compromised admin credential, and audit for lateral movement from the phone's network segment
response.adequacy: VoIP endpoints are often on flat network segments, so containment requires broader network review, not just the phone itself

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: Least-privilege control is undermined because the flaw is reachable by any admin-privileged account — a compromised or over-provisioned VoIP admin credential is sufficient to pivot to full command execution.

new_control_requirements.name: CONTROL-PANEL-PLUGIN-USER-SURFACE-MUST-NOT-REACH-ROOT-OPERATIONS
new_control_requirements.description: The Mitel phone's administrative management interface is the constrained user surface this control governs. The packet places the defect in a boot-process parameter the product fails to sanitize, and describes an attacker who already holds administrative privilege on that interface injecting shell metacharacters to escape the parameter context and execute arbitrary commands in the phone's underlying OS — a device-configuration surface wired straight through to an OS command context, which is the pattern the control forbids. Bound to this product, it means a value an administrator sets on a 6800, 6900 or 6900w Series handset or the 6970 Conference Unit is consumed by the boot process as data and never reaches a command interpreter, so that a phone-administration role stays a configuration role instead of becoming a shell on the handset. This is also why the least-privilege control cited as insufficient on this entry does not cover the path: the attacker uses a legitimate administrative account, so per-account privilege scoping is never the thing that fails — the failure is that the administrator role, correctly held, reaches arbitrary command execution. Preconditions: the vendor firmware update that moves a handset past the affected range is what repairs that boundary; this control states the property to verify, it does not implement it. Until that update lands on a given handset, the only operator-side lever is limiting which accounts and which network segments can reach the phones' management interface — that bounds who can present the injected parameter but does not close the path, because any account that legitimately administers a phone still reaches it, and it gives nothing at all once an administrator credential is in an attacker's hands. And because exploitation is confirmed, a handset whose management interface was reachable during the exposure window needs its running configuration compared against a known-good baseline rather than being closed on the update: commands that already executed in the phone's system context are not undone by loading new firmware.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet vector: a vulnerability in the Mitel 6800 Series, 6900 Series and 6900w Series SIP Phones, including the 6970 Conference Unit, through R6.4.0.HF1 (R6.4.0.136), could allow an authenticated attacker with administrative privilege to conduct an argument injection attack due to insufficient parameter sanitization during the boot process, with a successful exploit allowing execution of arbitrary commands within the context of the system (CWE-88). Packet attack_vector: the attacker already holds administrative access to the phone's management interface and injects shell metacharacters into a boot-process parameter to escape the intended parameter context. CISA KEV-listed 2025-02-12 with active_exploitation confirmed; poc_available true; RWEP 64 against CVSS 7.2. The packet records NIST-800-53-AC-6 (Least Privilege) and ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.8.9 (Configuration management) among the framework controls already cited as insufficient for this entry.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For this entry the expedited clock runs from the 2025-02-12 KEV listing, and the population it has to be measured against is the handsets themselves: every 6800, 6900 and 6900w Series phone and every 6970 Conference Unit whose running load falls in the affected range the packet names, through R6.4.0.HF1 (R6.4.0.136). Completion has to be counted per device against its reported firmware load, not as a site-level or platform-level statement that the phones were updated — a telephony estate is distributed across sites and the individual handset is precisely the asset class a server-and-workstation patch program has no row for, so an SLA measured on anything coarser than the per-device load will report green over handsets still running affected firmware. The distinguishing test: enumerate the handsets and conference units in service and confirm none reports a load at or below R6.4.0.HF1 (R6.4.0.136); a device absent from that enumeration is unmeasured, not compliant. Preconditions and limits: the packet records a vendor patch and registers no live-patch path, so the firmware update itself is the only remediation available — there is nothing to apply to a running handset in the meantime. Where a handset cannot be taken to the fixed load inside the window, the control's compensating-control branch must be written down explicitly rather than assumed, and for this flaw the honest compensating control is restricting which accounts and segments can reach the management interface; that bounds who can attempt the injection, it does not remove the unsanitized boot parameter, and it does not help where the administrative credential is already compromised.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet fields: cisa_kev true with kev_date 2025-02-12; active_exploitation confirmed; poc_available true; patch_available true; live_patch_available false with no live-patch notes recorded for this entry; RWEP 64 against CVSS 7.2. Affected range from the packet vector: Mitel 6800 Series, 6900 Series and 6900w Series SIP Phones, including the 6970 Conference Unit, through R6.4.0.HF1 (R6.4.0.136). The packet cites EU NIS2 Directive Art. 21 vulnerability handling as a framework control insufficient for this entry.

CVE-2025-21418.name: Microsoft Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock Heap-Based Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A local attacker who already has code execution on a Windows host (typically via a prior phishing-delivered payload) sends crafted IOCTL requests to the kernel-mode afd.sys driver, triggering a heap-based buffer overflow to corrupt kernel memory and escalate to SYSTEM privileges.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low (a standard authenticated local session is sufficient to reach the vulnerable IOCTL handler)
attack_vector.complexity: high — reliable kernel heap-overflow exploitation requires precise memory-layout control; no public exploit exists, suggesting a sophisticated actor developed it
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — identified through Microsoft's internal security response process. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the February 2025 cumulative update promptly; this was a zero-day so no pre-patch mitigation existed beyond limiting local code-execution opportunities (phishing/malware defenses)
prevention.adequacy: Patching only helps after release; the real gap during the zero-day window was preventing the initial-access step that made local exploitation possible

detection.what_would_have_worked: EDR rules for anomalous kernel-driver IOCTL activity and unexpected SYSTEM-privileged process creation from a standard user session
detection.adequacy: Kernel-level exploitation is specifically designed to operate below most EDR visibility, making this detection unreliable in practice

response.what_would_have_worked: Full re-image of any host where SYSTEM-level compromise is suspected, since kernel-level access can persist below OS-level remediation
response.adequacy: Kernel compromise materially raises the bar for confident remediation short of a full rebuild

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Monthly Patch Tuesday cadence is the fastest routine remediation path, but this flaw was exploited in the wild as a zero-day before the February 2025 patch existed.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: The afd.sys WinSock driver fix has to run on a KEV-tied clock across the whole Windows estate rather than ride the routine servicing cadence, because this entry has no alternative remediation path: the packet records patch_available true with live_patch_available false and no live-patch notes at all, so nothing closes the IOCTL path while the host keeps running. Escalation to SYSTEM is the second half of a chain whose first half is a phishing-delivered payload, which means every unpatched workstation that can run user-delivered code is a full-host compromise waiting on one foothold. Hosts that genuinely cannot take the update inside the window need a documented, time-bound decision about what untrusted code is allowed to execute on them, not an SLA extension.
new_control_requirements.evidence: cisa_kev is true with kev_date 2025-02-11 and active_exploitation confirmed; rwep_score 61 against a cvss of 7.8. patch_available is true, live_patch_available is false, and live_patch_notes is null, so the vendor update is the only remediation the packet records. The attack_vector describes a local attacker who already has code execution (typically via a prior phishing-delivered payload) sending crafted IOCTL requests to the kernel-mode afd.sys driver, triggering a heap-based buffer overflow to escalate to SYSTEM. The gaps citing this CVE — AU-Essential-8-Patch, ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8, NIST-800-53-SI-2 and NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management — are all routine-cadence flaw-remediation controls carrying no KEV-tied clock.

new_control_requirements.name: KERNEL-EXPLOITATION-DETECTION
new_control_requirements.description: Windows hosts need behavioural alerting on the post-exploitation signature of an afd.sys overflow — a user-mode process issuing anomalous IOCTLs to the AFD device, followed by a token swap or a SYSTEM-integrity child spawned from a non-SYSTEM parent — with the alert raised in seconds, not at the next log review. The defining constraint for this CVE is that defenders cannot validate their coverage by replaying a published exploit: exploitation is confirmed in the wild while no public PoC exists, so signature-and-replay verification is unavailable and detection has to key on the privilege-escalation behaviour itself. That telemetry is also the input the response and recovery plan depends on, since the escalation is what converts a phishing foothold into a host that must be rebuilt rather than cleaned, and it is the only visibility an operator has over the hosts still inside the patch window.
new_control_requirements.evidence: poc_available is false while active_exploitation is confirmed and cisa_kev is true (kev_date 2025-02-11) — in-the-wild exploitation with no public proof-of-concept to test defences against. The attack_vector records a local attacker with prior code execution sending crafted IOCTL requests to the kernel-mode afd.sys driver, corrupting kernel memory to escalate to SYSTEM privileges. UK-CAF-D1 (Response and recovery planning) is one of the framework gaps citing this CVE as evidence.

CVE-2025-21391.name: Microsoft Windows Storage Link Following Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A local attacker with standard user access creates a symbolic link that redirects a privileged Windows Storage file-management operation to an unintended target, allowing them to delete arbitrary files — including security event logs — and escalate privileges.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low (a standard authenticated local session is sufficient to stage the link-following condition)
attack_vector.complexity: low — link-following/race-style exploitation of storage operations is a well-understood technique once the vulnerable operation is identified
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — identified through Microsoft's internal security response process. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the February 2025 cumulative update promptly; this was exploited as a zero-day, so no pre-patch software mitigation existed
prevention.adequacy: Patch-only remediation addresses the flaw but not the log-deletion damage already caused during the zero-day exploitation window

detection.what_would_have_worked: Forward security/event logs to a separate, tamper-resistant log-collection pipeline (e.g. SIEM with write-once storage) so local log deletion doesn't erase the only copy
detection.adequacy: Only effective if remote log forwarding was already configured before the intrusion; many endpoints rely solely on the local event log

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat any host with unexplained gaps in local security logs as a likely privilege-escalation indicator and investigate via centrally-forwarded logs or endpoint telemetry instead
response.adequacy: Effective only where centralized logging exists independent of the compromised host

NIST-800-53-AU-9.gap: Protection-of-audit-information control is directly undermined — the observed exploitation pattern deletes security logs via link-following, defeating log-integrity assumptions.

new_control_requirements.name: ACTIVELY-EXPLOITED-OS-LPE-REMEDIATION-WINDOW-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Windows Storage is an OS component rather than an optional server role, so the exposed population is the whole Windows fleet and there is no subset an operator can enumerate and isolate instead of updating. The exploitation precondition the packet names is standard user access — the local attacker plants a symbolic link that redirects a privileged Windows Storage file-management operation to a target of their choosing — so account-privilege policy is not a containment story here: the flaw is the thing that converts a standard user into a privileged one, which is precisely why this control says privilege policy must not be relied on to hold the line. Applied to this entry, the Windows update carrying the fix has to be driven across every affected endpoint on the clock that started with the 2025-02-11 KEV listing rather than folded into the normal monthly ring, and the packet's live_patch_available: false with no live_patch_notes has to be treated as a hard planning fact — nothing can be applied to a running endpoint, so the rollout needs restart windows for the fleet and not just a deployment ring. One scheduling signal is actively misleading on this entry: poc_available is false while active_exploitation is confirmed, so a program that gates urgency on public proof-of-concept availability will hold this at routine severity indefinitely. The distinguishing test: enumerate installed build numbers across the fleet against the fixed build for each Windows SKU in the estate and confirm zero endpoints remain below it past the KEV due date — an attestation that 'standard users are not local administrators' passes cleanly while this path stays wide open.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: CISA KEV-listed 2025-02-11, active_exploitation confirmed, CVSS 7.1, RWEP 61, CWE-59. Attack path as recorded: 'A local attacker with standard user access creates a symbolic link that redirects a privileged Windows Storage file-management operation to an unintended target, allowing them to delete arbitrary files — including security event logs — and escalate privileges.' Remediation fields: patch_available true; live_patch_available false with live_patch_notes null. poc_available false, i.e. confirmed in-the-wild exploitation with no public PoC recorded.

CVE-2024-40891.name: Zyxel DSL CPE OS Command Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An attacker with a Telnet session to a legacy Zyxel DSL CPE device (using default or otherwise-obtained service-account credentials) sends management commands containing embedded shell metacharacters, which are passed unsanitized to the underlying OS shell and executed.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low (authenticated Telnet session using a service account such as supervisor/zyuser, often default or trivially obtained on legacy CPE)
attack_vector.complexity: low — no special conditions required beyond reaching the Telnet management port and authenticating
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — disclosed by VulnCheck security researchers; exploitation activity documented by GreyNoise. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: No vendor patch exists; the only durable prevention is decommissioning the EOL device or firewalling the Telnet management interface off the WAN entirely.
prevention.adequacy: Patch-based remediation is not available at all for this entry — BOD 22-01's remediation deadline can only be met via mitigation/decommissioning, not a vendor patch.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Egress monitoring for anomalous outbound scanning/C2 traffic from consumer/SMB router IP ranges, and Telnet exposure scanning of the managed fleet.
detection.adequacy: Detection is a compensating control only; most affected devices are unmanaged consumer/SMB equipment with no monitoring agent.

response.what_would_have_worked: ISP/operator-driven notification and forced decommissioning or firmware replacement of affected legacy CPE.
response.adequacy: Response is slow and diffuse because affected devices are distributed across many individual subscribers rather than a centrally managed fleet.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation is structurally impossible: Zyxel has declared these DSL CPE devices end-of-life/end-of-service with no patch planned, so the standard remediate-within-SLA control has no path to closure short of hardware replacement.

new_control_requirements.name: UNSUPPORTED-NETWORK-DEVICE-ENUMERATION-AND-RETIREMENT
new_control_requirements.description: The packet forecloses the interim half of this control before it begins: patch_available is false, the vector opens with the UNSUPPORTED WHEN ASSIGNED marker, and live_patch_notes records that no live-patch path exists for this EOL firmware and that the vendor's only guidance is to discontinue use of the device if it cannot be isolated from untrusted networks. So for these legacy Zyxel DSL CPE units there is no fixed build to reach and no patched state to record — every unit in service is a replacement item, and the requirement is an inventory naming each VMG4325-B10A and each related legacy Zyxel DSL CPE running firmware 1.00(AAFR.4)C0_20170615, with a dated removal date per unit rather than a remediation ticket that waits on firmware. Scope it to what the packet's affected and affected_versions name — VMG4325-B10A and the related legacy Zyxel DSL CPE builds sharing the same management-command codebase — because the packet maps this command-injection sink to that codebase and to no other Zyxel line, and sweeping every Zyxel device in the estate as an instance of this CVE manufactures replacement work against hardware no evidence implicates. Until a unit is gone, the only lever the packet leaves is the isolation the vendor names, and its precondition has to be stated rather than assumed: the injection is reached through the Telnet-exposed management command interface, so blocking Telnet at the WAN interface removes the path Censys observed on 1,500+ of these devices and the path GreyNoise saw scanned from January 2025 — but a DSL CPE exists to serve the LAN attached to it, and every client on that LAN still reaches the management interface with the default or service-account credentials the packet describes the attack using. For a unit serving a general user network there is no filter that removes the path, only isolation of that network from anything that matters. And because active exploitation is confirmed and Mirai variants recruited these routers into botnet infrastructure, a unit that was WAN-reachable during the exposure window is not made safe by filtering it now: the flaw yields OS command execution on the device itself, so it is a removal item rather than a reconfiguration item, and any credential that transited it should be rotated.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet fields: patch_available false, live_patch_available false, patch_required_reboot true with no patch to apply; live_patch_notes — "No live-patch path exists for this EOL firmware; the vendor's only guidance is to discontinue use of the device if it cannot be isolated from untrusted networks." The vector carries the UNSUPPORTED WHEN ASSIGNED marker and describes a post-authentication command injection in the management commands of the legacy DSL CPE Zyxel VMG4325-B10A firmware version 1.00(AAFR.4)C0_20170615, executed via Telnet; affected/affected_versions scope to VMG4325-B10A and related legacy Zyxel DSL CPE firmware builds sharing the same management-command codebase; CWE-78; cvss 8.8, rwep_score 70; poc_available false; cisa_kev true with kev_date 2025-02-11 and active_exploitation confirmed. active_exploitation_notes: GreyNoise observed mass scanning and exploitation attempts beginning January 2025 and Mirai botnet variants incorporated exploitation of this Telnet-based command injection, using it alongside CVE-2024-40890 to recruit EOL routers. framework_control_gaps: NIST-800-53-SI-2 records Zyxel declaring these devices end-of-life/end-of-service with no patch planned and no closure short of hardware replacement; NIST-800-53-CM-7 records Censys observing 1,500+ of these EOL devices with the Telnet management interface reachable directly from the WAN; UK-CAF-B4 records the Telnet management plane exposed to the untrusted WAN interface; ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8 records these units sitting outside the ISMS asset register.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For this entry only the control's third branch is reachable. Its requirement is a verified mitigation — patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls — on the KEV clock, and the packet records patch_available false and live_patch_available false with no live-patch path for this EOL firmware, so the clock that opened with the 2025-02-11 KEV listing can only be answered by the compensating action the vendor names: isolate the device from untrusted networks, or discontinue use. That is precisely what the two frameworks cited here cannot express — Essential Eight's patch-within-48-hours-of-active-exploitation expectation is unmeetable because no patch exists, and NIS2 vulnerability handling assumes an eventual vendor fix that will never ship for this hardware — so the compensating action has to be recorded as the terminal deliverable against the KEV date, not as a temporary state pending firmware. Operationally, every affected unit needs a dated, evidenced record of either its removal or its Telnet management interface being unreachable from the WAN, produced against the listing date rather than left as an open remediation ticket. Distinguishing test, keyed on the exploitation path the packet documents: from outside the device's WAN interface, attempt a Telnet connection to each unit and issue a management command; anything that answers is within reach of the scanning and exploitation GreyNoise observed from January 2025, and a vulnerability-management report carrying this CVE as "no patch available, risk accepted" while the interface answers has recorded the exposure rather than mitigated it. Precondition: the isolation is a mitigation only while it holds, and it depends on a WAN-side filter surviving firmware resets, ISP re-provisioning and user reconfiguration on hardware the operator generally does not manage — which is why the vendor's own guidance ends at discontinuing use rather than at isolation.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet fields: cisa_kev true with kev_date 2025-02-11 and active_exploitation confirmed; patch_available false; live_patch_available false; live_patch_notes — "No live-patch path exists for this EOL firmware; the vendor's only guidance is to discontinue use of the device if it cannot be isolated from untrusted networks." attack_vector: an attacker with a Telnet session to a legacy Zyxel DSL CPE device, using default or otherwise-obtained service-account credentials, sends management commands containing embedded shell metacharacters that are passed unsanitized to the underlying OS shell. active_exploitation_notes: GreyNoise observed mass scanning and exploitation attempts against exposed Zyxel legacy DSL CPE devices beginning January 2025. framework_control_gaps: AU-Essential-8-Patch — "Essential 8's patch-within-48-hours-of-active-exploitation guidance is unmeetable since no patch exists; the only compensating action is decommissioning or isolating the device from the internet"; NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management — "NIS2 operators relying on this hardware have no vendor remediation SLA at all post-EOL; typical vulnerability-management timelines assume an eventual vendor fix that will never ship."

CVE-2024-40890.name: Zyxel DSL CPE OS Command Injection Vulnerability (CGI)

attack_vector.description: An attacker with an authenticated session sends a crafted HTTP POST request to the CGI management program on a legacy Zyxel DSL CPE device; the CGI program passes request parameters unsanitized to the underlying OS shell, achieving command execution.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low (authenticated HTTP session using a service account such as supervisor/zyuser, often default or trivially obtained on legacy CPE)
attack_vector.complexity: low — a single crafted HTTP POST is sufficient once authenticated
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — disclosed by VulnCheck security researchers; exploitation activity documented by GreyNoise. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: No vendor patch exists; the only durable prevention is decommissioning the EOL device or restricting the CGI management interface from the WAN entirely.
prevention.adequacy: Patch-based remediation is not available at all for this entry — BOD 22-01's remediation deadline can only be met via mitigation/decommissioning, not a vendor patch.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Web-application-firewall or perimeter logging on the CGI endpoint for shell-metacharacter payloads in POST bodies, plus fleet-wide exposure scanning.
detection.adequacy: Detection is a compensating control only; most affected devices are unmanaged consumer/SMB equipment with no monitoring agent.

response.what_would_have_worked: ISP/operator-driven notification and forced decommissioning or firmware replacement of affected legacy CPE.
response.adequacy: Response is slow and diffuse because affected devices are distributed across many individual subscribers rather than a centrally managed fleet.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: Boundary protection is absent by design: the CGI management program is reachable via HTTP POST from the untrusted WAN interface with no network-layer restriction.

new_control_requirements.name: UNSUPPORTED-NETWORK-DEVICE-ENUMERATION-AND-RETIREMENT
new_control_requirements.description: The packet settles the patch question before the control begins: patch_available is false, the CVE text is marked UNSUPPORTED WHEN ASSIGNED, and the vendor's only recorded guidance is to discontinue use of the device if it cannot be isolated from untrusted networks. There is no fixed firmware to reach and therefore no interim state — for these units the terminal state is removal or replacement, and the enumeration half is what makes that actionable: inventory every Zyxel legacy DSL CPE in service with its model and running firmware, covering the related legacy models sharing the same CGI codebase that the packet's affected_versions name rather than only the VMG4325-B10A the vector headlines, since an estate that standardised on a sibling model would otherwise report clean. Each unit becomes a dated replacement item; a risk acceptance with no removal date leaves a KEV-listed device under confirmed mass exploitation in service indefinitely, and it stays exposed to everything else found in that abandoned firmware, not only this command injection. Precondition on the isolation half, which the vendor guidance itself makes conditional: the flaw is reached by an HTTP POST to the CGI management program, so removing WAN-side reachability of that interface takes the unit out of the internet-facing path the trackers observed from January 2025 — but a DSL CPE exists to serve the client network behind it, and every client on that network still reaches the CGI management surface, so for a unit serving a general user network isolation bounds who can reach the path rather than removing it. The post-authentication framing is not a barrier either: the packet places the session on a default or service account, so the precondition is credentials that ship with the device rather than anything an attacker must first steal. And because active exploitation is confirmed and the outcome is OS command execution on the device itself, a unit that was reachable during the window is not made safe by reconfiguration — it is replaced, and credentials that transited it are rotated.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: patch_available false, live_patch_available false, live_patch_notes 'No live-patch path exists for this EOL firmware; the vendor's only guidance is to discontinue use of the device if it cannot be isolated from untrusted networks.' vector begins '**UNSUPPORTED WHEN ASSIGNED**' and describes post-authentication command injection in the CGI program of the legacy DSL CPE Zyxel VMG4325-B10A firmware 1.00(AAFR.4)C0_20170615 via a crafted HTTP POST request; affected_versions extends to 'related legacy Zyxel DSL CPE firmware builds sharing the same CGI codebase'; affected records the session as an 'authenticated (default/service-account) session'. cisa_kev true, kev_date 2025-02-11, active_exploitation confirmed, CVSS 8.8, RWEP 70, CWE-78. active_exploitation_notes: GreyNoise and Mirai botnet trackers observed mass scanning/exploitation of exposed devices via crafted HTTP POST requests against the CGI management program beginning January 2025. The NIST-800-53-SI-2 gap states remediation is structurally impossible with no path to closure short of hardware replacement; the NIST-800-53-SC-7 gap states the CGI management program is reachable via HTTP POST from the untrusted WAN interface with no network-layer restriction; the ISO-27001-2022-A.5.21 gap states the devices are vendor-abandoned with no patch path.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: This control's three states resolve unusually on this entry, and that is the point of attaching it: state (a), binary patch deployed, is permanently unreachable. patch_available is false and live_patch_available is false with no live-patch path recorded for the abandoned firmware, so a Zyxel legacy DSL CPE that has been isolated from untrusted networks sits permanently in state (b) — compensating control active, no binary patch — and one that has not sits in state (c), full exposure, while its CGI management program answers HTTP POSTs from the WAN. The requirement here is that the compliance record says exactly that: an isolated VMG4325-B10A or sibling legacy unit must appear as a compensating-control state carrying a dated replacement action, never as remediated and never as an open-ended accepted risk, because unlike a patch-pending entry there is no future vendor event that converts the state — the only thing that closes it is the device leaving the estate. Precondition on what may be recorded as the compensating control: it has to be isolation actually in force and verified from outside, since 'the router sits behind the ISP connection' is an assertion about topology rather than evidence that the CGI interface is unreachable. The residual-risk statement attached to state (b) must also carry the two facts that bound it — LAN-side clients still reach the management surface, and the authenticating credential is a device default or service account — otherwise the record reads as containment while the exploited path remains available to anything on the client network.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: patch_available false, live_patch_available false, live_patch_notes recording no live-patch path for this EOL firmware and vendor guidance to discontinue use of the device if it cannot be isolated from untrusted networks; poc_available false but active_exploitation confirmed with kev_date 2025-02-11 (KEV ransomware use flagged Unknown). The NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management gap states that operators relying on this hardware have no vendor remediation SLA at all post-EOL and that typical vulnerability-management timelines assume an eventual vendor fix that will never ship; the AU-Essential-8-Patch gap states the patch-within-48-hours-of-active-exploitation guidance is unmeetable since no patch exists and the only compensating action is decommissioning or isolating the device from the internet.

attack_vector.description: An attacker with a low-privileged authenticated session to a Cityworks-hosted IIS server submits a crafted serialized object that, upon deserialization, achieves remote code execution on the underlying Windows/IIS host — used in the wild to stage Rust-based loaders that deploy Cobalt Strike/VShell.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low (authenticated Cityworks user session)
attack_vector.complexity: low — a single crafted request against the deserialization endpoint is sufficient once authenticated
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — identified via incident response and reported by Trimble/CISA. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply Cityworks 15.8.9 / 23.10 promptly and restrict IIS/Cityworks management access to trusted networks (VPN/allow-list) rather than exposing it directly to the internet.
prevention.adequacy: Patch alone is insufficient against a zero-day: the exploitation window opened before the patch existed, so network-layer restriction of the management interface is a necessary compensating control.

detection.what_would_have_worked: EDR alerting on anomalous child processes from w3wp.exe and on Rust-compiled loader binaries staging Cobalt Strike/VShell.
detection.adequacy: Effective if deployed, but several victims reportedly reached the post-exploitation staging phase before detection, indicating monitoring maturity gaps.

response.what_would_have_worked: Isolate the affected IIS host, rotate credentials used by the Cityworks service account, and hunt for the Rust-loader/Cobalt Strike/VShell IOCs shared by Trimble/CISA across the fleet.
response.adequacy: Timely response depends on having the Trimble/CISA IOC set pre-loaded into detection tooling, which is not universal across critical-infrastructure operators.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The emergency patches (15.8.9 / 23.10, released Jan 28-29 2025) landed only after in-the-wild zero-day exploitation was already underway, showing standard patch-SLA timelines don't cover a pre-disclosure exploitation window.

new_control_requirements.name: SERVICE-INTERNAL-PROTOCOL-DESERIALIZATION-HARDENING
new_control_requirements.description: Cityworks reaches its deserialization sink over an ordinary authenticated application request to the IIS site, so only one half of this control is a lever here and the other half must not be claimed. The bind-the-listener-and-authenticate-the-peer half gives nothing: the packet's exploitation precondition is a low-privileged authenticated Cityworks session, which every legitimate field and office user already holds, and the deployments the packet describes as exploited are internet-facing by design for local-government and utility users — there is no network position to remove that does not also remove the product's function. The load-bearing half is constraining what arriving content the service is permitted to construct or evaluate: the Cityworks request path must not inherit safety from the fact that the caller authenticated, and the deserializer must be bound to an explicit set of expected types rather than reconstructing whatever object graph the submitted payload names. That is exactly why the least-privilege control cited against this entry passes its attestation while the flaw stays fully exploitable — the attacker is a legitimate low-privileged account behaving like one, so per-account privilege scoping is never the thing that fails and no access decision is ever wrong. Precondition: this states the property the vendor build must hold, it does not implement it. Cityworks 15.8.9 and Cityworks with Office Companion 23.10 are what establish it, and until a deployment is on those builds nothing on the operator side constrains the sink, because the request that reaches it is indistinguishable from a legitimate authenticated one. Measure completion per component on the version the running IIS deployment actually serves: the packet gives Office Companion its own fixed build, so a site that took the Cityworks update alone is not remediated.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet vector: 'Trimble Cityworks versions prior to 15.8.9 and Cityworks with office companion versions prior to 23.10 are vulnerable to a deserialization vulnerability. This could allow an authenticated user to perform a remote code execution attack against a customer's Microsoft Internet Information Services (IIS) web server.' cwe_refs CWE-502. affected: 'Trimble Cityworks GIS-centric asset-management software deployed on Microsoft IIS, including the Cityworks with Office Companion add-on, vulnerable to a .NET deserialization flaw reachable by an authenticated user.' affected_versions: 'Cityworks < 15.8.9', 'Cityworks with Office Companion < 23.10'. The NIST-800-53-AC-6 gap states exploitation only requires a low-privileged authenticated session (PR:L), so the deserialization surface itself needs to be constrained regardless of the caller's privilege level; the ISO-27001-2022-A.8.28 gap states the root cause is unsafe deserialization and that account-level trust in a low-privileged authenticated user cannot compensate. active_exploitation confirmed against internet-facing Cityworks/IIS deployments at local-government and utility operators; patch_available true, live_patch_available false, live_patch_notes null, patch_required_reboot false.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: The packet dates exploitation of Cityworks to around January 2025, the emergency builds 15.8.9 and Office Companion 23.10 to 28-29 January 2025, and the KEV listing to 2025-02-07. For this CVE the control's 'whichever is later' clause does real work: patch availability was the trigger that had already passed, and the interval between the vendor's emergency release and a site's next scheduled application-update window is the whole of the operator-controllable exposure. Concretely for a Cityworks estate that means the emergency build is driven out on an incident clock rather than folded into the normal application-update cycle, with each site's remediation recorded as the version its running IIS deployment serves and both components tracked separately, since Office Companion carries its own build number. The sector profile the packet records — water and wastewater, energy, transportation — is why the clock has to be the incident one rather than the cadence one, since these are the operators for whom a documented vulnerability-handling procedure is what currently satisfies the obligation. Precondition, stated because this is where a KEV SLA is routinely over-claimed: the control bounds the post-release window only. The packet records this as a zero-day exploited before the vendor build existed, so no SLA reaches the period in which the documented victims were actually compromised. And because the packet records custom Rust-based loaders staging VShell and Cobalt Strike in memory on the IIS host, an installation upgraded to 15.8.9 without triage carries whatever was staged on it into the fixed build — reaching the fixed version closes the sink, not the intrusion.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: cisa_kev true, kev_date 2025-02-07, active_exploitation confirmed, cvss 8.8, rwep_score 50, poc_available false, patch_available true, live_patch_available false, live_patch_notes null. The NIST-800-53-SI-2 gap states: 'The emergency patches (15.8.9 / 23.10, released Jan 28-29 2025) landed only after in-the-wild zero-day exploitation was already underway, showing standard patch-SLA timelines don't cover a pre-disclosure exploitation window.' active_exploitation_notes: 'Actively exploited as a zero-day beginning around January 2025 against internet-facing Cityworks/IIS deployments at local-government and utility operators; Trimble-shared IOCs indicate attackers deployed custom Rust-based loaders to stage the VShell and Cobalt Strike post-exploitation frameworks in memory... the affected sectors span water/wastewater, energy, and transportation.' The AU-Essential-8-Patch gap states the 48-hour guidance could not be met because the vendor's own emergency patch trailed the observed zero-day exploitation start date; the NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling gap states critical-infrastructure operators running Cityworks had no coordinated emergency-patch SLA matching that timeline.

CVE-2025-0411.name: 7-Zip Mark of the Web Bypass Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A victim opens a spear-phished, homoglyph-spoofed double-encapsulated 7-Zip archive; because 7-Zip fails to propagate the outer archive's Mark-of-the-Web to the inner archive's extracted files, script files (.js/.wsf/.url) run without triggering Windows SmartScreen or Office Protected View, executing attacker code (observed delivering SmokeLoader).
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated remote attacker; requires user interaction to open the crafted archive)
attack_vector.complexity: high — requires social-engineering (homoglyph filename spoofing) plus a specifically-crafted double-encapsulated archive structure
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — identified in the wild by Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative Threat Hunting team. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Update to 7-Zip 24.09+ and enforce Essential-8-style application hardening blocking direct execution of .js/.wsf/.url files extracted from archives.
prevention.adequacy: Patch alone is insufficient without also blocking risky script-file execution, since 7-Zip lacks auto-update and the campaign already ran as a zero-day for months before the fix existed.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Email-gateway detection of nested/double archives and homoglyph filename spoofing; EDR alerting on script interpreters (wscript/cscript) launched from freshly-extracted archive contents.
detection.adequacy: Effective when deployed, but homoglyph spoofing is specifically designed to defeat naive extension-based filtering.

response.what_would_have_worked: Hunt for SmokeLoader C2 indicators and script-interpreter execution chains following archive extraction across the fleet; block identified C2 infrastructure.
response.adequacy: Timely only if IOCs from Trend Micro's published analysis are ingested promptly.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: Malicious-code protections that gate on Mark-of-the-Web (SmartScreen prompts, Protected View) are bypassed entirely by the double-archive technique, so endpoint controls relying solely on MotW propagation are insufficient.

new_control_requirements.name: ARCHIVE-CONTENT-TYPE-PROVENANCE
new_control_requirements.description: The archive tool itself must carry the Mark-of-the-Web from the downloaded outer archive onto every file it writes — including the files it writes while extracting an archive that was itself extracted — and must decide how to render or launch an entry from its verified content type rather than from the name shown in the extraction listing. Both halves are load-bearing for this specific chain: the target receives a double-encapsulated 7-Zip archive whose entries carry homoglyph-spoofed names, and 7-Zip drops the outer archive's mark when it extracts the inner one, so the script files land on disk indistinguishable from files the user authored locally. Until 24.09 or later has actually been pushed to the fleet, treat any nested archive that 7-Zip extracts as mark-stripped by default: open it in a detonation chamber, not on a user endpoint, and do not rely on the displayed filename to judge what an entry is.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: 'The specific flaw exists within the handling of archived files. When extracting files from a crafted archive that bears the Mark-of-the-Web, 7-Zip does not propagate the Mark-of-the-Web to the extracted files' (CWE-693). The recorded path is a spear-phished, homoglyph-spoofed double-encapsulated 7-Zip archive whose extracted .js/.wsf/.url files execute attacker code, observed delivering SmokeLoader. User interaction is required — the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file. KEV-listed 2025-02-06, active_exploitation confirmed, poc_available true, CVSS 7.0, RWEP 68.

new_control_requirements.name: DOWNLOAD-PROVENANCE-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Script hosts and shortcut handlers must be blocked from running .js, .wsf and .url content that arrived through a download path, and that block must not be conditional on a reputation verdict — in this chain SmartScreen and Office Protected View never render a verdict at all, because the extracted files carry no mark for them to evaluate. Enforce provenance at the execution boundary instead (WDAC/AppLocker rules covering wscript/cscript and the shortcut handler, or removing script-host associations for user-writable extraction directories), so a mark-stripped payload dropped by a 7-Zip extraction is refused when it tries to run rather than when it tries to earn a reputation. Malware protection alone is the control this entry shows failing: the loader ran because the operating system had no reason to treat the file as internet-sourced.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: the extracted .js/.wsf/.url script files 'run without triggering Windows SmartScreen or Office Protected View, executing attacker code (observed delivering SmokeLoader)'. The flaw class is CWE-693, a protection-mechanism failure — the bypassed mechanism is the provenance mark itself. KEV-listed 2025-02-06 with active_exploitation confirmed and poc_available true. The entry's own citing gaps already record NIST 800-53 SI-3 (Malicious Code Protection), ISO/IEC 27001 A.8.7 (Protection against malware) and NIST 800-53 CM-7 (Least Functionality) as insufficient here.

new_control_requirements.name: PROTECTION-MECHANISM-FAILURE-CLASS-REGRESSION
new_control_requirements.description: 7-Zip carries no auto-update channel, so the fixed build only exists on an endpoint once someone has packaged and pushed 24.09 or later — and that push is only meaningful if a Mark-of-the-Web bypass battery is re-run against the build that actually landed. Keep that battery as a standing asset and make sure it includes the nested case this entry demonstrates (outer archive bearing the mark, inner archive extracted from it, script file extracted from that), not just a single-level download test, because the single-level test passes on a build that still drops the mark one layer down. Run it on every 7-Zip redistribution across the fleet and treat a software-inventory report showing '24.09 deployed' with no accompanying bypass result as unverified. Extend the same battery to every other archive tool operators are permitted to install: the packaging tool, not Windows, decides whether the mark survives extraction.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet live_patch_notes: '7-Zip has no built-in auto-update mechanism; enterprises must manually redistribute 24.09 or later, unlike browser-class software with silent auto-update.' live_patch_available is false, so there is no vendor-side path that reaches endpoints without the organization packaging and pushing the build. The defect is a protection-mechanism failure (CWE-693) against the Mark-of-the-Web / SmartScreen class, KEV-listed 2025-02-06 with active_exploitation confirmed and poc_available true — a working bypass primitive for the class is public, so the regression battery has real material to test with.

CVE-2024-21413.name: Microsoft Outlook Improper Input Validation Vulnerability (MonikerLink)

attack_vector.description: An attacker sends an email containing a crafted 'file://' moniker hyperlink with a '!' new-window parameter; when the recipient clicks it, Outlook bypasses Office Protected View and opens the linked remote document in edit mode, enabling NTLM hash leakage via an attacker SMB share or remote code execution.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated remote attacker; requires the recipient to click the crafted link)
attack_vector.complexity: low — a single crafted email link is sufficient, no additional conditions
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — discovered and reported by Check Point Research. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the February 2024 Outlook security update fleet-wide and block outbound SMB (445) to the internet at the perimeter.
prevention.adequacy: Patch availability preceded KEV addition by a year, showing patch-SLA policy alone did not drive timely remediation across the installed base — boundary controls on outbound SMB provide a necessary independent layer.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Email-gateway detection of moniker-scheme ('file://...!') links in inbound mail, and SIEM alerting on outbound NTLM authentication to non-corporate hosts.
detection.adequacy: Effective when deployed but requires email-gateway rules specifically tuned for the moniker-link pattern, which many default configurations lack.

response.what_would_have_worked: Force NTLM credential rotation for any user who triggered an outbound SMB authentication to an untrusted host, and hunt for follow-on RCE indicators.
response.adequacy: Timely only if outbound SMB/NTLM telemetry is already being collected and alerted on.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: Boundary protection blocking outbound SMB (445) to arbitrary external hosts would have prevented NTLM hash relay/capture even where the client-side Protected View bypass succeeded.

new_control_requirements.name: PROTECTION-MECHANISM-FAILURE-CLASS-REGRESSION
new_control_requirements.description: The mechanism this CVE defeats is Office Protected View itself: per the packet, a crafted 'file://' moniker hyperlink carrying the '!' new-window parameter makes Outlook bypass Protected View and open the linked remote document in edit mode when the recipient clicks it. That makes an attestation of the form 'Protected View is enforced by policy' simultaneously true and worthless — the policy is enforced and the document opens outside it, so a user-application-hardening review that inspects the policy finds nothing wrong. For this CVE the control means the moniker-link primitive becomes a permanent case in the estate's Protected-View / untrusted-document test battery, re-executed on every Office and Outlook update rather than exercised once while remediating this CVE, because a mechanism that has been bypassed once is a mechanism whose future updates need proving rather than assuming. Distinguishing test, keyed to the behaviour the packet documents rather than to a stand-in: send a managed workstation at the fixed build an email whose body carries a 'file://' moniker hyperlink with the '!' new-window parameter pointing at a share you control, click it, and check two observables — that the linked document opens in Protected View rather than edit mode, and that the workstation makes no authentication attempt to that share. The second observable is the one a naive test drops: the packet records NTLM hash leakage to an attacker SMB share as an outcome distinct from code execution, so an outbound authentication attempt is the signal that the primitive still works even when the document render looks contained, and a test that watches only the render will pass over it. Precondition: this is a verification control, not a mitigation. It tells an operator whether the protection class is actually restored on a given build; it restores nothing itself, and it gives nothing to a client that has not yet taken the vendor update. A battery that runs only at remediation time also cannot see a later regression, which is the entire reason for tying it to every update rather than to this ticket.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet fields for CVE-2024-21413 (Microsoft Outlook Improper Input Validation Vulnerability): cwe_refs CWE-20; vector 'Microsoft Outlook Remote Code Execution Vulnerability'; attack_vector 'An attacker sends an email containing a crafted file:// moniker hyperlink with a ! new-window parameter; when the recipient clicks it, Outlook bypasses Office Protected View and opens the linked remote document in edit mode, enabling NTLM hash leakage via an attacker SMB share or remote code execution.' cisa_kev true with kev_date 2025-02-06; active_exploitation confirmed; poc_available true; cvss 9.8; rwep_score 74. patch_available true, live_patch_available false, live_patch_notes null. Citing gaps recorded on this entry: AU-Essential-8-Patch, ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8 (Management of technical vulnerabilities), NIS2-Art21-patch-management, NIST-800-53-SC-7 (Boundary Protection), NIST-800-53-SI-2 (Flaw Remediation) and UK-CAF-B4 (System security).

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: What the clock governs on this entry is distribution, not availability: the packet records patch_available true against a CVE from the 2024 identifier series that CISA did not list until 2025-02-06, with exploitation confirmed and a public PoC. The remediation unit is also unusual for a KEV item — the vulnerable code is the Outlook client on every user's machine, not a server or an appliance, so the SLA has to be measured as the count of Outlook installs reporting the fixed build and closed against the estate's install inventory, not against a change ticket for a single system. The packet registers no live-patch path and carries no live-patch note for this entry, so each install reaches remediation only by taking the vendor update; there is no interim state in which the client is running fixed code. Precondition on the compensating-control branch, which is where this gets over-claimed: for the window before the update lands, the outbound leg the packet names — NTLM authentication to an attacker-controlled SMB share — can be restricted at the boundary, and that is what the entry's boundary-protection gap points at, but it bounds only the credential-leak half. The packet records remote code execution as a separate outcome that this restriction does not address, and it does nothing where the link's destination is reachable inside the estate rather than across the boundary being filtered, so it is a bound on one outcome for one class of destination, not a substitute for the update. Second precondition: the update closes the client path forward and recovers nothing backward. Credential material already leaked during the exposure window stays valid after every client is patched, so any account whose workstation authenticated outward to an untrusted host in that window is a rotation item and a hunt item, not a line that clears when the install count reaches 100 percent.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet fields for CVE-2024-21413: attack_vector 'An attacker sends an email containing a crafted file:// moniker hyperlink with a ! new-window parameter; when the recipient clicks it, Outlook bypasses Office Protected View and opens the linked remote document in edit mode, enabling NTLM hash leakage via an attacker SMB share or remote code execution.' cisa_kev true with kev_date 2025-02-06 against a CVE in the 2024 identifier series; active_exploitation confirmed; poc_available true; cvss 9.8; rwep_score 74; cwe_refs CWE-20. patch_available true, live_patch_available false, live_patch_notes null — no live-patch path and no live-patch note is recorded for this entry. The citing gaps are dominated by patch-timeline controls (AU-Essential-8-Patch, NIS2-Art21-patch-management, NIST-800-53-SI-2, ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8), with NIST-800-53-SC-7 (Boundary Protection) recorded alongside them.

attack_vector.description: An attacker with local access places a malicious 'dal_keepalives.dll' in the application directory of the legitimate, signed mDNSResponder.exe (part of Audinate's Dante Application Library for Windows); when the trusted binary runs, it loads the attacker's DLL and executes code in the context of the trusted process.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none beyond local access to the filesystem (PR:N); requires the user/attacker to trigger execution of mDNSResponder.exe (UI:R)
attack_vector.complexity: low — placing a same-named DLL in the application's search path is sufficient, no additional conditions
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — discovered and reported by Check Point Research (CPR-Zero). No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Update to Dante Application Library for Windows v1.2.1+ (mDNSResponder.exe v1.3.2) and enforce application-hardening controls restricting DLL loading to trusted system paths.
prevention.adequacy: Patch adoption depends on every downstream OEM that bundles Dante Application Library repackaging and redistributing the fix, so patch alone is not a fast or complete remediation path.

detection.what_would_have_worked: EDR rules alerting on unsigned/unexpected DLLs loaded by signed binaries (image-load monitoring) for mDNSResponder.exe specifically.
detection.adequacy: Effective when deployed, but broadcast/pro-audio production workstations are frequently outside standard EDR coverage.

response.what_would_have_worked: Remove the malicious DLL, verify integrity of the Dante Application Library installation, and audit for other side-loadable directories on affected hosts.
response.adequacy: Requires awareness that Dante software is present, which is often overlooked in general IT asset inventories.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least-functionality/secure-configuration baselines should prevent a signed executable from loading DLLs out of a user-writable application directory; safe DLL search-order hardening wasn't applied.

new_control_requirements.name: TIER-3-DEPENDENCY-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: The vulnerable executable here is not something an operator installs by name. The packet identifies mDNSResponder.exe as part of Audinate's Dante Application Library for Windows, so the binary an attacker abuses arrives on a Windows host as a component of whatever product embeds that library, under that product's name in the installed-software list. Applied to this CVE, the control means the software inventory and SBOM carry the Dante Application Library and the mDNSResponder.exe it installs as components in their own right — each with its own version and its own fix state, recorded separately from the product that shipped them — because a remediation program that enumerates only installed applications has no row to act on when the KEV entry names the library rather than the application. Scope this to what the packet establishes: locate copies of that named library and executable. The packet ties the defect to mDNSResponder.exe improperly specifying how, and from which folder, it loads a DLL, and to a malicious dal_keepalives.dll dropped in that executable's own application directory; it provides no mapping of the defect into other signed binaries, so treating every DLL-loading signed executable in the estate as an instance of this CVE would manufacture findings against software no evidence implicates. The distinguishing test: search the estate's Windows hosts for mDNSResponder.exe on disk and reconcile every hit against an inventory record naming the Dante Application Library and its version; hits with no matching record are exactly the population the flaw-remediation process cannot currently reach, and they will not appear on any patch report. Precondition and limit: an inventory locates the component, it does not remediate it. The packet records that a vendor patch exists, so each located copy still has to be carried to the fixed library; a copy installed by software that is not under management is remediated by removing that software, not by recording the component as inventoried.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet vector: mDNSResponder.exe is vulnerable to DLL sideloading — the executable improperly specifies how to load the DLL, from which folder and under what conditions, so a malicious attacker can use the valid and legitimate executable to load malicious files (CWE-114, CWE-426). Packet attack_vector: an attacker with local access places a malicious dal_keepalives.dll in the application directory of the legitimate, signed mDNSResponder.exe, part of Audinate's Dante Application Library for Windows; the trusted binary then loads the attacker's DLL and executes code in the context of the trusted process. CISA KEV-listed 2025-02-06 with active_exploitation confirmed; patch_available true; RWEP 40 against CVSS 7.8. The packet cites EU NIS2 Art. 21 supply chain security measures and NIST SP 800-53 SI-2 (Flaw Remediation) among the framework controls insufficient for this entry.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: This entry is the case the control's 'whichever is later' wording exists for. The CVE identifier is from 2022 and the packet records a vendor patch as available, but the KEV listing — and with it the evidence of confirmed in-the-wild exploitation — did not arrive until 2025-02-06. A risk-based vulnerability-management cycle that triaged this at disclosure saw a local-access DLL sideload with no public proof-of-concept, which is precisely the profile such a cycle files below its action threshold and never revisits; the packet still carries poc_available false today, so a triage weighted on public exploit code would deprioritize it while it is in fact being exploited. Applied to this product, the control means the KEV listing date reopens the item and starts an expedited clock over every located copy of the Dante Application Library and its mDNSResponder.exe, with the verified state being the library version present on each host rather than the currency of the application that bundled it. Preconditions and limits: the packet registers no live-patch path, so there is no interim fix to apply — a copy is either carried to the fixed library or it is exposed. Where that cannot happen inside the window, the control's compensating-control branch has to be documented rather than implied, and for this flaw the defensible compensating control follows directly from the packet's own exploitation step: constrain write access to mDNSResponder.exe's application directory so that no identity other than one performing a vendor update can place a DLL there. State its bounds honestly — it does nothing on a host where the attacker already holds the privilege needed to rewrite that directory or its permissions, and it does not remove a dal_keepalives.dll planted before the restriction was applied, so a host that ran the vulnerable configuration during the exposure window needs that directory's contents compared against the vendor's file set rather than being closed on the update.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet fields: cve id CVE-2022-23748 with cisa_kev true and kev_date 2025-02-06; active_exploitation confirmed; poc_available false; patch_available true; live_patch_available false with no live-patch notes recorded; RWEP 40 against CVSS 7.8. Packet attack_vector establishes the exploitation step as an attacker with local access placing a malicious dal_keepalives.dll in the application directory of the legitimate, signed mDNSResponder.exe. The packet cites ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.8.8 (Management of technical vulnerabilities) among the framework controls insufficient for this entry.

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated remote attacker submits crafted SQL injection payloads to the CyberoamOS WebAdmin login/authentication endpoint, executing arbitrary SQL statements against the backend database — in observed cases used to create unauthorized administrative accounts on the appliance.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated remote attacker)
attack_vector.complexity: low — direct SQL injection against a network-exposed login endpoint, no special conditions
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — reported to and fixed by Sophos. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the December 2020 hotfix; for appliances that are now EOL/EOS, isolate or decommission the WebAdmin interface from any untrusted network.
prevention.adequacy: The hotfix closed the flaw in 2020, but the product's subsequent EOL/EOS status means operators who never applied it now have no vendor remediation path at all — only isolation or replacement remains.

detection.what_would_have_worked: WAF/IPS signatures for SQL injection patterns on the WebAdmin login endpoint, and monitoring for unexpected new administrative accounts on the appliance.
detection.adequacy: Effective when deployed, but EOL appliances are frequently excluded from modern security-monitoring tooling and asset inventories.

response.what_would_have_worked: Audit all local admin accounts on the appliance for unauthorized additions, rotate credentials, and review WebAdmin access logs for injection payload patterns.
response.adequacy: Requires the appliance to be within scope of routine account/log auditing, which EOL devices often are not.

NIST-800-53-AC-3.gap: Unauthenticated SQL injection against the WebAdmin login endpoint bypasses access enforcement entirely at the authentication layer itself, before any access-control policy is evaluated.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: The packet does not stop at 'unauthenticated SQL injection' — it records the observed outcome as the creation of unauthorized administrative accounts on the appliance, which is an implant built out of the product's own account model rather than a file dropped on disk. Applying the December 2020 hotfix closes the injection point at the WebAdmin authentication endpoint and removes nothing an attacker already created through it, so for any CyberoamOS unit that was reachable before the hotfix landed the default disposition is export-config, rebuild or replace, and rotate every credential the appliance holds or terminates — not hotfix-in-place followed by closing the ticket. The audit that decides this cannot be run against the appliance's own account list on its own terms: an attacker-created administrator is indistinguishable from a legitimate one by privilege alone, so the list has to be reconciled against an authoritative roster of who is supposed to hold WebAdmin access, and any account that cannot be attributed to a person is the finding. State the limit rather than recording this as remediation: it is a detection-and-recovery control, not a fix. It tells the operator whether the box is trustworthy today, and on a platform that will receive no further updates a clean answer has a short shelf life.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: CWE-89; CISA KEV-listed 2025-02-06 with active_exploitation confirmed; CVSS 9.8, RWEP 73, poc_available true. attack_vector: 'An unauthenticated remote attacker submits crafted SQL injection payloads to the CyberoamOS WebAdmin login/authentication endpoint, executing arbitrary SQL statements against the backend database — in observed cases used to create unauthorized administrative accounts on the appliance.' live_patch_available false; live_patch_notes record a hotfix distributed December 4, 2020 (including to EOL versions 10.6.2+). NIST-800-53-SI-2 and NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management are recorded as citing gaps.

new_control_requirements.name: UNSUPPORTED-NETWORK-DEVICE-ENUMERATION-AND-RETIREMENT
new_control_requirements.description: The packet's live_patch_notes carry the whole decision: a hotfix was distributed December 4, 2020, including to EOL versions 10.6.2+, but CyberoamOS is now fully end-of-life/end-of-service per CISA's required action and no further updates will be issued for remaining deployments. That makes the hotfix worth applying to any unit that never took it, and worthless as a posture — it settles this defect and leaves the next WebAdmin defect with no fix path at all. Applied to this product, the control means every surviving CyberoamOS unit carries an end-of-support date in the asset inventory together with a dated replacement decision, because the packet's exploitation path is an unauthenticated remote request to the appliance's web management surface, so reachability is the entire precondition and the inventory is what tells the operator where reachability exists. Until replacement lands, the WebAdmin surface comes off every untrusted segment. Name the precondition instead of claiming the surface is gone: that restriction holds only while it is enforced from every segment an attacker can occupy; it does not cover a unit whose WebAdmin must stay reachable for remote administration, which has to be moved behind an authenticated gateway performing its own enforcement, since the appliance's own authentication is precisely what the injection bypasses; and it does nothing for a unit that already carries an attacker-created administrator. The distinguishing test: from each untrusted segment, attempt to load WebAdmin on every inventoried unit — anything that answers is reachable by the exact request the packet describes, and a risk-acceptance record with no replacement date leaves a KEV-listed device on a retired platform in service indefinitely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet live_patch_notes, verbatim: 'A hotfix was distributed December 4, 2020 (including to EOL versions 10.6.2+), but CyberoamOS is now fully end-of-life/end-of-service per CISA's required action — no further updates will be issued for remaining deployments.' live_patch_available false. Vector: 'An SQL injection vulnerability in the WebAdmin of Cyberoam OS through 2020-12-04 allows unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary SQL statements remotely.'
