Because the packet records continuous cryptomining and webshell campaigns against exposed T3/IIOP interfaces, an instance that answered from an untrusted network needs examining for an already-planted webshell or miner rather than being closed on the patch record.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: affected records that an unauthenticated attacker with network access to the T3 or IIOP protocol can send a malicious serialized object deserialized by the Oracle Coherence library, resulting in full server takeover; CVSS 9.8 with vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N. NIST-800-53-SC-7 gap: the most effective compensating control — disabling or firewalling T3/IIOP from untrusted networks — is a boundary-protection measure, not a patch, and many affected servers left T3/IIOP internet-reachable long after patching. NIS2-Art21-network-security gap: EU operators running WebLogic as middleware need network-layer segmentation of T3/IIOP as a standing control, independent of patch status. active_exploitation_notes: exploited in the wild almost immediately after the April 2020 patch and the May 2020 public PoC release, and still targeted by opportunistic scanners and cryptomining/webshell campaigns against exposed WebLogic T3/IIOP interfaces, prompting the CISA KEV addition in January 2025. poc_available true; active_exploitation confirmed.

new_control_requirements.name: SCANNER-PAPER-COMPLIANCE-TEST
new_control_requirements.description: The packet states the divergence this control exists to test: technical vulnerability management marks the control satisfied once the April 2020 patch is recorded as applied, yet CISA added this to KEV in January 2025 — 'patched in inventory' and 'not exploitable' are different statements wherever a shadow WebLogic instance was missed. A scan that reports this closed by reading a patch level from the hosts already in the asset register is paper compliance for exactly this CVE, because the instances driving a five-year exploitation tail are the ones the register does not contain: WebLogic embedded inside a vendor product or appliance, a dev or DR clone of production, an instance stood up for a migration and never retired. The operational test that separates the two is to discover by protocol response rather than by asset record — sweep the internal estate, the cloud ranges and the external perimeter for anything answering T3 or IIOP, and for every responder establish which release it is running against the four the packet names as affected (10.3.6.0.0, 12.1.3.0.0, 12.2.1.3.0, 12.2.1.4.0) and whether the Oracle Coherence deserialization path it is executing carries the fix. A programme that reports zero vulnerable WebLogic hosts while a T3 listener answers somewhere has measured its inventory, not its estate. Preconditions: this finds instances, it does not remediate them — each responder still needs the vendor patch, and while the packet records no host reboot as required and no live-patch path, completion has to be read from the release the running server process reports, since the process holding the listener is the one executing the vulnerable deserialization path and a patch applied on disk under a still-running server is not yet in force. And because a public PoC has existed since May 2020 and campaigns have been continuous, a newly discovered exposed instance should be triaged as potentially already compromised rather than merely unpatched.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8 gap: technical vulnerability management marks A.8.8 satisfied once the April-2020 patch is recorded as applied, yet KEV addition in 2025 proves 'patched in inventory' and 'not exploitable' diverge for this T3/IIOP deserialization flaw wherever a shadow WebLogic instance was missed. UK-CAF-B2 gap: asset inventories that fail to track exposed middleware protocol ports (T3/IIOP) leave legacy WebLogic deployments exploitable years after a patch exists. AU-Essential-8-Patch gap: patch-application timelines alone do not explain multi-year persistence of exploitation against a patched vulnerability — unpatched shadow/legacy instances are the likely driver. NIST-800-53-SI-2 gap: patched in April 2020 yet CISA found active in-the-wild exploitation warranting KEV addition in January 2025. affected_versions: 10.3.6.0.0, 12.1.3.0.0, 12.2.1.3.0, 12.2.1.4.0. patch_available true, patch_required_reboot false, live_patch_available false, live_patch_notes null. poc_available true, with the public PoC recorded as released May 2020.

CVE-2024-3393.name: Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS Malicious DNS Packet Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated attacker sends a specially crafted DNS packet through the firewall's data plane; on devices with DNS Security logging enabled, parsing the packet crashes the firewall and forces a reboot, with repeated attempts pushing the device into maintenance mode.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated, network-reachable data plane)
attack_vector.complexity: low in principle, but requires the target to have a DNS Security or Advanced DNS Security license with logging enabled — a common but not universal production configuration
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — found and disclosed by Palo Alto Networks. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the PAN-OS 10.1.15 / 10.2.14 / 11.1.5 / 11.2.3+ patch, or apply the interim workaround of disabling DNS Security logging
prevention.adequacy: The interim workaround (disabling logging) reduces the firewall's DNS-threat visibility as a side effect, so it is a stopgap, not a durable fix.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Monitor firewall uptime/reboot telemetry and data-plane crash logs for repeated unscheduled reboots correlated with inbound DNS traffic
detection.adequacy: Detects the symptom (reboot) but by the time it fires the perimeter defense is already degraded.

response.what_would_have_worked: Failover to a redundant firewall pair, apply the emergency patch or workaround, and review whether the outage window was used to mask other intrusion attempts
response.adequacy: High-availability firewall pairs mitigate the direct outage but do not by themselves close the underlying flaw.

NIST-800-53-SI-4.gap: Perimeter monitoring needs to detect repeated malformed-packet-triggered reboots as an availability incident, since the firewall itself becomes the outage rather than merely logging an alert.

UK-CAF-D1.gap: Response and recovery planning must account for the firewall entering maintenance mode under repeated attack, since the perimeter defense device itself becomes unavailable.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-DEVICE-ZERODAY-SLA-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: The tier as written covers pre-auth RCE on the trust boundary; this CVE shows it has to cover pre-auth availability loss on the same devices. An unauthenticated packet arriving through the firewall's data plane reboots it, and repeated packets drive it into maintenance mode — the trust boundary stops enforcing policy without the attacker ever touching the management plane or holding a credential. A 14/30-day operating-system patch window is meaningless against that: the device whose uptime every other control depends on is remotely switchable-off by anyone who can reach it. The tier requirement for this entry is the vendor PAN-OS update deployed on the KEV clock, or the exposed DNS-inspection path taken out of service until it can be, and there is no live-patch option that avoids the restart.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA KEV-listed 2024-12-30 with active_exploitation confirmed; RWEP 58, CVSS 7.5. The packet's vector: 'A Denial of Service vulnerability in the DNS Security feature of Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS software allows an unauthenticated attacker to send a malicious packet through the data plane of the firewall that reboots the firewall. Repeated attempts to trigger this condition will cause the firewall to enter maintenance mode.' patch_available true; live_patch_available false; live_patch_notes null; poc_available false; CWE-754.

new_control_requirements.name: CONFIGURATION-SIDE-LIVE-PATCH-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: The packet conditions the crash on DNS Security logging being enabled, which means there is a configuration-side route out of the exploitable state that does not wait for the PAN-OS update or its restart window. That route is only useful if it was inventoried before the KEV listing: which firewalls have that logging enabled, what detection coverage the organisation gives up while it is off, who is authorised to change it under an incident clock, and how the change is verified on each device. Because live_patch_available is false for this entry, an operator has exactly two options — the configuration change now, or the vendor update plus restart later — and frameworks that only recognise the second leave the hours in between uncovered on an actively exploited firewall.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The packet's attack_vector states the crash occurs 'on devices with DNS Security logging enabled', tying reachability to a configuration state. live_patch_available false and live_patch_notes null — no in-place hot fix is recorded. patch_available true. CISA KEV-listed 2024-12-30, active_exploitation confirmed, RWEP 58, CVSS 7.5.

new_control_requirements.name: FIREWALL-EGRESS-TELEMETRY-SEPARATE-TRUST-ZONE
new_control_requirements.description: The device that would record this attack is the device the attack knocks over. A firewall that reboots on a crafted DNS packet — and that after repeated packets sits in maintenance mode — is not forwarding anything during the window that matters, so on-box threat and system logs are the worst possible place to hold the evidence that an outage was an attack rather than a hardware or software fault. Continuous forwarding of syslog and threat logs to a SIEM in a separate trust zone (separate management plane, separate credentials, separate authentication path) is what converts 'the firewall rebooted again' into a correlated repeat-attempt pattern with source data, and it is what gives responders a timeline while the device itself is unreachable. That matters more here than for a typical exploit because there is no public PoC to signature against — the reboot pattern is the detection.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Per the packet, 'Repeated attempts to trigger this condition will cause the firewall to enter maintenance mode', and the triggering packet arrives unauthenticated through the data plane. poc_available false — no public exploit artifact to build a signature from. CISA KEV-listed 2024-12-30 with active_exploitation confirmed; RWEP 58, CVSS 7.5; CWE-754.

CVE-2021-44207.name: Acclaim Systems USAHERDS Use of Hard-Coded Credentials Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: USAHERDS ships with a static, product-wide ASP.NET MachineKey (ValidationKey/DecryptionKey). An attacker who obtains the actual key value — APT41 acquired it through undisclosed means — can forge a __VIEWSTATE payload that passes MAC validation; the server deserializes it, executing attacker code.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none for exploitation once the static key is known, but the attacker must first obtain the actual key value through a separate vulnerability, leak, or reverse engineering
attack_vector.complexity: high — the key is not publicly disclosed by any advisory, so real-world exploitation (as by APT41) required independent acquisition of the key material
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — found and disclosed by Mandiant. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Deploy the vendor patch that removes the hardcoded key and regenerate a unique MachineKey per installation
prevention.adequacy: A version-number patch alone is inadequate unless each deployment's MachineKey is individually rotated, since the vulnerability is the shared key material itself, not a code logic bug.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Monitor IIS logs for anomalous ViewState deserialization activity and unexpected new files/scheduled tasks on the USAHERDS web server
detection.adequacy: Effective for catching post-exploitation activity but cannot detect the initial forged-ViewState request without deep ASP.NET-specific instrumentation most organizations lack.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rotate the MachineKey, hunt for APT41 DEADEYE malware and webshells, and review lateral movement from the compromised host into the broader state-government network
response.adequacy: Matches Mandiant's documented response to the actual APT41 campaign, which required full incident response across multiple state agencies.

NIST-800-53-IA-2.gap: Static, product-wide cryptographic key material (the ASP.NET MachineKey) undermines authentication assurance for every deployment sharing the same hardcoded value, regardless of individual organizations' IA controls.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: EU-equivalent public-sector operators of niche vertical software need vendor attestation that cryptographic key material is unique per deployment, which standard vulnerability management processes rarely verify.

new_control_requirements.name: FRAMEWORK-DEFAULT-SECRET-DETECTION
new_control_requirements.description: USAHERDS ships the same ASP.NET MachineKey (ValidationKey/DecryptionKey) in every install, so the secret an attacker needs to forge material the server will trust comes from the product rather than from the target — and the packet records that APT41 already holds the value. That inverts the usual remediation order: no amount of account hygiene, password policy or session management on the operator's side reduces this exposure, because the forged __VIEWSTATE passes MAC validation before any account is consulted, which is exactly why the cited ISO A.5.15 access-control and NIST IA-2 user-authentication attestations pass cleanly while the path stays open. Gate the deployment on key uniqueness instead: after moving the instance off the affected build (the packet places the flaw in USAHERDS through 7.4.0.1), verify that the instance's machineKey validation and decryption values are unique to that instance and match neither the product-shipped constant nor any other instance you operate, and hold the server out of service until they do. Re-run the check after every restore-from-image, VM template clone or server rebuild, since those are the operations that quietly reintroduce the shipped key onto a host that was previously remediated. The precondition that must be stated: rotating the key closes the forgery path forward only — it does not evict an attacker who already achieved code execution through a forged __VIEWSTATE before rotation, so an instance exposed while carrying the shipped key needs forensic triage of the web application's process and content in addition to the key change. Distinguishing test: read the machineKey values from two independently deployed instances and from a freshly restored image; identical values on any pair means the deserialization path is still forgeable by anyone holding the constant.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: CWE-798 use of hard-coded credentials; vector 'Acclaim USAHERDS through 7.4.0.1 uses hard-coded credentials.' attack_vector states USAHERDS ships with a static, product-wide ASP.NET MachineKey (ValidationKey/DecryptionKey), that an attacker who obtains the key value — 'APT41 acquired it through undisclosed means' — can forge a __VIEWSTATE payload that passes MAC validation, and that the server deserializes it, executing attacker code. CVSS 8.1, RWEP 42, CISA KEV-listed 2024-12-23, active_exploitation 'confirmed', poc_available false. patch_available true; live_patch_available false with live_patch_notes null. Cited gaps include ISO-27001-2022-A.5.15 (Access control), NIST-800-53-IA-2 (Identification and Authentication, Organizational Users) and NIST-800-53-SI-2 (Flaw Remediation).

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: The clock on this entry opened with the 2024-12-23 KEV listing against confirmed in-the-wild exploitation, and the remediation shape leaves no shortcut: the packet records a vendor patch with no live-patch path, so the only way the fix reaches a USAHERDS instance is by taking it off the affected build (through 7.4.0.1) and through the vendor update, with the service interruption that implies. For this application the control means that upgrade is scheduled against the KEV clock rather than against the general application-patching cadence the cited AU ISM 1546 and NIST SI-2 attestations are measured on — a line-of-business web application inside a periodic patch cycle is precisely the population that carried this flaw into a KEV listing years after the affected build was identified. The condition to state plainly: meeting the SLA on version alone is not sufficient remediation here, because the vulnerable primitive is a shipped secret rather than a code defect the update independently guarantees to re-key; the version move is the SLA-bearing action and the key-uniqueness verification recorded alongside it is what makes the instance actually non-forgeable. Distinguishing test: for each USAHERDS instance, compare the deployed build against the affected range and the completion date against the 2024-12-23 listing; an instance recorded as 'scheduled in the next maintenance cycle' is an accepted exposure on an actively exploited path, not a remediation.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: CISA KEV-listed 2024-12-23, active_exploitation 'confirmed', RWEP 42, CVSS 8.1. Vector places the flaw in 'Acclaim USAHERDS through 7.4.0.1'. patch_available true; live_patch_available false with live_patch_notes null, so no live-patch path is recorded for this entry. Cited gaps include NIST-800-53-SI-2 (Flaw Remediation), AU-ISM-1546 (Patch operating systems and applications), NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management (Vulnerability handling) and UK-CAF-B4 (System security).

CVE-2024-12356.name: BeyondTrust Privileged Remote Access (PRA) and Remote Support (RS) Command Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted WebSocket-upgrade HTTP request with malicious Sec-WebSocket-Protocol / X-Ns-Company header values that are concatenated unsanitized into a shell command run as the appliance's site user, yielding remote command execution on the PAM appliance itself.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated network request)
attack_vector.complexity: low — a single crafted HTTP request with malformed headers triggers command execution; a public Metasploit module fully automates it
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — identified by BeyondTrust after detecting compromise of its own hosted infrastructure. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Vendor patch (24.3.1+) plus network isolation of the PAM appliance's management/API surface from downstream sensitive systems
prevention.adequacy: Patch alone is insufficient because the breach chain relied on a stolen vendor API key, not a defect any customer-side patch would have closed

detection.what_would_have_worked: Anomaly detection on PAM/remote-support API key usage from unfamiliar source contexts, and WAF/IDS signatures for shell metacharacters in WebSocket upgrade headers
detection.adequacy: Most customers had no visibility into vendor-side API key misuse, which is the layer where this campaign actually pivoted

response.what_would_have_worked: Immediate API-key rotation, appliance isolation, and forensic review of PRA/RS session logs for any of the 17 known-compromised SaaS instances
response.adequacy: Response depended on BeyondTrust's own disclosure timeline; affected customers had limited independent means of detecting the compromise

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The actual breach vector was a compromised vendor SaaS API key, not a direct customer-side flaw; CAF B4 (supply chain) requires modeling vendor-side compromise blast radius for privileged remote-access providers, which most customers had not done.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: BeyondTrust Privileged Remote Access and Remote Support exist to broker privileged sessions into other systems, and the packet's path ends with command execution on that broker itself — an unauthenticated crafted WebSocket-upgrade request whose Sec-WebSocket-Protocol / X-Ns-Company header values are concatenated unsanitized into a shell command run as the appliance's site user. For this product the control means an appliance whose HTTP surface was reachable during the exposure window is handled as attacker-held rather than as a patch item: configuration and session artifacts captured for forensics first, the appliance rebuilt from vendor media, and every credential the appliance stored, brokered, or that authenticated through it during the window rotated. Applying the vendor update closes the injection sink and removes nothing the attacker wrote or read through it, and on a privileged-access appliance what it read is the credential set for the downstream estate — which is why a remediation that ends at 'the fix is deployed' understates this CVE specifically. Precondition and limits: this is an incident-response default, not a preventive measure. It presumes the operator can bound an exposure window (the packet gives the 2024-12-19 KEV listing as the anchor and no per-unit indicator of compromise), and it does not tell an operator whether a given appliance was actually reached. Where session and access logs live only on the appliance the attacker had command execution on, absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, so reachability during the window — not a confirmed detection — has to be the trigger. Rebuild-and-rotate is also not free: it interrupts the remote-support function the appliance provides, which is the reason the patch-in-place shortcut gets taken.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: CWE-77 command injection; an unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted WebSocket-upgrade HTTP request with malicious Sec-WebSocket-Protocol / X-Ns-Company header values that are concatenated unsanitized into a shell command run as the appliance's site user, yielding remote command execution on the PAM appliance itself. CISA KEV-listed 2024-12-19; active_exploitation confirmed; poc_available true; CVSS 9.8; RWEP 74. patch_available true, live_patch_available false, with no live-patch note recorded — the vendor update is the only remediation the packet registers, and it is exactly the step this control says is insufficient on its own once exploitation is confirmed.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-DEVICE-ZERODAY-SLA-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: A Privileged Remote Access / Remote Support appliance is a remote-access trust boundary — it accepts connections from technicians outside the protected network — and the packet's request arrives unauthenticated over that same HTTP surface. So the remediation clock for this CVE cannot be the general application-patching SLA the AU Essential Eight and boundary-protection attestations are measured against: the requirement is the vendor fix deployed, or the vulnerable HTTP/WebSocket surface withdrawn from untrusted networks, measured from the 2024-12-19 KEV listing rather than from the next maintenance window. Precondition, and it is the whole difficulty on this product: withdrawing the surface is only available where remote technicians can still reach the appliance another way — an internal-only deployment, or an interposed VPN or authenticating proxy that terminates the connection before the appliance's own handler ever parses the upgrade headers. On an appliance published to the internet so external support staff can connect, which is the deployment this product is bought for, there is no isolation lever that preserves the function, and the vendor update is the only path; the isolation half then applies only to management and API surfaces that have no need to be publicly reachable. Note also what isolation does not do: it bounds who can send the crafted request, it does not repair the unsanitized concatenation, so any caller inside a permitted segment still reaches command execution. The packet records no live-patch mechanism, so there is no in-place option that avoids taking the vendor update.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: unauthenticated network request against the appliance's WebSocket-upgrade path yields remote command execution on the PAM appliance itself; CWE-77. CISA KEV-listed 2024-12-19; active_exploitation confirmed; poc_available true; CVSS 9.8; RWEP 74. patch_available true; live_patch_available false, with no live-patch note recorded.

new_control_requirements.name: PEN-TEST-SCOPE-INCLUDES-SECURITY-PRODUCTS
new_control_requirements.description: The vulnerable product here is itself a security control — the privileged remote access and remote support tier that brokers privileged sessions — which is precisely the class this control says must appear in test scope as attack surface rather than as a defense to work behind. Bound to this CVE that means the PRA/RS appliance's public HTTP surface, and specifically its WebSocket upgrade handling, is a tested surface in its own right: the defect lives in how attacker-supplied Sec-WebSocket-Protocol and X-Ns-Company header values are carried into a shell command, and no amount of testing the systems reached through the appliance would surface it. Scope language has to name the appliance and its API surface explicitly, because scope statements typically enumerate the estate the privileged-access tool protects and silently exclude the tool. Precondition and limits: this is an assurance control, not a mitigation. It changes the probability of finding the next defect in this surface and does nothing for an appliance already exposed to this one, and because the code is the vendor's, what it produces is a vendor report plus an operator exposure decision — not a fix the operator can write, which is the same reason a secure-coding attestation over the operator's own code passes cleanly while this path stays open. Keep the scope addition to the products the packet names, Privileged Remote Access and Remote Support; extending it to other security products is a decision to make on their own evidence, not on this entry.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: the affected product is BeyondTrust Privileged Remote Access (PRA) and Remote Support (RS) — a privileged-access product — and the flaw is a CWE-77 command injection reached by an unauthenticated crafted WebSocket-upgrade HTTP request through the Sec-WebSocket-Protocol / X-Ns-Company headers, executing as the appliance's site user. poc_available true; active_exploitation confirmed; CISA KEV-listed 2024-12-19; CVSS 9.8; RWEP 74.

CVE-2022-23227.name: NUUO NVRmini2 Devices Missing Authentication Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated attacker uploads a specially crafted encrypted TAR archive to the NVRmini2 user-import handler, which has no authentication check, to create an arbitrary administrator account; combined with a separate directory-traversal bug in the device's bundled BusyBox (CVE-2011-5325), the same upload chain overwrites files under the web root to achieve root-level code execution.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated network request)
attack_vector.complexity: low — a public PoC and Metasploit module fully automate both the account-creation and file-overwrite chain
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — found and disclosed by independent researcher Pedro Ribeiro. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: No vendor patch exists; the only effective prevention is removing NVRmini2 devices from the network or air-gapping them behind a dedicated management VLAN
prevention.adequacy: Because NUUO has never fixed the flaw, patch-based remediation guidance is inapplicable — CISA's own required action is decommissioning, not patching

detection.what_would_have_worked: Monitoring for unauthenticated TAR uploads to the NVR's HTTP interface and alerting on new administrator accounts appearing outside change-management windows
detection.adequacy: Most NVRmini2 deployments (small business, physical security) lack any network monitoring layer capable of catching this

response.what_would_have_worked: Immediate device isolation, credential/user-database review, and firmware reflash or hardware replacement
response.adequacy: Reflashing does not fix the underlying flaw since it exists in all released firmware; full replacement is the only durable response

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical vulnerability management assumes an eventual vendor patch — NUUO has not responded to disclosure and the flaw persists in the latest firmware, so remediation-SLA-based controls cannot be satisfied and must fall back to decommissioning.

new_control_requirements.name: UNSUPPORTED-NETWORK-DEVICE-ENUMERATION-AND-RETIREMENT
new_control_requirements.description: The NVRmini2 is a network video recorder, and this packet resolves the patch-versus-replace question in one direction: patch_available is false and no live-patch path is recorded, so there is no fixed build for an operator to reach. That makes each unit in service a replacement item rather than a remediation-clock item, and the requirement is an inventory naming every NVRmini2 with its firmware level - the packet scopes the defect to builds 'through 3.11' - together with a vendor-obtained answer on whether a fixed firmware exists for that hardware, rather than an assumption in either direction. Any unit for which the vendor produces a fix belongs on a remediation clock; every unit for which it does not belongs on a dated removal or replacement schedule, because a risk acceptance with no removal date leaves a KEV-listed device carrying a public PoC and confirmed exploitation in service indefinitely. Scope the inventory to what the packet names - NUUO NVRmini2 - not to every recorder or camera on the estate; the packet ties the missing authentication check to handle_import_user.php on this product and provides no mapping into other video hardware, so treating all surveillance appliances as instances of this CVE manufactures removal work against devices no evidence implicates. The distinguishing test is per unit rather than per estate: produce, for each NVRmini2 in service, its firmware level and the vendor's answer on a fix - an asset register that records the device as 'segmented' or 'monitored' with no removal date has recorded the exposure rather than removed it. Precondition, and it is why this cannot end at a segmentation entry in the risk register: the exposure being scored is an unauthenticated archive upload that creates an arbitrary account, so restricting which segments can reach the device bounds who can send that upload but repairs nothing, and with no vendor fix recorded there is no update behind which that interim state resolves. Because active_exploitation is confirmed and the primitive is account creation, a unit that was reachable during the exposure window may already carry an attacker-created account and, through the CVE-2011-5325 chain the packet names, attacker-written files under the web root; isolating that unit afterwards does not clear it, and its accounts and configuration must be treated as attacker-controlled until it is removed.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet records patch_available: false, live_patch_available: false, live_patch_notes: null - no fixed build is recorded for this entry. CISA KEV-listed 2024-12-18, active_exploitation confirmed, poc_available true, CVSS 9.8, RWEP 79. Vector: 'NUUO NVRmini2 through 3.11 allows an unauthenticated attacker to upload an encrypted TAR archive, which can be abused to add arbitrary users because of the lack of handle_import_user.php authentication. When combined with another flaw (CVE-2011-5325), it is possible to overwrite arbitrary files under the web root and achieve code execution as root.' Citing gaps include AU-Essential-8-Patch, ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8 and NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.

new_control_requirements.name: DEVICE-MANAGEMENT-GATEWAY-CONFIG-ENDPOINT-AUTH-INPUT-NEUTRALIZATION
new_control_requirements.description: The NVRmini2's web interface is the device's configuration plane, and the defect is that plane's file-accepting endpoint making no authorization decision at all: the packet places the missing check in handle_import_user.php, which takes an encrypted TAR archive from an unauthenticated caller and imports users from it, so an attacker creates an arbitrary account without ever presenting a credential. Bound to this product, the control means a configuration endpoint that accepts an uploaded archive authorizes its caller before the archive is processed, and resolves and validates every destination path the import writes before the write executes - the chained CVE-2011-5325 step the packet names is exactly that second half failing, with archive content overwriting files under the web root and ending in code execution as root. This is also why the identification-and-authentication and identity-and-access gaps cited on this entry pass their attestations while the path stays open: the attacker never authenticates as any NVR user, so per-account authentication and privilege scoping are never consulted - the account model is bypassed rather than abused, and an attestation that every recorder administrator authenticates at login reads clean. Distinguishing test: from a segment with no operational need to administer the recorder, send an unauthenticated upload to the user-import handler on a bench unit and confirm it is refused before anything is imported or written to disk. Precondition, and it is decisive on this entry: endpoint-side authorization and path validation are properties a vendor fix would have to establish, and this packet records patch_available false with no live-patch path, so there is no update behind which this control resolves. The only operator-side lever left is reachability - restricting which segments can reach the management interface bounds the population that can send the upload, but leaves the endpoint fully exploitable to anything inside the permitted segment, and it is unavailable wherever the recorder's web interface must stay reachable for normal viewing and administration. Treat reachability restriction as a holding measure attached to a removal date, never as closure of the endpoint.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet vector: 'NUUO NVRmini2 through 3.11 allows an unauthenticated attacker to upload an encrypted TAR archive, which can be abused to add arbitrary users because of the lack of handle_import_user.php authentication. When combined with another flaw (CVE-2011-5325), it is possible to overwrite arbitrary files under the web root and achieve code execution as root.' CWE-306 (missing authentication), CVSS 9.8, RWEP 79, poc_available true, active_exploitation confirmed, CISA KEV-listed 2024-12-18. patch_available: false and live_patch_available: false, with live_patch_notes null. Citing gaps include NIST-800-53-IA-2 (Identification and Authentication), UK-CAF-B2 (Identity and access control) and NIST-800-53-CM-7 (Least Functionality).

CVE-2021-40407.name: Reolink RLC-410W IP Camera OS Command Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An authenticated attacker sends a crafted HTTP request to the camera's SetDdns network-configuration API with shell metacharacters embedded in the DDNS domain field, which the device passes unsanitized into a system-level command, achieving OS command execution.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low (authenticated device-admin session required)
attack_vector.complexity: low — a single crafted API request triggers the injection once authenticated
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — found and disclosed by Cisco Talos researcher Francesco Benvenuto. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the vendor firmware fix (released 2022-01-19) and disable remote admin access on cameras that don't need it
prevention.adequacy: A patch has existed for years, but consumer/SMB camera fleets commonly run unpatched firmware indefinitely, which is why this was still being exploited enough to warrant a 2024 KEV addition

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on SetDdns API calls containing shell metacharacters and monitoring outbound connections from camera management VLANs
detection.adequacy: Most deployments have no logging or monitoring on the camera's local management interface

response.what_would_have_worked: Isolate the camera, capture firmware/process state, reflash to patched firmware, and rotate any credentials used on the device
response.adequacy: Feasible once detected, but detection is the weak link for unmonitored IoT camera fleets

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Many affected cameras remain on end-of-life firmware years after the fix shipped; Essential 8's patch-application pillar requires an inventory and update mechanism that consumer IoT vendors typically don't provide.

CVE-2019-11001.name: Reolink Multiple IP Cameras OS Command Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An authenticated admin submits shell metacharacters in the addr1 field of the camera's TestEmail notification-test feature, which the device executes directly as an OS command running as root, giving the attacker full device control.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low (authenticated admin session required)
attack_vector.complexity: low — a single crafted form submission, fully scripted in the public PoC
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — found via the VDOO community disclosure effort and independent researcher mcw0. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply a vendor firmware fix if available for the specific model, or replace/isolate devices where no fix exists
prevention.adequacy: No confirmed firmware fix is documented for all affected models; CISA's required action itself defaults to discontinuing use if mitigation is unavailable

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on TestEmail configuration submissions containing shell metacharacters and monitoring for unexpected root-level process spawns on the camera
detection.adequacy: Consumer/SMB camera deployments almost never have this level of local monitoring

response.what_would_have_worked: Isolate and remove the device from the network, rotate any shared/admin credentials, and replace with a supported model
response.adequacy: Without a patch, response is limited to containment and replacement rather than remediation

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: No confirmed vendor firmware fix has been identified for all affected models, and CISA's own required action notes the product may be EoL/EoS; flaw remediation cannot be satisfied where no patch exists.

CVE-2018-14933.name: NUUO NVRmini Devices OS Command Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted request to upgrade_handle.php invoking the writeuploaddir command with shell metacharacters embedded in the uploaddir parameter, resulting in direct OS command execution on the NVR.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated network request)
attack_vector.complexity: low — public Exploit-DB PoCs and a Metasploit module fully automate exploitation
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — publicly disclosed by independent security researchers via Exploit-DB. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: No vendor patch exists for this end-of-life product line; the only effective prevention is removing the device from the network or isolating it on a dedicated management VLAN
prevention.adequacy: Patch-based remediation is not possible; CISA's required action is discontinuing use of the product, which many deployments have not done

detection.what_would_have_worked: Monitoring for unauthenticated requests to upgrade_handle.php outside scheduled firmware-upgrade windows
detection.adequacy: Most physical-security NVR deployments have no network monitoring layer capable of catching this

response.what_would_have_worked: Immediate device isolation and replacement, since no firmware fix can remediate the flaw
response.adequacy: Reflashing does not help — the flaw is present in all released firmware for this product line

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: NUUO has declared the NVRmini line end-of-life with no fix; flaw-remediation SLAs cannot be met where no vendor patch exists, so the required action is decommissioning rather than patching.

CVE-2024-55956.name: Cleo Multiple Products Unauthenticated File Upload Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated attacker imports a file that lands in the Cleo product's default Autorun directory; the platform's default configuration automatically executes files placed there as Bash or PowerShell commands, giving the attacker code execution on the host with no credentials required.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated network request)
attack_vector.complexity: low — the exploitation mechanic requires only placing a file where the platform's default configuration will auto-execute it
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — active exploitation first identified by Huntress threat-intelligence researchers. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the vendor patch (5.8.0.24+) and disable Autorun-directory auto-execution as a compensating control during the zero-day window
prevention.adequacy: Patching alone is insufficient for the zero-day window itself — disabling auto-execution of unauthenticated file drops was the only mitigation available before the fix shipped

detection.what_would_have_worked: Monitoring the Autorun directory for unexpected file creation and alerting on PowerShell/Bash child processes spawned by the Cleo Java process
detection.adequacy: Huntress-style managed detection caught this quickly, but self-monitored deployments without EDR on the MFT host missed it for days

response.what_would_have_worked: Immediate isolation of the Cleo host, hunting for the Malichus Java backdoor, and forensic review of all files landed via unauthenticated import since December 3, 2024
response.adequacy: Cl0p's campaign moved from initial access to data exfiltration quickly, so response speed was critical and many victims were compromised before detection

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Application hardening (disabling unnecessary auto-execution features like Autorun-directory command execution) would have closed this vector even before the vendor patch existed.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: The packet puts the flaw in a default: 'an unauthenticated user can import and execute arbitrary Bash or PowerShell commands on the host system by leveraging the default settings of the Autorun directory', on Cleo Harmony, VLTrader and LexiCom before 5.8.0.24. That gives a Cleo estate two states a compliance verdict must not collapse into one. The first is a host on 5.8.0.24 or later, where the defect is gone. The second is a host on an earlier build with the Autorun directory's auto-execution turned off by configuration — the execution trigger is closed, and the residual risk in that state is concrete for this product: the unauthenticated import path itself is untouched, so attacker-chosen files still land on the host, and the setting is a product default, so any operation that reapplies defaults (a configuration restore, a reinstall, an upgrade path that re-writes them) silently returns the host to full exposure with nothing in the version string to show it. The requirement is that the second state is reported as a distinct compensating-control state with a dated action item to reach the fixed build, and never as 'patched per SLA'. Distinguishing test: per Cleo host, report the product build and the Autorun auto-execution setting as two separate fields, and re-read the setting after every upgrade, restore and reinstall. An inventory whose only field is 'Cleo: remediated' cannot tell a 5.8.0.24 host from one whose mitigation was reverted by a default-restoring operation, and both read compliant. Precondition: disabling the auto-execution bounds the trigger — it does not remove the defect and it evicts nothing. The packet records active_exploitation as confirmed, so a host that ran a pre-5.8.0.24 build while reachable is not made clean by the configuration change; that host belongs on the response path, and the configuration state describes only what an attacker can do to it from this point forward.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: 'Cleo Multiple Products Unauthenticated File Upload Vulnerability', cwe_refs CWE-77, cvss 9.8, rwep_score 54, poc_available false. Vector: 'In Cleo Harmony before 5.8.0.24, VLTrader before 5.8.0.24, and LexiCom before 5.8.0.24, an unauthenticated user can import and execute arbitrary Bash or PowerShell commands on the host system by leveraging the default settings of the Autorun directory.' attack_vector: 'An unauthenticated attacker imports a file that lands in the Cleo product's default Autorun directory; the platform's default configuration automatically executes files placed there as Bash or PowerShell commands, giving the attacker code execution on the host with no credentials required.' cisa_kev true, kev_date 2024-12-17, active_exploitation confirmed. patch_available true; live_patch_available false (live_patch_notes null). Citing gaps closed here: NIST-800-53-CM-7 (Least Functionality), ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9 (Configuration management), AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening (User application hardening).

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Cleo Harmony, VLTrader and LexiCom sit at the trust boundary by function — the packet's attack path requires that an unauthenticated party can reach an instance and import a file to it — and the packet's outcome is arbitrary Bash or PowerShell execution on the host with no credential required. With active exploitation recorded as confirmed, upgrading to 5.8.0.24 removes the import-to-execute path and removes nothing the executed commands already wrote or started. The control's default therefore binds here: for any instance that was reachable while running a build before 5.8.0.24, export the configuration for review, rebuild the host from a known-good image onto the fixed build rather than upgrading over the running state, and rotate every credential the instance held — a file-transfer platform's stored credentials reach outward to the partners it exchanges with, so the rotation scope does not stop at this host. This is what the flaw-remediation gap recorded on this entry is pointing at: the exposure window opened before a fix existed, so 'the host is on 5.8.0.24' answers what an attacker can do next and says nothing about what already happened. Precondition, stated rather than implied: rebuilding is a response action for an instance that was reachable during the exposure window. It prevents nothing, and it is not a substitute for the fixed build — a rebuilt instance that comes back on an earlier build is exposed again immediately, since the packet records the vendor fix as available and no live-patch path. It also reaches only artefacts on the instance itself; anything the executed commands pushed to another host is outside what rebuilding this one can undo and needs its own scope.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet vector: 'In Cleo Harmony before 5.8.0.24, VLTrader before 5.8.0.24, and LexiCom before 5.8.0.24, an unauthenticated user can import and execute arbitrary Bash or PowerShell commands on the host system by leveraging the default settings of the Autorun directory.' attack_vector adds that the platform's default configuration 'automatically executes files placed there as Bash or PowerShell commands, giving the attacker code execution on the host with no credentials required'. cwe_refs CWE-77, cvss 9.8, rwep_score 54, poc_available false. cisa_kev true, kev_date 2024-12-17, active_exploitation confirmed. patch_available true; live_patch_available false (live_patch_notes null). Citing gaps closed here: NIS2-Art21-incident-handling (Incident handling) and NIST-800-53-SI-2 (Flaw Remediation).

CVE-2024-35250.name: Microsoft Windows Kernel-Mode Driver Untrusted Pointer Dereference Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A local attacker with code execution on the host issues a crafted IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY request to the Kernel Streaming Service driver, manipulating the RequestorMode field to bypass a security check so the driver dereferences an attacker-controlled pointer, elevating the calling process to SYSTEM.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low (requires existing local code execution as a standard user)
attack_vector.complexity: low — a public PoC and Metasploit module fully automate the elevation once local code execution is achieved
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — found by DEVCORE researchers and demonstrated at Pwn2Own Vancouver 2024. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the June 2024 Patch Tuesday cumulative update, which requires a reboot to take effect
prevention.adequacy: The patch is fully effective once applied and rebooted, but the reboot requirement is exactly what causes real-world deployment lag on servers with strict maintenance windows

detection.what_would_have_worked: EDR rules for anomalous DeviceIoControl calls to MSKSSRV.SYS and unexpected SYSTEM-level token elevation on endpoints
detection.adequacy: Most EDR products did not ship specific detections for this driver's IOCTL abuse pattern until after public PoC release

response.what_would_have_worked: Isolate the host, capture a memory image before reboot, and hunt for known PoC/Metasploit artifacts and unexpected SYSTEM processes
response.adequacy: Standard EoP response is effective but depends on detection triggering in the first place, which is the weaker link here

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: EU operators running unpatched Windows kernel-mode driver updates past the reboot-requiring maintenance window remain exploitable for privilege escalation; Art. 21 patch management must account for reboot-dependent kernel fixes specifically.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: This is a local elevation of privilege, and at CVSS 7.8 it competes for a patch slot against remotely reachable criticals - but it is KEV-listed with confirmed exploitation and a public PoC, and its function is to convert code execution an intruder already holds into SYSTEM. The KEV clock therefore has to cover the whole workstation and server fleet rather than an internet-facing subset, because the precondition (the attacker already runs code on the host) is satisfied by whatever phishing or commodity-malware step precedes it. No live-patch path is registered for this entry, so a host remains exploitable until the vendor update is actually installed on it - fleet completion, not deployment start, is the measure.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA KEV-listed 2024-12-16 with active_exploitation 'confirmed' and poc_available true; CVSS is 7.8 against an RWEP of 77. patch_available is true, live_patch_available is false, and live_patch_notes is null. The entry's attack path begins with a local attacker who already has code execution on the host.

new_control_requirements.name: KERNEL-EXPLOITATION-DETECTION
new_control_requirements.description: The escalation happens entirely inside one host: a process the attacker already controls sends a crafted IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY request to the Kernel Streaming Service driver with a manipulated RequestorMode field and comes back running as SYSTEM. There is no network stage to intercept and no privilege the defender can withhold - the caller is an ordinary user process right up until it is not, which is why least privilege is listed as insufficient for this entry. What remains is behavioural detection of the escalation itself: monitoring rules that fire within a minute on kernel-driver IOCTL sequences from unexpected callers and on a process token changing to SYSTEM without a legitimate service-start or elevation path, kept running on patched hosts as well as unpatched ones.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The entry's attack path is a local attacker with code execution on the host issuing a crafted IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY request to the Kernel Streaming Service driver, manipulating the RequestorMode field to bypass a security check so the driver dereferences an attacker-controlled pointer, elevating the calling process to SYSTEM. NIST-800-53-AC-6 (Least Privilege) is among the framework controls this entry already cites as insufficient.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Between the KEV listing and the moment a given host is running the fixed build, this entry has nothing to put in the mitigation column: it registers no live-patch path and no live-patch notes, so there is no interim vendor mitigation to report as active. Audit reporting must place every not-yet-updated host in the 'no mitigation, no patch' class rather than the 'mitigating pending patch' class a vulnerability-management process will otherwise accept, so residual exposure to a kernel LPE with confirmed exploitation is counted as a host list with a time-bound action, not described as remediation in progress.
new_control_requirements.evidence: For this entry live_patch_available is false and live_patch_notes is null, while patch_available is true; active_exploitation is 'confirmed' and it was CISA KEV-listed 2024-12-16.

CVE-2024-20767.name: Adobe ColdFusion Improper Access Control Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated attacker sends crafted requests to the ColdFusion admin API/PMS servlet to read arbitrary files on the server filesystem, exposed only because the admin panel itself was reachable from the internet.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated, but only reachable if the admin panel is internet-exposed)
attack_vector.complexity: high — CVSS AC:H reflects the nonstandard prerequisite that the admin panel be exposed to the internet
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — reported to Adobe via standard vendor disclosure. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply APSB24-14 and, independently, never expose the ColdFusion admin panel to the internet (restrict to internal/VPN access).
prevention.adequacy: Patching alone is insufficient if the admin panel remains internet-facing; network segmentation is the compensating control.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on any external source reaching CFIDE/adminapi or PMS servlet paths, and on reads of config files like password.properties.
detection.adequacy: Detection is a fallback; the primary control is not exposing the admin interface at all.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rotate any credentials/keys stored in exposed config files, review admin-panel access logs for prior exploitation, restrict panel access.
response.adequacy: Credential rotation is necessary once exposure is confirmed, since file read alone can leak reusable secrets.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: Boundary protection was insufficient — the vulnerability is only reachable because the ColdFusion admin panel was exposed to the internet in the first place.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: Vulnerability handling processes did not flag an internet-facing admin interface as an unacceptable exposure ahead of exploitation.

new_control_requirements.name: ENTERPRISE-ERP-MANAGEMENT-FUNCTION-AUTHENTICATION
new_control_requirements.description: The ColdFusion Administrator is the management surface on this entry, and the packet places the defect behind it: an unauthenticated attacker sends crafted requests to the ColdFusion admin API / PMS servlet and reads arbitrary files on the server filesystem, with no user interaction required. Bound to this product, the control means each administrative endpoint on that admin API decides its own caller's authorization before performing the file operation — an unauthenticated request is refused by the endpoint itself, not by whatever fronts it — and the Administrator surface is segmented so an untrusted caller cannot present the request in the first place. The packet makes that second half unusually concrete for a KEV entry: it states that exploitation requires the admin panel be exposed to the internet, so on a deployment where the Administrator answers only from an internal or VPN-reached segment, the published path has no origin to come from. The access-control gap recorded against this entry is cited precisely because no account is authenticated anywhere on this path: the attacker holds no ColdFusion administrator credential, so per-account access rules are never consulted, and an access-control attestation showing every ColdFusion administrator named, provisioned and reviewed passes cleanly while the read succeeds. Distinguishing test: from an untrusted network segment, issue unauthenticated requests to the admin API / PMS servlet paths on a staging ColdFusion instance and confirm each is refused before any file is read. Preconditions: the endpoint-side authorization is a property the vendor update establishes — this control states what to verify, it does not implement it. Removing internet reachability bounds who can send the request, and the packet gives that reachability as the exploit's stated prerequisite, but it does not repair the access control: any caller inside the permitted segment still reaches it, so a compromised internal host, a jump box or a partner-network path satisfies the precondition in full, and the measure is unavailable where the Administrator must stay reachable for operational reasons. And because the primitive is an arbitrary file read with exploitation confirmed, an instance that was internet-reachable before remediation has to have the secrets held in the files it could serve treated as read and rotated — neither the update nor the segmentation recovers what already left.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet fields for CVE-2024-20767 (Adobe ColdFusion Improper Access Control Vulnerability): cwe_refs CWE-284; vector 'ColdFusion versions 2023.6, 2021.12 and earlier are affected by an Improper Access Control vulnerability that could result in arbitrary file system read. An attacker could leverage this vulnerability to access or modify restricted files. Exploitation of this issue does not require user interaction. Exploitation of this issue requires the admin panel be exposed to the internet.'; attack_vector 'An unauthenticated attacker sends crafted requests to the ColdFusion admin API/PMS servlet to read arbitrary files on the server filesystem, exposed only because the admin panel itself was reachable from the internet.' cisa_kev true with kev_date 2024-12-16; active_exploitation confirmed; poc_available true; cvss 7.4; rwep_score 70. patch_available true, live_patch_available false, live_patch_notes null. Citing gaps recorded on this entry include ISO-27001-2022-A.5.15 (Access control) and NIST-800-53-SC-7 (Boundary Protection), alongside AU-Essential-8-Patch, NIST-800-53-SI-2, NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management and UK-CAF-B4.

new_control_requirements.name: SCANNER-PAPER-COMPLIANCE-TEST
new_control_requirements.description: This entry carries two independent conditions, and a scan verdict that checks only the first is paper compliance: the packet names the affected levels (ColdFusion 2023.6, 2021.12 and earlier) and separately states that exploitation requires the admin panel be exposed to the internet. Those two checks fail in opposite directions — a host at a fixed build whose Administrator still answers from the internet keeps every subsequent admin-surface defect on the published path, and a host below the fixed build that no untrusted network can route to is not on that path at all — so a vulnerability-management program that reports ColdFusion remediation as a build number has scored the wrong condition. The operational test this entry requires runs from outside: from each untrusted origin the panel could be reachable from, request the admin API / PMS servlet paths against every ColdFusion host and record whether anything answers, and report that result alongside the build level rather than in place of it. Precondition, and it is the one that makes this test worth anything: a reachability check proves only what is unreachable from the vantage point actually used. A host that one scan origin cannot route to may still answer through a cloud load-balancer rule, a partner link, a management VPN, or a hostname the scan never resolved, so a clean result from a single origin is not an exposure verdict — and an exposure check that has never returned a positive against a host known to be published is a broken check rather than a clean estate, and must be proven against a known-reachable instance before any absence is believed. The check also has to be applied retrospectively: the primitive is an arbitrary file read and exploitation is confirmed, so a host that answered externally at any point in the exposure window has to be handled as having served its files, which no version-based verdict will ever surface.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet fields for CVE-2024-20767: the vector states 'ColdFusion versions 2023.6, 2021.12 and earlier are affected by an Improper Access Control vulnerability that could result in arbitrary file system read' and, separately, 'Exploitation of this issue requires the admin panel be exposed to the internet'; attack_vector records an unauthenticated attacker reading arbitrary files via the ColdFusion admin API/PMS servlet, 'exposed only because the admin panel itself was reachable from the internet'. cisa_kev true with kev_date 2024-12-16; active_exploitation confirmed; poc_available true; cvss 7.4; rwep_score 70; patch_available true. The citing gaps this addresses are the remediation-and-handling ones recorded on the entry: AU-Essential-8-Patch (Patch operating systems), NIST-800-53-SI-2 (Flaw Remediation) and NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management (Vulnerability handling).

CVE-2024-50623.name: Cleo Multiple Products Unrestricted File Upload Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted POST request with a path-traversal filename to the Cleo Synchronization endpoint, writing an arbitrary file into the autorun directory that Cleo executes automatically, yielding remote code execution.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated)
attack_vector.complexity: low — CVSS AC:L, no special conditions beyond network reachability
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — identified via active-exploitation telemetry and reported to Cleo. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the fully-patched 5.8.0.24 release (not just 5.8.0.21) and restrict MFT appliance management/sync ports to trusted networks.
prevention.adequacy: The vendor's first patch (5.8.0.21) was itself insufficient, so patch-and-forget was not adequate — verification of full remediation was required.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Monitor the Cleo autorun directory for new files and alert on any child process spawned by the Cleo Java process.
detection.adequacy: Detection would have caught exploitation faster than the multi-day gap observed before mass compromise was identified.

response.what_would_have_worked: Isolate compromised MFT hosts, rotate all credentials handled by the file-transfer service, and hunt for ransomware staging activity given confirmed ransomware use.
response.adequacy: Given confirmed ransomware follow-on activity, rapid isolation is essential to prevent lateral movement from the compromised MFT host.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The initial vendor fix shipped in 5.8.0.21 was itself incomplete and was bypassed (tracked separately as CVE-2024-55956), so patch-SLA compliance alone did not close the exposure window.

DORA-Art10.gap: Financial-sector file-transfer exposure via MFT appliances was not adequately tested for resilience against this exploitation chain.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: This entry is the incomplete-patch sequence the control exists for, and the packet states it outright: the fix shipped in 5.8.0.21 was itself incomplete and was bypassed, tracked separately as CVE-2024-55956, with the products recorded fully patched only in 5.8.0.24. Applied to Cleo, the requirement has three parts. The remediation target is 5.8.0.24 or later, not the first fix — an estate that closed this CVE at 5.8.0.21 recorded remediation while the arbitrary-write path into the autorun directory stayed open through the December 2024 ransomware campaign. The scope is all three products the packet names: Harmony, VLTrader and LexiCom are each recorded affected before 5.8.0.21, so an inventory built around the Harmony servers leaves the VLTrader and LexiCom installs on the identical write path, and each must be enumerated and shown at the fixed build in its own right. And the verdict on a first fix in a sequence is 'unproven', not 'closed': the second CVE on the same primitive raises rather than lowers the expectation of a third, so a vendor's assertion that a build closes the flaw is evidence to be tested, not accepted, which is precisely what the packet's ICT-supply-chain gap says no framework requires. Completion is measured on the version the running Cleo service reports rather than on the installer having been executed. Distinguishing test: against a staging install left at 5.8.0.21, replay the unauthenticated crafted POST carrying a traversal filename at the Synchronization endpoint and confirm nothing is written into the autorun directory — a patch metric that went green at 5.8.0.21 passes every cadence attestation while the write path remains exploitable.
new_control_requirements.evidence: affected_versions: 'Harmony before 5.8.0.21 (initial fix incomplete)', 'VLTrader before 5.8.0.21', 'LexiCom before 5.8.0.21', 'fully patched in 5.8.0.24'; the NIST-800-53-SI-2 gap states the initial fix in 5.8.0.21 was itself incomplete and was bypassed (tracked separately as CVE-2024-55956), so patch-SLA compliance alone did not close the exposure window; the AU-Essential-8-Patch gap states patch-compliance was met by applying 5.8.0.21 yet that fix was bypassable and the appliances were mass-exploited by ransomware anyway; the ISO-27001-2022-A.5.21 gap states the ICT-supply-chain control does not require validating that a vendor's fix actually closes the flaw; the UK-CAF-B4 gap states system-security lifecycle management did not catch that the patched version remained exploitable; attack_vector describes an unauthenticated crafted POST with a path-traversal filename to the Cleo Synchronization endpoint writing into the autorun directory; CVSS 9.8, RWEP 74, poc_available true, cisa_kev true (2024-12-13); patch_available true, live_patch_available false, patch_required_reboot false, live_patch_notes null.

new_control_requirements.name: ENDPOINT-MGMT-DEPLOYMENT-CHANNEL-INTEGRITY
new_control_requirements.description: The primitive the packet describes is an arbitrary file write that lands in the Cleo autorun directory — a directory whose contents the product executes automatically — so on Harmony, VLTrader and LexiCom the directories the server holds and acts on are a privileged execution channel, not application data, and must be monitored as one. The requirement: file-integrity monitoring on the Cleo installation and on the autorun directory in particular, alerting on any file appearing there that does not correspond to a sanctioned operator action or a vendor update, together with alerting on child processes spawned by the Cleo service. The detection has to key on that shape and no other, because the shape is all the exploit produces. An attacker doing exactly what the packet describes sends a well-formed POST, causes a file to be written, and then lets the product run it through its ordinary autorun behaviour: nothing crashes, no exploit tooling signature is present on the host, and the execution is performed by the legitimate service. A rule keyed on service crashes, on known-bad hashes, or on anomalous inbound request volume would miss it; a rule keyed on unexpected writes into autorun plus the service's subsequent child process would not. This is also the control that retains value after 5.8.0.24 lands, since the upgrade closes the write path but removes nothing already written through it. Precondition: it requires the file-integrity and process telemetry to have been collected and forwarded off the server before the drop — against an actor holding code execution on that host, an alert stream retained only on the host is not evidence, and a rule authored afterwards against telemetry nobody was collecting produces nothing.
new_control_requirements.evidence: attack_vector: 'An unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted POST request with a path-traversal filename to the Cleo Synchronization endpoint, writing an arbitrary file into the autorun directory that Cleo executes automatically, yielding remote code execution'; affected names Cleo Harmony, VLTrader and LexiCom and records unauthenticated upload/download leading to RCE through the autorun feature; active_exploitation_notes records at least ten businesses' Cleo servers confirmed compromised via arbitrary file write leading to RCE, with activity dating to 2024-12-03 and spiking 2024-12-08; DORA-Art10 is cited on this entry as 'Detection of anomalous activities and ICT-related incidents'; patch_available true with the fully-patched level recorded as 5.8.0.24.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: The packet records confirmed compromise, not merely exposure: at least ten businesses' Cleo servers compromised via arbitrary file write leading to RCE, mass exploitation from 3 December 2024 spiking on 8 December by a Termite-affiliated ransomware actor, and a KEV entry flagged ransomware Known. Upgrading Harmony, VLTrader and LexiCom to 5.8.0.24 closes the write path and leaves intact whatever was written into the autorun directory and executed before the upgrade. So for any Cleo server that was internet-reachable while running a build at or below 5.8.0.21 during that window, the default response is exporting the configuration for review, rebuilding at 5.8.0.24, and rotating every credential configured on the server — not upgrading in place and closing the ticket on the version number. Preconditions this control must not be recorded without. The rebuild decision depends on establishing whether the server was reachable and at which build during the window; where that cannot be evidenced, it is treated as exposed rather than clean. Taking an MFT server out of service for rebuild interrupts the partner transfers it exists to perform, so the action needs a scheduled path with the transfer partners rather than being assumed free — an unscheduled rebuild requirement is the one most likely to be quietly downgraded to an in-place upgrade. And the rebuild removes server-resident persistence only: files the actor moved through the server, and any encryptor deployment that already reached hosts beyond it, are incident-response scope that rebuilding the Cleo server does not recover.
new_control_requirements.evidence: active_exploitation confirmed; active_exploitation_notes: 'Mass-exploited from early December 2024 (activity dating to Dec 3, spiking Dec 8) by a Termite-affiliated ransomware actor; at least ten businesses' Cleo servers were confirmed compromised via arbitrary file write leading to RCE. CISA KEV flags ransomware use as Known.'; attack_vector records the arbitrary file write into the autorun directory that Cleo executes automatically; affected_versions records the products affected before 5.8.0.21 and fully patched in 5.8.0.24; the NIST-800-53-SC-7 gap records the MFT appliances as directly internet-reachable with no additional network segmentation; the NIST-800-53-SI-2 gap records that patch-SLA compliance alone did not close the exposure window; patch_available true, live_patch_available false.

CVE-2024-49138.name: Microsoft Windows Common Log File System (CLFS) Driver Heap-Based Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A local attacker with low privileges triggers a heap-based buffer overflow in the CLFS kernel driver via crafted log-file structures, escalating to SYSTEM privileges — commonly used as a precursor step before ransomware deployment.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low (requires existing local code execution as a standard user)
attack_vector.complexity: low — CVSS AC:L, no special access conditions beyond local code execution
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — reported by CrowdStrike via standard vendor disclosure. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the December 2024 Patch Tuesday update promptly, since this was exploited as a zero-day before release.
prevention.adequacy: Patching is necessary but was not sufficient pre-disclosure; endpoint detection for anomalous SYSTEM escalation is a needed compensating control against the next CLFS zero-day in this recurring pattern.

detection.what_would_have_worked: EDR rules for unexpected SYSTEM-privilege child processes spawned from standard-user sessions and anomalous .blf file activity.
detection.adequacy: Behavioral detection is important given this is the fifth actively-exploited CLFS LPE since 2022 — signature-based defenses lag each new variant.

response.what_would_have_worked: Isolate hosts showing SYSTEM-token anomalies, hunt for ransomware staging or lateral movement toward domain controllers.
response.adequacy: Given CLFS LPE flaws are routinely chained into ransomware deployment, rapid isolation is critical to prevent domain-wide impact.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Standard OS patch-SLA cadence did not cover this flaw, which was already being exploited as a zero-day before the fix shipped.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch-operating-system control is necessarily reactive to a pre-disclosure zero-day exploitation window.

new_control_requirements.name: ACTIVELY-EXPLOITED-OS-LPE-REMEDIATION-WINDOW-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: CLFS is a kernel-mode driver of Windows itself, so the heap overflow the packet describes executes below every account boundary the endpoint estate is audited on: the attacker begins as a low-privileged local user who is legitimately entitled to be on the host and ends as SYSTEM. That is why AC-6 and UK-CAF-B2 are recorded as insufficient against this entry — constraining what the user's account may do never contains an escalation that does not consult the account model, and a least-privilege or identity-and-access attestation reads clean while the path stays fully open. The enforceable lever is the remediation window: drive the Windows update carrying the CLFS fix across the whole affected fleet on the clock that opened with the 2024-12-10 KEV listing rather than folding it into the next monthly rollup, and measure completion by each host's installed build rather than by "approved" or "downloaded" in the management console. The packet records a vendor patch and no live-patch path, so the fix does not reach the driver already resident in a running kernel — a host on which the update is pending completion still runs the vulnerable CLFS driver and counts as exposed, not remediated. Sequence the fleet by where a low-privileged foothold is most likely to already exist: the packet describes this escalation as a step commonly taken before ransomware deployment, so ordinary user endpoints where initial-access payloads land are the priority, not only servers.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: CWE-122 heap-based buffer overflow in the Windows CLFS driver. attack_vector: "A local attacker with low privileges triggers a heap-based buffer overflow in the CLFS kernel driver via crafted log-file structures, escalating to SYSTEM privileges — commonly used as a precursor step before ransomware deployment." CISA KEV 2024-12-10, active_exploitation confirmed, RWEP 81, CVSS 7.8, patch_available true, live_patch_available false. Citing gaps include NIST-800-53-AC-6 (Least Privilege) and UK-CAF-B2 (Identity and access control).

new_control_requirements.name: KERNEL-EXPLOITATION-DETECTION
new_control_requirements.description: Because the escalation runs inside a kernel driver and never consults the account model, the transition itself is the only place it becomes visible — and the packet states precisely what an exploit doing this emits: a low-privileged local process driving the CLFS logging path with crafted log structures, and then that process or its lineage acting with SYSTEM authority. Build the rule on that pairing: CLFS log creation or manipulation by a process running as an ordinary user, followed within a short window by a SYSTEM-authority token on that process or a SYSTEM-integrity child in the same lineage. Explicitly do not key it on the driver or host faulting — a working exploit corrupts the heap without crashing, so a crash-derived rule is blind on exactly the runs that succeed — and do not key it on the name or hash of a known tool, because the packet records a public proof-of-concept and a recompiled binary defeats that on the first attempt. Distinguishing test: detonate the available proof-of-concept on an instrumented staging host and confirm the rule fires on the log-manipulation-then-SYSTEM sequence, rather than confirming only that kernel telemetry is being collected. Preconditions: this detects, it does not prevent — the escalation completes, and the value is the dwell time removed before the ransomware step the packet names; and the alert must leave the host, because a process that has just reached SYSTEM can stop a local agent and clear a local log, so a rule whose only evidence stays on the compromised endpoint is silent at the moment it fires.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: attack_vector describes a low-privileged local attacker triggering the CLFS heap overflow "via crafted log-file structures, escalating to SYSTEM privileges — commonly used as a precursor step before ransomware deployment"; poc_available true; active_exploitation confirmed; CISA KEV 2024-12-10; CWE-122.

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated attacker sends a GET request (instead of POST) to a DNS/FTP reset-status endpoint to bypass authentication middleware, then injects shell metacharacters in the statusfile parameter to execute arbitrary OS commands.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated)
attack_vector.complexity: low — CVSS AC:L, no special conditions beyond crafting the HTTP request
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — publicly disclosed via researcher blog post. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the vendor patch (commit 1c0c6cb) and restrict CyberPanel's admin/API ports to trusted networks.
