new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: The packet describes exactly the conditions under which patch-in-place is the wrong default: a mass-exploited zero-day on an internet-facing gateway, CISA-flagged ransomware-associated, with the traversal chaining to CVE-2024-21887 command injection for unauthenticated RCE across the Connect Secure and Policy Secure fleet. The runbook for these appliances must therefore assume that any Connect Secure 9.x or 22.x or Policy Secure 9.x or 22.x unit reachable from the internet during the exposure window was compromised until evidence says otherwise, and default to capturing the running configuration for analysis, rebuilding the appliance onto the fixed release, and rotating every credential and certificate the device held or brokered — VPN user credentials and session material, the appliance's own administrative accounts, any directory or authentication-service account it bound with, and its device certificates. This is precisely what the two network-security gaps on the entry miss: NIS2's obligations and CAF's resilient-network expectations both treat the remote-access gateway as a trusted enforcement point, so once it reports the fixed version the framework's questions are answered — while an implant installed through the RCE chain survives the upgrade untouched and keeps the position the gateway grants. Preconditions, all three load-bearing: the rebuild only helps if the unit comes up on the fixed release and is rebooted onto it, since the packet records no live-patch path and a reboot requirement; a configuration restored wholesale from a backup taken after the exposure began can carry the attacker's changes back in, so it is reviewed rather than replayed; and rebuilding the appliance does nothing about access the attacker already converted into a foothold behind it, so the internal follow-on investigation and the credential rotation are part of this runbook rather than a later phase.

CVE-2024-21887.name: Ivanti Connect Secure and Policy Secure Command Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An administrator-context request (reachable unauthenticated when paired with CVE-2023-46805) injects OS commands into an ICS/IPS web-component endpoint, executing arbitrary code and enabling webshell deployment on the appliance.
attack_vector.privileges_required: high (authenticated administrator) alone, but effectively none when chained with the CVE-2023-46805 auth bypass
attack_vector.complexity: low — a single crafted request; public tooling automates the full unauthenticated chain
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — found in-the-wild by Volexity, coordinated with Ivanti/Mandiant. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the interim mitigation then the firmware fix and reboot, factory reset before upgrade, and reduce internet exposure of the gateway.
prevention.framework_requiring_it: CISA BOD 22-01 (KEV remediation, added 2024-01-10); CISA ED 24-01
prevention.adequacy: No patch existed at disclosure; interim mitigation and reset guidance carried the load, and patch alone did not clear implanted webshells.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Run the external Integrity Checker Tool, hunt for webshells under dana-na, and monitor for command metacharacters in web-component API calls.
detection.adequacy: The built-in ICT was subverted, so only the external tool plus network telemetry is trustworthy.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat the appliance as compromised: factory reset, rotate every secret/cert it held, and rebuild before returning to service.
response.adequacy: Post-RCE persistence required a full reset and credential rotation, not just an upgrade.

NIST-800-53-SI-4.gap: System monitoring does not natively cover a closed appliance whose own Integrity Checker Tool was subverted by attackers, so command-injection and webshell activity evaded the expected detection surface.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Network-security duties assume the gateway enforces trust, but command injection on the appliance itself runs inside the trust boundary the control relies on.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: Security-monitoring expectations were defeated because operators lacked telemetry from the appliance and the built-in integrity check was tampered with, hiding the command-execution stage.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The patch objective could not apply during a zero-day with no fix; interim mitigation plus factory reset were required beyond the normal patch SLA.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical-vulnerability management offers no route for a KEV appliance command-injection zero-day where only a temporary mitigation existed before a patch.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: For Ivanti Connect Secure 9.x/22.x and Policy Secure 9.x/22.x, the packet records the outcome of exploitation and not only the flaw: crafted requests to the ICS/IPS web components executed arbitrary OS commands, and webshells (GIFTEDVISITOR, WIREFIRE) were dropped across the fleet while this was still a zero-day. Applying the fixed release and rebooting — which the packet records as the only remediation path, with no vendor live-patch mechanism — restores the code but removes nothing an attacker wrote to the appliance during the exposure window. So for any ICS/IPS unit that was reachable between the 2024-01-10 KEV listing and the fixed release, the default runbook must be: export the configuration for review, rebuild the appliance from the vendor image onto the fixed release, and rotate every credential and certificate the appliance held or brokered — VPN user credentials, appliance administrator credentials, and any service account reachable through it — rather than patching in place and closing the item. The packet also removes the usual reassurance that would otherwise justify patch-in-place: the appliance's own Integrity Checker Tool was subverted by the attackers, so a clean on-box integrity result is not evidence the unit is clean, and 'ICT reports no changes' cannot be the basis for skipping the rebuild. Preconditions: the rebuild holds only if the unit returns on the fixed release — a rebuilt appliance restored to a pre-fix build is immediately re-exploitable through the same web-component path — and rebuilding does not retract credential material already exfiltrated, which is why rotation runs as part of the same action rather than as a later phase.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet records a mass-exploited zero-day, CISA-flagged ransomware-associated, KEV-listed 2024-01-10 with active_exploitation 'confirmed' and poc_available true; webshells named as GIFTEDVISITOR and WIREFIRE dropped 'across the fleet', and the path becomes fully unauthenticated RCE when chained with the CVE-2023-46805 auth bypass. patch_available true, patch_required_reboot true, live_patch_available false with live_patch_notes 'No vendor live-patch mechanism; remediation requires applying the fixed release and rebooting'. The AU-Essential-8-Patch gap states 'interim mitigation plus factory reset were required beyond the normal patch SLA', and the NIST-800-53-SI-4 gap states the appliance's 'own Integrity Checker Tool was subverted by attackers'.

new_control_requirements.name: FIREWALL-EGRESS-TELEMETRY-SEPARATE-TRUST-ZONE
new_control_requirements.description: Both monitoring gaps recorded on this entry are on-box-trust failures: the packet states operators lacked telemetry from the Ivanti appliance and that its built-in integrity check was tampered with, so the two records an operator would consult after the fact were under the control of an attacker who held command execution on the box. For ICS/IPS the requirement is that the appliance continuously forward web-component request logs, administrative-action logs and authentication logs to a collector in a separate trust zone — different management plane, different credentials, different authentication path — so the record of exploitation survives the appliance that was exploited. The detection built on that feed has to key on what the packet describes this exploit doing: crafted requests to ICS/IPS web-component endpoints that result in OS command execution; an administrator-context request against those endpoints with no corresponding successful administrator authentication, which is the shape the packet records when the flaw is chained with CVE-2023-46805 and becomes unauthenticated; and subsequent requests to web-accessible paths that are not part of the vendor image, which is how a planted webshell is reached. Rules written around appliance crashes, malware signatures, or named exploit tooling would miss every stage of that — the packet describes well-formed requests to legitimate endpoints and a webshell as the artifact, not a crash. Precondition: this only produces evidence if the off-box collection was already running before the intrusion, which for a closed appliance is exactly where it is least often configured; and once a unit is compromised its own on-box logs cannot be used to fill the gap retrospectively, because the attacker had command execution on the system that wrote them.
new_control_requirements.evidence: NIST-800-53-SI-4 gap: 'System monitoring does not natively cover a closed appliance whose own Integrity Checker Tool was subverted by attackers, so command-injection and webshell activity evaded the expected detection surface.' UK-CAF-C1 gap: 'Security-monitoring expectations were defeated because operators lacked telemetry from the appliance and the built-in integrity check was tampered with, hiding the command-execution stage.' Vector: a command injection in web components of Ivanti Connect Secure (9.x, 22.x) and Ivanti Policy Secure (9.x, 22.x) where an authenticated administrator sends specially crafted requests to execute arbitrary commands; the packet records the same path as unauthenticated when chained with CVE-2023-46805, used to drop webshells. active_exploitation 'confirmed'.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: The packet records this as exploited before any fix existed, with only a temporary mitigation available in the interim — the state that compliance reporting on ICS/IPS could not express, because it has no verdict between 'vulnerable' and 'patched per SLA'. For this CVE the requirement is that an Ivanti Connect Secure or Policy Secure appliance carrying the interim mitigation with no fixed release installed be recorded as its own state — mitigation active, no fixed build — with a dated action item attached, and that the state age against the 2024-01-10 KEV listing rather than resetting the clock on the day the mitigation was applied. Two consequences are specific to this entry. Any defect in the interim mitigation reopens a command-injection path that the packet already shows was being exploited at scale across the fleet, so the residual risk in state (b) here is not theoretical. And the mitigation says nothing about units already compromised: the packet records that a factory reset was required alongside it, so an appliance in this state that was reachable during the exposure window sits on the rebuild path at the same time and must not be closed on the mitigation record. This control is a reporting requirement, not a defence — it makes the residual exposure countable; what removes it is the fixed release and the reboot the packet records as required, with no live-patch alternative.
new_control_requirements.evidence: ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8 gap: 'Technical-vulnerability management offers no route for a KEV appliance command-injection zero-day where only a temporary mitigation existed before a patch.' AU-Essential-8-Patch gap: 'The patch objective could not apply during a zero-day with no fix; interim mitigation plus factory reset were required beyond the normal patch SLA.' Packet fields: cisa_kev true with kev_date 2024-01-10, active_exploitation 'confirmed', patch_available true, patch_required_reboot true, live_patch_available false.

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated attacker appends ?public=true to Joomla 4.x REST config/user endpoints; the improper access check returns the application configuration, including MySQL username, password, and host, which is reused for deeper access.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated REST request)
attack_vector.complexity: low — a single GET request; the exact URL is public and templated in scanners
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — reported to the Joomla project and fixed in 4.2.8. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrade to Joomla 4.2.8, restrict the /api endpoints, and rotate database credentials that may have been disclosed.
prevention.adequacy: The update fixes the access check, but any credentials leaked while exposed remain valid until rotated — patch alone leaves the secret compromised.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on requests to /api/index.php/v1/config/* and ?public=true patterns from untrusted sources.
detection.adequacy: Single-request disclosure is fast; detection is largely retrospective.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rotate the database password and any secrets in the config, and review DB access logs for use of leaked credentials.
response.adequacy: Without credential rotation, remediation is incomplete.

NIST-800-53-AC-3.gap: Access enforcement is exactly what failed at the application tier; the compensating layer (a network device) is not required to authenticate REST endpoints, so the improper access check leaks config regardless.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: Vulnerability-management duties address the CVE but not the downstream harm — leaked database credentials must be rotated, which patch-tracking alone does not trigger.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: Identity and access-control expectations assume endpoint authorization is enforced; a broken access check exposes secrets that then enable credentialed follow-on access.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The patch objective closes the endpoint but does not mandate rotating the database password that was disclosed while the site was vulnerable.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical-vulnerability management does not chain to secrets rotation, leaving leaked DB credentials valid after the Joomla update.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: The packet establishes the fact this control exists for: the unauthenticated request returns the application configuration including the MySQL username, password and host, and those credentials are reused for deeper access. The vendor fixed release stops the endpoint from serving that configuration; it does not invalidate a credential that has already been served. With a public PoC and confirmed in-the-wild exploitation against a version range as wide as 4.0.0 through 4.2.7, any site that was reachable before it was upgraded has to be treated as having disclosed those secrets. Bound to this entry the requirement is that the response for an exposed site is upgrade plus rotation, in that order and both recorded: rotate the database credential and every other secret carried in the site configuration, then review what that database account could reach and what was done with it across the exposure window, scoping the review from the site's own request logs rather than from whether anything looks wrong in the CMS — nothing needs to look wrong, because the exploit is a well-formed GET that returns 200. Note which half of this control the packet supports: it establishes configuration disclosure and credential reuse, not code execution on the web server, so the rebuild default the control specifies for a pre-auth RCE is not what this entry calls for; the config-exfiltration and credential-rotation half is, and it is the half the cited patching and vulnerability-management controls miss entirely, because their completion criterion is the installed version. Precondition: rotation closes the disclosed credential and nothing else. If the deeper access the packet describes was already used to establish something durable — an application account, or a change to stored content — rotating the database password does not remove it, and a site that cannot account for its exposure window needs its administrative accounts and content compared against a known-good state rather than being closed on the upgrade record.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: Joomla! 4.0.0 through 4.2.7; "An improper access check allows unauthorized access to webservice endpoints" (CWE-284). Attack path per the packet: "An unauthenticated attacker appends ?public=true to Joomla 4.x REST config/user endpoints; the improper access check returns the application configuration, including MySQL username, password, and host, which is reused for deeper access." CISA KEV-listed 2024-01-08 with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation; poc_available true; CVSS 5.3 against RWEP 68; patch_available true, live_patch_available false, live_patch_notes: "No vendor live-patch mechanism; remediation requires applying the vendor fixed release."

new_control_requirements.name: ENTERPRISE-ERP-MANAGEMENT-FUNCTION-AUTHENTICATION
new_control_requirements.description: Read past the product class in this control's name to what it requires — a management function that authorizes its own caller instead of inheriting a verdict — because the Joomla webservice layer is where this product takes its access decision and this CVE is that decision being made from the request. The packet has an unauthenticated caller appending ?public=true to the 4.x REST config and user endpoints, and the improper access check handing back the application configuration. Bound to this product, the control means each webservice endpoint authorizes its caller itself before the handler runs and before any configuration value is serialized into a response, rather than honouring a flag the caller supplies; and the REST API surface answers only from networks with an operational need for it, so an arbitrary internet client cannot present the request at all. The access-enforcement and identity-and-access controls cited on this entry are cited precisely because they do not reach this path: the attacker never holds a Joomla account, so per-account privilege scoping is never consulted, and an attestation showing every administrator authenticates with correctly scoped roles passes cleanly while an unauthenticated GET returns the database password. Distinguishing test: from a network with no operational need for the API, issue unauthenticated requests to the config and user webservice endpoints on a staging site with the caller-supplied public flag set, and confirm each is refused before the handler runs and before anything is emitted — testing that the administrator login requires authentication demonstrates nothing about this path. Precondition: the endpoint-side check is a property the vendor fixed release establishes; this control states what to verify, it does not implement it. On a site still in the 4.0.0-4.2.7 range, restricting reachability bounds who can send the request but closes nothing — anything inside the permitted set still receives the configuration — and that restriction is unavailable where the site's own integrations consume those endpoints from outside a trusted segment.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: Joomla! 4.0.0 through 4.2.7, improper access check allowing unauthorized access to webservice endpoints (CWE-284); the unauthenticated request path is ?public=true against the Joomla 4.x REST config/user endpoints, returning the application configuration. CISA KEV-listed 2024-01-08 with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation; poc_available true; CVSS 5.3, RWEP 68; patch_available true with live_patch_available false and remediation stated as applying the vendor fixed release. NIST-800-53-AC-3 (Access Enforcement) and UK-CAF-B2 (Identity and access control) are cited as insufficient on this entry.

CVE-2016-20017.name: D-Link DSL-2750B Devices Command Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A remote unauthenticated attacker sends a request to login.cgi with shell metacharacters in the cli parameter; the CGI passes it to a shell, executing arbitrary commands typically used to install botnet malware.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated, pre-login CGI)
attack_vector.complexity: low — a single crafted HTTP request; automated by IoT botnet loaders
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — public exploit since 2016, adopted by Mirai-class botnets. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Replace the end-of-life DSL-2750B (no fixed firmware exists), and where still deployed disable remote/WAN management and block login.cgi from untrusted networks.
prevention.adequacy: There is no patch, so KEV remediation can only be met by decommissioning or isolating the device — patching is impossible.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Monitor for login.cgi requests carrying cli= command payloads and for CPE fetching remote binaries.
detection.adequacy: Residential/edge CPE rarely has centralized logging, so detection coverage is thin.

response.what_would_have_worked: Remove the device from service and replace it; assume any exposed unit is or was botnet-infected.
response.adequacy: Reboot/reflash is only temporary on an unpatchable device that will be reinfected.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least-functionality guidance would disable remote management on the CPE, but the device exposes login.cgi by default and, being end-of-life, offers no patch — the durable control is decommissioning, which flaw-remediation processes do not schedule.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Network-security duties do not compel replacing or isolating an unpatchable, internet-facing end-of-life router that cannot be remediated in place.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Resilient-network expectations do not force retirement of legacy CPE whose vendor has issued no fix, leaving a permanently exploitable node on the estate.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The patch objective is unachievable because no patch exists; the control provides no fallback of mandated replacement for end-of-life hardware.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical-vulnerability management assumes a fix path; for an EOL device with an unauthenticated RCE it has no remediation to apply short of removal.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: Network-reachable end-of-life devices with no vendor patch path must be isolated and decommissioned within a bounded window; mandatory compensating segmentation applies until removal since no remediation exists.
new_control_requirements.evidence: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2016-20017

CVE-2023-41990.name: Apple Multiple Products Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A malicious iMessage attachment is processed without any user interaction; parsing a crafted font via the undocumented Apple-only ADJUST TrueType instruction corrupts memory and executes code, seeding the multi-stage Triangulation implant.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (zero-click; delivered via iMessage, requires no victim action)
attack_vector.complexity: high — bespoke exploit chain built by a capable actor, though victim-side it is fully automatic
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — discovered by Kaspersky researchers (Operation Triangulation). No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the Apple updates (iOS 15.7.8/16.3 and companions) promptly and enable Lockdown Mode for high-risk users to disable auto-processing of risky attachments.
prevention.adequacy: Patch closes the font flaw, but as a zero-click 0-day it was exploited before a fix existed; Lockdown Mode is the only pre-patch compensating control for targeted users.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Run Kaspersky's triangle_check against device backups and monitor for the anomalous post-exploit network/data-usage patterns of TriangleDB.
detection.adequacy: Mobile forensics is specialized and after-the-fact; real-time detection on the device is minimal.

response.what_would_have_worked: Update and reboot affected devices, and for confirmed targets consider device replacement plus credential/session rotation.
response.adequacy: Advanced implants may persist across the delivery chain; replacement is the conservative response for high-value targets.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation depends on Apple's patch, but a zero-click 0-day is weaponized before any patch exists; the SLA cannot cover the pre-disclosure exploitation window against high-value mobile targets.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Patch-management obligations do not address a client-side, zero-interaction mobile exploit delivered via iMessage, where there is no user action or perimeter control to interrupt the chain.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Resilient-system expectations assume a controllable OS update cadence, but mobile OS 0-days require rapid forced updates and lockdown postures the control does not mandate.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The operating-system patch objective is defeated by a 0-day with no fix at time of exploitation; the Essential Eight has no mobile zero-click compensating control.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical-vulnerability management provides no play for a targeted mobile 0-day; only enrolling high-risk users in Apple Lockdown Mode meaningfully reduces exposure, which the control does not require.

new_control_requirements.name: MOBILE-ZERO-CLICK-HARDENING
new_control_requirements.description: High-risk mobile users must operate in a reduced-attack-surface mode (e.g. Lockdown Mode) that disables automatic processing of untrusted message attachments, fonts, and link previews, closing the zero-click delivery path patch SLAs cannot outrun.
new_control_requirements.evidence: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-41990

CVE-2023-27524.name: Apache Superset Insecure Default Initialization of Resource Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An attacker takes one of Superset's well-known default SECRET_KEY values, signs a session cookie carrying an admin identity (e.g. with flask-unsign), and is authenticated as administrator, then abuses admin database/SQL features toward code execution.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated; the forged cookie substitutes for a login)
attack_vector.complexity: low — default keys are public and cookie forging is a one-liner with off-the-shelf tools
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — reported by Horizon3.ai. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Set a unique, high-entropy SECRET_KEY (superset_config.py or SUPERSET_SECRET_KEY) and upgrade to 2.1.0+, which refuses the default; rotate the key and invalidate existing sessions.
prevention.adequacy: Upgrading helps, but the true fix is changing the secret and rotating it; a version bump without a strong SECRET_KEY leaves prior forged sessions/data exposure risk.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Detect session cookies that validate against known default keys and anonymous-to-admin transitions in Superset logs.
detection.adequacy: Requires application-log visibility that many deployments do not centralize.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rotate SECRET_KEY and all database credentials reachable from Superset, invalidate sessions, and review for unauthorized queries/exports.
response.adequacy: Without key and credential rotation, an attacker who already forged admin access may retain footholds.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Secure-configuration/least-functionality controls do not, by default, verify that a shipped default cryptographic secret was changed at deployment; Superset started fine with the insecure default, so the control gap is unenforced configuration.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: Vulnerability-management duties cover the CVE but not the systemic root cause — inventorying deployments still running a known default SECRET_KEY, which needs config auditing rather than patch tracking.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: Identity and access-control expectations assume session tokens are unforgeable; a predictable signing key lets an attacker mint admin sessions, defeating access policy at the framework layer.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Application-hardening guidance does not specifically require changing framework default secrets, so the forgeable session key persists in hardened-looking deployments.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: Configuration-management as written does not mandate detecting and remediating unchanged vendor-default secrets, which is precisely what makes this session-forgery reachable.

new_control_requirements.name: FRAMEWORK-DEFAULT-SECRET-DETECTION
new_control_requirements.description: Deployment gating that fails any release shipping or running an unrotated framework default cryptographic secret (APP_KEY / SECRET_KEY and equivalents), which turn a leaked constant into session forgery and RCE.
new_control_requirements.evidence: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-27524

CVE-2023-29300.name: Adobe ColdFusion Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted serialized-object payload to a network-reachable ColdFusion endpoint; a gadget class (e.g. JdbcRowSetImpl) drives deserialization into arbitrary code execution, typically dropping a web shell.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated, network)
attack_vector.complexity: low — no user interaction and public gadget/Nuclei tooling exists
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — reported to Adobe / analyzed by ProjectDiscovery. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply ColdFusion 2018u17 / 2021u7 / 2023u1 (or later); restrict admin/AJAX endpoints and run ColdFusion under a low-privilege service account.
prevention.adequacy: Patch is decisive, but the exploitation window opened before many operators patched; segmentation alone does not block a request to the legitimate endpoint.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on new web shell files under CFIDE/webroot and on java-runtime processes spawning shells; inspect for deserialization gadget strings.
detection.adequacy: Detection catches post-exploitation but not the single deserialization POST that grants code execution.

response.what_would_have_worked: Isolate the host, hunt for web shells and persistence, rotate secrets accessible to the ColdFusion account, and rebuild if compromised.
response.adequacy: Effective only after the fact; ransomware association raises the cost of delayed response.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: A standard 30-day flaw-remediation SLA is far longer than the observed window between disclosure and mass web-shell deployment; an emergency out-of-band ColdFusion patch was required well inside any routine cycle.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical-vulnerability management catalogs the CVE but does not compel the emergency patch cadence a top-EPSS, ransomware-linked preauth RCE demands.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Baseline patch-management cadence does not force the rapid remediation an actively-exploited internet-facing app-server RCE requires; the KEV due date (2024-01-29) is tighter than typical SLAs.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: System-security/patch controls do not on their own detect the initial deserialization POST, which reaches a legitimate application endpoint and blends with normal ColdFusion traffic.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The 48-hour internet-facing patch target is frequently missed on legacy ColdFusion estates, leaving a preauth RCE exposed after public gadget chains dropped.

CVE-2023-38203.name: Adobe ColdFusion Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated attacker submits a serialized payload using a gadget class (JdbcRowSetImpl) that Adobe's deserialization denylist did not block, achieving RCE — a bypass of the fix for the related CVE-2023-29300.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated, network)
attack_vector.complexity: low — no user interaction; public gadget analysis and Nuclei tooling exist
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — ProjectDiscovery research. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply ColdFusion 2018u18 / 2021u8 / 2023u2 (or later); move deserialization to an allowlist and least-privilege the service account.
prevention.adequacy: The re-patch is decisive, but the denylist bypass shows blocklist-based mitigation is structurally fragile.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Watch for JNDI/RMI egress from the ColdFusion process and new web shells; flag gadget-class strings in requests.
detection.adequacy: Post-exploitation only; the triggering request looks like normal endpoint traffic.

response.what_would_have_worked: Isolate, hunt for web shells and persistence, rotate credentials, and rebuild on confirmed compromise.
response.adequacy: Reactive; ransomware linkage increases the cost of any delay.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The out-of-band Adobe fix for this denylist bypass landed days after disclosure; a routine flaw-remediation SLA cannot keep pace with a chained, actively-exploited preauth RCE.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least-functionality/deny-by-default at the object layer is exactly what Adobe's denylist attempted and failed — an allowlist-based deserialization policy, not a blocklist, is required, which this control does not by itself mandate.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical-vulnerability management does not compel the emergency re-patch that a fix-bypass zero-day demands within days.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Vulnerability-handling processes assume a single patch closes the issue; a denylist bypass requires re-remediation, which routine handling under-covers.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Network/patch controls do not detect a deserialization POST to a legitimate endpoint using a not-yet-blocked gadget class.

attack_vector.description: An attacker crafts an Excel file whose Number-format string contains Perl code; when a service embedding Spreadsheet::ParseExcel parses the file, the module passes the format string into a string eval and executes the attacker's code.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (attacker supplies a file; delivery is via email/upload to the parsing service)
attack_vector.complexity: low — public PoC exists; exploitation is triggered simply by the target parsing the file
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Barracuda/Mandiant incident response. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrade the embedded module to Spreadsheet::ParseExcel 0.66; inventory appliances for the bundled copy and disable/patch the eval path.
prevention.adequacy: Patch fixes the eval, but operators must first discover the module inside an appliance they cannot directly patch.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Sandbox inbound attachments and alert on the mail-parsing process spawning perl/shells or making outbound connections.
detection.adequacy: Behavioral detection is the main hope where the vulnerable library is embedded and unpatchable by the operator.

response.what_would_have_worked: Isolate affected appliances, hunt for SEASPY/SALTWATER-style implants, and follow Barracuda's guidance (replace rather than patch compromised ESG units).
response.adequacy: Barracuda advised device replacement for compromised ESG appliances, underscoring the limits of remediation.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation targets first-party software; a vulnerability in a transitive Perl dependency embedded in an appliance is invisible to patch cycles that track the appliance version, not its bundled modules.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical-vulnerability management rarely enumerates deep third-party library dependencies inside an appliance, so the vulnerable Spreadsheet::ParseExcel copy goes untracked.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Perimeter/network controls do not stop a malicious document delivered as a legitimate email attachment to a mail-security appliance whose job is to parse it.

DORA-Art-9.gap: ICT protection expectations do not by themselves compel SBOM-level visibility into embedded parsing libraries that a supply-chain-style document exploit abuses.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Application-hardening guidance focuses on macro/Office hardening on endpoints, not on server-side spreadsheet parsers that eval format strings.

new_control_requirements.name: TIER-3-DEPENDENCY-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: The vulnerable code here is a third-party Perl module, and the packet's exploitation path is 'a service embedding Spreadsheet::ParseExcel' — so an operator's exposure is a property of software it bought or built on, not of anything its own package list names. Bound to this CVE, the requirement is that the component inventory resolve to the depth at which Spreadsheet::ParseExcel actually sits — inside an appliance image, a container layer, or a vendor product that ingests spreadsheets — and record the module version, obtained from the supplier's SBOM or a direct written answer wherever the operator cannot inspect the image itself. Hold the scope there: the packet ties the string-eval sink to this module and the services embedding it, and provides no mapping from the defect into other spreadsheet-parsing code, so widening the sweep to every library in the estate that reads Excel files manufactures findings and rework against components no evidence implicates. The vulnerability-management and flaw-remediation controls cited as insufficient for this entry fail at their input rather than in their process: both act on an asset register, and a module bundled three levels down never reaches one, so the programme can be fully conformant and never open a ticket for a KEV-listed remote code execution it is running every day. Distinguishing test: for each product in the estate that ingests spreadsheets, ask whether it embeds Spreadsheet::ParseExcel and at what version, and require the answer to come from the supplier — because querying the operator's own package manager returns 'not installed' on a fully exposed system, which is the specific way this check gets recorded as clean. Precondition and limit: inventory is visibility, not remediation. The packet records a vendor fixed release as available and no live-patch mechanism, so every copy the inventory surfaces still has to be taken to that release by whoever controls it; for a bundled copy that is the embedding vendor, and until they ship it the operator's position is a known-exposed parsing path to be constrained, not a closed finding.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: 'Spreadsheet::ParseExcel version 0.65 is a Perl module used for parsing Excel files. Spreadsheet::ParseExcel is vulnerable to an arbitrary code execution (ACE) vulnerability due to passing unvalidated input from a file into a string-type "eval"', with the issue stemming from evaluation of Number format strings within the Excel parsing logic; attack vector records that the code executes when 'a service embedding Spreadsheet::ParseExcel parses the file'; CWE-95 and CWE-94; CISA KEV-listed 2024-01-02 with active_exploitation confirmed and poc_available true; RWEP 66 / CVSS 7.8; patch_available true and live_patch_available false, with the live-patch note recording that 'remediation requires applying the vendor fixed release'. ISO 27001:2022 A.8.8, NIST 800-53 SI-2 and DORA Art.9 are the framework controls recorded as insufficient for this entry.

new_control_requirements.name: MULTI-TRIGGER-DEPENDENCY-EXECUTION-POLICY
new_control_requirements.description: This CVE adds a dependency-execution trigger that no policy enumerates: document-parse time. The packet has the module passing a Number-format string out of an attacker-crafted Excel file into a Perl string eval, so the attacker's code runs when a service performs an ordinary data-processing operation on a business document — not when the dependency is installed, imported, or built. Every safeguard an estate is likely to hold is keyed to a moment that is never reached: ignore-scripts defaults and lockfile pinning govern install time, build sandboxes govern compile time, and none of them is consulted when a mail-handling service, a reporting job, or an upload handler opens the attachment. Applied here, the policy must list document/data-parse time alongside install, import and build time as an execution trigger, and every service that feeds files into Spreadsheet::ParseExcel must run under an identity scoped to that job alone — no credentials the parse itself does not need, no interactive shell, and constrained egress — so that code executed out of a format string lands somewhere that cannot reach the estate's secrets or call outward. The user-application-hardening control cited as insufficient here is aimed at a different machine entirely: it governs macro, OLE and add-in behaviour in an Office client on a user's endpoint, while this code executes inside a server-side Perl process with that service's privileges, on a file no person may ever open. Distinguishing test: feed a file whose Number-format string carries a Perl payload to a staging instance of each service that parses spreadsheets through this module, and confirm from the service account's own context that the payload can neither read credentials nor open an outbound connection — an attestation covering endpoint Office hardening passes cleanly while the server-side parse path executes attacker code unimpeded. Precondition: this constrains what the executed code can reach; it does not stop the execution. The packet records a vendor fixed release with no live-patch path, so every copy still has to be taken to that release, and the least-privilege identity is worth nothing on a service whose parse job simply inherited the application's main credentials — which is the normal case, and the thing to change first.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: the flaw stems from 'the evaluation of Number format strings (not to be confused with printf-style format strings) within the Excel parsing logic', passing unvalidated input from a file into a string-type eval; attack vector records that an attacker crafts an Excel file whose Number-format string contains Perl code and the module executes it when a service embedding Spreadsheet::ParseExcel parses the file; CWE-95 and CWE-94; KEV 2024-01-02, active_exploitation confirmed, poc_available true; patch_available true, live_patch_available false, remediation is applying the vendor fixed release. AU Essential Eight user application hardening, NIS2 Art.21 security of network and information systems, and UK CAF B4 (System security) are the framework controls recorded as insufficient for this entry.

CVE-2023-7024.name: Google Chromium WebRTC Heap Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A remote attacker serves a crafted HTML page that drives WebRTC into a heap buffer overflow, corrupting the heap in the renderer to gain code execution in the browser process context.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (remote; requires the victim to visit a page)
attack_vector.complexity: low for the victim (a single page visit), though exploit development is sophisticated and was used in targeted attacks
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Google Threat Analysis Group. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Enforce Chrome auto-update to 120.0.6099.129+ and require browser relaunch across the fleet; deploy site-isolation and reduced attack surface for high-risk users.
prevention.adequacy: The update fixes the flaw only once every Chrome process is restarted; unrestarted browsers stay vulnerable.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Endpoint telemetry on renderer crashes and anomalous child processes from the browser; block/monitor known malicious infrastructure.
detection.adequacy: Client-side memory-corruption exploitation is hard to detect at the network layer; the delivering page looks like normal web traffic.

response.what_would_have_worked: Force-update and relaunch browsers, investigate targeted users for follow-on implants, rotate credentials entered in-browser.
response.adequacy: Reactive; targeted-operation use means high-value users may already be compromised.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: A monthly or slower browser-update SLA leaves a client-side zero-day exploitable via any web page; auto-update must be enforced, which flaw-remediation policy often does not treat as urgent for endpoints.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical-vulnerability management tends to prioritize server/appliance patches; a browser heap-overflow zero-day needs endpoint-fleet-wide forced restart to take effect.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Baseline patch cadence does not force the near-immediate browser relaunch across a fleet that a drive-by client zero-day requires.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Endpoint/patch controls do not detect exploitation delivered as ordinary web content to a legitimately running browser.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The application-patch target for browsers is frequently unmet on managed fleets, and 'patched' Chrome is not protected until every process is restarted.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: This is a heap buffer overflow in the WebRTC component of Chrome/Chromium reachable from a crafted HTML page, so the delivery path is ordinary browsing and every endpoint that renders web content is in the exploit population — the update ring is the whole of the remediation, and any ring that stages security-channel browser updates behind a validation window is holding a fleet on exploitable code while the pages that exploit it are already being served. Scope the ring from the packet's affected field rather than from the vector's headline product: it records Google Chrome / Chromium and downstream Chromium browsers, and the exploitation notes state the flaw affects the broad Chromium browser base, so every Chromium-based browser deployed in the estate has to be covered at that product's own fixed build. An estate standardised on a downstream Chromium browser will report clean if the check keys only on Chrome reaching 120.0.6099.129. Measure completion on the build the running browser process is executing, not on the installed package: patch_required_reboot is false, which means no machine reboot is required, not that the fix is live on deployment — a browser process that has been running since before the update keeps executing the pre-fix WebRTC code until it is relaunched, which is what the packet's own gap statements mean by needing a fleet-wide forced restart. Precondition: the ring reaches only browsers under management policy. A per-user or otherwise unmanaged Chromium install on a managed host is outside the ring, and the ring's compliance percentage will not show it; that copy is remediated by bringing it under management or removing it, not by the ring.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet vector: 'Heap buffer overflow in WebRTC in Google Chrome prior to 120.0.6099.129 allowed a remote attacker to potentially exploit heap corruption via a crafted HTML page.' affected: 'Google Chrome / Chromium (and downstream Chromium browsers) — heap buffer overflow in the WebRTC component reachable from a crafted HTML page'; affected_versions: 'Google Chrome prior to 120.0.6099.129'. active_exploitation_notes: exploited in the wild as a Chrome zero-day found by Google's Threat Analysis Group, 'fixed in Chrome 120.0.6099.129/130; affects the broad Chromium browser base'. cisa_kev true, kev_date 2024-01-02, active_exploitation 'confirmed', patch_available true, patch_required_reboot false, live_patch_available false with live_patch_notes 'No vendor live-patch mechanism; remediation requires applying the vendor fixed release.' Cited gaps: NIST-800-53-SI-2 'auto-update must be enforced, which flaw-remediation policy often does not treat as urgent for endpoints'; ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8 'a browser heap-overflow zero-day needs endpoint-fleet-wide forced restart to take effect'; NIS2-Art21-patch-management 'Baseline patch cadence does not force the near-immediate browser relaunch across a fleet that a drive-by client zero-day requires.'

new_control_requirements.name: SCANNER-PAPER-COMPLIANCE-TEST
new_control_requirements.description: For this CVE the paper-compliance trap is specific and the packet states it outright: a scan that reads the installed Chrome/Chromium version off disk and reports the endpoint patched at 120.0.6099.129 is measuring the wrong thing, because the browser process that has been running since before the update is still executing the vulnerable WebRTC code. The operational test that distinguishes real remediation: on a sample of endpoints, compare the build the running browser process itself reports against the fixed build, and treat any host whose on-disk build is at or above the fix while the running process reports lower as exposed rather than remediated. Run the same comparison for every Chromium-based browser the estate deploys, since the packet places the defect in Chromium's WebRTC component and not solely in Chrome. This matters more here than for a server patch because of how endpoints are used — a laptop that is suspended and resumed for weeks without the browser ever being closed is the normal case, not the exception, so the population of 'installed but not yet running the fix' endpoints does not drain on its own. Precondition: this test measures state, it does not change it. It tells the operator which endpoints still owe a browser relaunch and gives nothing on a host where the relaunch is never forced; enforcing the relaunch is the update-ring control's job, not this one. It is also not an exploitation check — the packet's system-security gap notes the attack arrives as ordinary web content to a legitimately running browser, so a clean version comparison says nothing about whether a page already exploited the endpoint during the exposure window.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet gap AU-Essential-8-Patch: 'The application-patch target for browsers is frequently unmet on managed fleets, and "patched" Chrome is not protected until every process is restarted.' Corroborating packet fields: patch_required_reboot false; live_patch_available false with live_patch_notes 'No vendor live-patch mechanism; remediation requires applying the vendor fixed release'; affected 'Google Chrome / Chromium (and downstream Chromium browsers)'; fixed build per vector 'prior to 120.0.6099.129'. Gap UK-CAF-B4: 'Endpoint/patch controls do not detect exploitation delivered as ordinary web content to a legitimately running browser.'

CVE-2023-49897.name: FXC AE1021, AE1021PE OS Command Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An attacker who can authenticate to the router (often via default/weak credentials) submits a crafted value to a management parameter that is passed to an OS shell without sanitization, executing arbitrary commands and typically installing a Mirai-variant bot.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low (authenticated to the device management interface)
attack_vector.complexity: low — a single crafted authenticated request; weaponized by an automated botnet
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Akamai SIRT. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply FXC fixed firmware, change default credentials, and remove the management interface from untrusted networks.
prevention.adequacy: Firmware fixes the injection, but unmanaged edge devices are seldom updated, so credential hygiene and exposure reduction are essential compensations.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Monitor router egress for ELF payload retrieval and DDoS beaconing; alert on management-plane logins from unexpected sources.
detection.adequacy: Most operators lack telemetry on CPE routers, so conscription is noticed only via outbound abuse.

response.what_would_have_worked: Factory-reset and re-flash, rotate credentials, and block C2 infrastructure.
response.adequacy: Effective per-device but hard to scale across a dispersed CPE fleet.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SOHO/edge routers like the AE1021 rarely receive centrally managed patches, so a firmware fix does not reach the exposed fleet within the KEV window.

NIST-800-63B-rev4.gap: Because exploitation requires a login, weak/default/reused router credentials directly enable the injection; authenticator strength for embedded-device admin accounts is routinely unaddressed.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Network-security baselines seldom cover edge CPE devices whose management plane is reachable and whose command injection turns a valid login into RCE.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Proactive security-event discovery does not extend to consumer-grade routers, so botnet conscription goes unnoticed until the device emits DDoS traffic.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch targets assume managed IT assets; unmanaged FXC edge routers fall outside the patch program entirely.

CVE-2023-47565.name: QNAP VioStor NVR OS Command Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An attacker authenticated to a VioStor NVR submits a crafted value to a web-interface field that reaches an OS shell unsanitized, executing arbitrary commands and typically installing a Mirai-variant bot for DDoS.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low (authenticated to the NVR web interface, often via default/weak credentials)
attack_vector.complexity: low — one crafted authenticated request; automated botnet weaponization
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Akamai SIRT. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrade to QVR 5.0.0+ (or retire the EoL device), change default credentials, and remove the NVR from internet exposure.
prevention.adequacy: Because the affected models are legacy, replacement/segmentation is often the only real fix; patch alone may be unavailable for the oldest units.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Monitor NVR egress for payload retrieval and DDoS beaconing; alert on management logins from unexpected sources.
detection.adequacy: Standalone appliances usually lack telemetry; abuse is seen only downstream.

response.what_would_have_worked: Isolate and re-image or decommission the NVR, rotate credentials, and block C2.
response.adequacy: Reactive; EoL status makes long-term remediation a replacement decision.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The fix requires migrating off end-of-life QVR 4.x to QVR 5.0.0+, which is a device-replacement/upgrade effort a flaw-remediation SLA cannot satisfy within the KEV window.

NIST-800-63B-rev4.gap: Exploitation requires a login, so weak/default/reused NVR admin credentials are the enabling condition; authenticator strength on legacy appliances is unmanaged.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Network-security baselines rarely inventory internet-exposed NVRs, leaving their reachable management plane open to command injection.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Vulnerability management tends to overlook end-of-life video-surveillance appliances that no longer receive routine updates.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Security-event discovery does not extend to standalone NVRs, so botnet conscription surfaces only as outbound DDoS abuse.

CVE-2023-6448.name: Unitronics Vision PLC and HMI Insecure Default Password Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated attacker with network reachability to an exposed Unitronics PLC/HMI authenticates using the publicly known factory default password and gains administrative control, enabling defacement, logic changes, or process disruption.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated network access; the default credential is public)
attack_vector.complexity: low — no exploit code needed, just the known default password and a reachable management port
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — coordinated disclosure / CISA-EPA incident response. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Change the default password (upgrade VisiLogic to 9.9.00+), remove the PLC/HMI from internet exposure, and place it behind a segmented OT boundary/VPN.
prevention.adequacy: Changing the credential closes the primary path, but network exposure of the OT management protocol must also be eliminated.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on external logins to PCOM/TCP 20256 and on unexpected PLC state changes; monitor HMI defacement.
detection.adequacy: Many OT networks lack monitoring on the management protocol, so intrusion is noticed only after disruption.

response.what_would_have_worked: Restore known-good PLC logic, rotate all device credentials, and remove internet exposure; coordinate with sector CISA/EPA guidance for water utilities.
response.adequacy: Effective but safety-critical processes may be disrupted before response begins.

NIST-800-53-IA-2.gap: Identification/authentication controls that permit a shared factory default password to remain active provide no real assurance; the device ships pre-authenticated to anyone who knows the default.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: Least-privilege is meaningless when the sole administrative account uses a universally known default credential reachable from the network.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Exposing an OT management protocol (PCOM/20256) to the internet is the enabling condition; network-security baselines frequently omit OT/ICS segmentation for small PLC estates.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: Identity and access control for OT devices seldom enforces mandatory default-credential change on commissioning, leaving critical-service PLCs trivially accessible.

AU-ISM-1546.gap: Privileged/default-account controls are inconsistently applied to embedded OT devices, so the factory password persists on safety-relevant equipment.

new_control_requirements.name: OT-DEFAULT-CREDENTIAL-ELIMINATION
new_control_requirements.description: No internet-reachable OT device (PLC/HMI/RTU) may ship or run with a vendor-default or blank administrative credential; enforce mandatory credential rotation at commissioning and segment the OT management plane from untrusted networks.
new_control_requirements.evidence: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-6448

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated attacker sends a path-traversal HTTP request to Qlik Sense that yields an anonymous session, allowing further requests to unauthorized backend endpoints; combined with CVE-2023-41265 this reaches remote code execution.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated, network)
attack_vector.complexity: low — public Nuclei template and ZeroQlik chain exist; used at scale by Cactus ransomware
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Praetorian research. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the Qlik Sense patch for the relevant train (Aug 2023 IR / May 2023 Patch 4 / Feb 2023 Patch 8 / Nov 2022 Patch 11 / Aug 2022 Patch 13) and restrict the Qlik proxy from untrusted networks.
prevention.adequacy: Patching is decisive, but the medium base score led many to deprioritize it despite its role as the chain's entry point.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on anonymous-session creation and traversal-style request paths against the Qlik proxy; monitor Qlik services spawning shells.
detection.adequacy: The auth-bypass request looks like ordinary HTTP; without app-aware logging the initial access is invisible.

response.what_would_have_worked: Isolate the Qlik host, hunt for the CVE-2023-41265 follow-on and Cactus tooling, rotate the Qlik service-account credentials, and rebuild if compromised.
response.adequacy: Reactive; ransomware chaining means fast containment is critical.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The path-traversal fix shipped as scattered per-release patches across many Qlik Sense trains; a single flaw-remediation SLA struggled to cover an estate on mixed patch levels before ransomware weaponization.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: A boundary/WAF permitting the request to the legitimate Qlik Sense endpoint does not stop a traversal that generates an anonymous session; the request is valid at the network layer.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical-vulnerability management under-prioritized a CVSS-6.5 path traversal that becomes critical only when chained, so patching lagged the exploited chain.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: Severity-driven vulnerability programs deprioritize a medium-rated auth-bypass primitive that is the first link of an RCE ransomware chain.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: Security monitoring often lacks visibility into anonymous-session creation inside the BI application, so the initial-access step goes undetected.

attack_vector.description: A remote attacker tunnels an HTTP request inside a raw HTTP request so the Qlik backend repository app executes it under the service account, escalating privileges; combined with the CVE-2023-41266 anonymous session it yields unauthenticated remote code execution.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low as scored, but effectively none when chained with CVE-2023-41266's anonymous session
attack_vector.complexity: low — public ZeroQlik chain; scope-change (S:C) escalation to the service account
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Praetorian research. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the fixed Qlik Sense train (and the follow-up for CVE-2023-48365), least-privilege the Qlik service account, and restrict the proxy from untrusted networks.
prevention.adequacy: The first patch was incomplete, so operators had to re-remediate; least-privilege limits blast radius of the service-account RCE.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Deploy request-smuggling-aware inspection and alert on Qlik services spawning shells or tunneled backend requests.
detection.adequacy: Standard WAFs may not normalize the ambiguous raw request that carries the tunneled payload.

response.what_would_have_worked: Isolate the host, hunt for Cactus tooling and persistence, rotate the service-account credentials, and rebuild on compromise.
response.adequacy: Reactive; the RCE runs with service-account rights, so credential rotation and host rebuild are essential.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Qlik's first fix was incomplete (superseded by CVE-2023-48365), so a single flaw-remediation cycle left the RCE chain reachable; re-remediation was required.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: Boundary/WAF inspection does not reliably normalize the ambiguous raw HTTP request that drives the tunneling, so the smuggled request passes through to the backend.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: Least-privilege gaps let the Qlik service account (under which tunneled requests execute) run with broad rights, amplifying the RCE into full host compromise.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: Vulnerability programs treat the fix as complete after one patch, but the incomplete-fix follow-up (CVE-2023-48365) required a second remediation the process did not anticipate.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: CAF Objective C security monitoring does not mandate HTTP-request-smuggling-aware detection, so the tunneled request that reaches the backend and yields service-account RCE is not surfaced.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight patch-application maturity treats the first Qlik advisory as complete, but the incomplete-fix follow-up (CVE-2023-48365) required a second remediation cycle the model does not anticipate.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical vulnerability management closed the first advisory but not the request-smuggling primitive the incomplete fix left reachable until the follow-up patch.

new_control_requirements.name: ENTERPRISE-ERP-MANAGEMENT-FUNCTION-AUTHENTICATION
new_control_requirements.description: Qlik Sense Enterprise for Windows terminates the raw HTTP request in a front tier and hands work to the backend server hosting the repository application, and this CVE is that split failing: the packet describes an attacker tunneling an HTTP request inside the raw HTTP request so the backend executes it, under the service account, with elevated privilege. The inner request never passes the front tier's authorization decision, so the backend acts on a caller nothing authorized. Bound to this product, the control means the repository application's privileged operations authorize their own caller rather than inheriting a verdict from the tier that fronts them, and the Qlik front-end surface answers only from segments with an operational need to reach it, so an untrusted caller cannot present a raw request to that tier at all. The least-privilege gap recorded against this entry does not close this path: the tunneled request runs under the Qlik service account, and chained with the CVE-2023-41266 anonymous-session flaw the packet names, the attacker holds no Qlik account, so per-user privilege scoping is never consulted and an AC-6 attestation passes cleanly while the path stays open. Distinguishing test: from a segment with no business need to reach the analytics platform, send a staging deployment a raw request carrying a second, tunneled request aimed at a privileged repository endpoint and confirm the backend refuses it before the operation runs, rather than relying on the front tier having stripped it. Precondition: consistent request parsing between the two tiers is a property the vendor fixed release establishes — this control states what to verify and where to segment, it does not repair the parser. Until the fixed build is in place, restricting reachability bounds who can send the raw request but leaves the tunneling path fully exploitable to anything inside the permitted segment, and it is unavailable where the deployment must serve a broad user population.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: CWE-444; an HTTP Request Tunneling flaw in Qlik Sense Enterprise for Windows allowing a remote attacker to elevate privilege by tunneling HTTP requests in the raw HTTP request, sending requests that get executed by the backend server hosting the repository application. The packet's attack path adds that execution occurs under the service account and that, combined with the CVE-2023-41266 anonymous session, it yields unauthenticated remote code execution. CISA KEV-listed 2023-12-07, active_exploitation confirmed, poc_available true, RWEP 70 against CVSS 9.9.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: The packet names five maintenance tracks with a different fixed build on each — August 2023 IR, May 2023 Patch 4, February 2023 Patch 8, November 2022 Patch 11, August 2022 Patch 13 — so on this CVE the SLA's failure mode is a mis-measured deadline rather than a missed one. A server sitting on November 2022 Patch 10 is current by its own track's reckoning and still carries the tunneling path. Applied here, the remediation clock opened by the 2023-12-07 KEV listing is measured per deployment against the fixed build named for that deployment's own track, not against whether the deployment is up to date within its track. The packet records a vendor fixed release and no live-patch mechanism, so nothing closes this without taking each deployment through the update; during that window the compensating half of the control is restricting who can reach the Qlik front end, which bounds the attacker population and does not close the flaw. Distinguishing test: produce, per Qlik Sense Enterprise deployment, its maintenance track and its installed build, and compare each against the fixed build named for that track — an estate whose patch report shows every server current has not answered this question. And because active exploitation is confirmed and the packet has the tunneled request executing under the service account, a deployment reachable during the exposure window is not remediated by the update alone: the update closes the path but removes nothing already done through it, so such a server needs forensic triage and service-account credential rotation rather than being closed on the patch.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: affected versions are May 2023 Patch 3 and earlier, February 2023 Patch 7 and earlier, November 2022 Patch 10 and earlier, and August 2022 Patch 12 and earlier; the fix is recorded as August 2023 IR, May 2023 Patch 4, February 2023 Patch 8, November 2022 Patch 11, and August 2022 Patch 13. CISA KEV-listed 2023-12-07, active_exploitation confirmed, poc_available true, RWEP 70 against CVSS 9.9. patch_available true, live_patch_available false, live_patch_notes: no vendor live-patch mechanism, remediation requires applying the vendor fixed release. The packet's attack path records execution under the service account.

CVE-2023-33107.name: Qualcomm Multiple Chipsets Integer Overflow Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A local, already-present unprivileged application issues a crafted IOCTL to the Adreno GPU (kgsl) driver; an integer overflow during shared-virtual-memory assignment corrupts kernel memory and escalates privileges, typically as one stage of a mobile exploit chain.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low (local; requires code execution as an unprivileged app on the device)
attack_vector.complexity: high — reliable kernel memory-corruption exploitation is sophisticated and was used in targeted attacks
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Qualcomm/Google TAG/Project Zero indications of in-the-wild use. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the OEM security update carrying the December 2023 Qualcomm patch level and reboot; restrict sideloading so a malicious app cannot reach the driver.
prevention.adequacy: Patch is decisive but gated on the OEM/carrier update chain; devices without an available build stay exposed.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Mobile EDR/attestation flagging anomalous kgsl IOCTL usage or unexpected privilege transitions.
detection.adequacy: On-device detection of a kernel LPE is limited, especially within a targeted spyware chain.

response.what_would_have_worked: Update firmware, re-image high-risk devices, and investigate for follow-on implants on targeted users.
response.adequacy: Reactive; targeted use means compromise may precede any available OEM patch.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The fix must traverse Qualcomm to Android OEM to carrier before reaching devices; this multi-hop patch chain routinely exceeds any flaw-remediation SLA, leaving the LPE exploitable for months.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least-functionality does not constrain a legitimate GPU IOCTL surface (kgsl) that any installed app can reach; the privileged driver interface is exposed by design.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Vulnerability management for mobile fleets depends on OEM update availability the organization does not control, so a known-exploited kernel LPE stays open on unpatched handsets.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Patch-management cadence cannot force firmware/driver updates onto devices whose vendor has not yet shipped the OEM build, undermining timely remediation of a KEV kernel flaw.

AU-ISM-1546.gap: Mobile-device hardening controls rarely account for a GPU-driver LPE that undoes app-sandbox isolation once a malicious app is already present.

new_control_requirements.name: ACTIVELY-EXPLOITED-OS-LPE-REMEDIATION-WINDOW-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: This is a confirmed-exploited local privilege escalation reached from an ordinary unprivileged application through a GPU driver IOCTL, and the packet records no vendor live-patch mechanism — remediation is applying the fixed release and rebooting. For this CVE that means the fixed release is driven across the affected estate on the KEV clock rather than folded into the next routine device-update cycle, and the reboot is treated as part of remediation rather than as a follow-up, since an installed-but-not-restarted device is still running the vulnerable kgsl code. Because the packet scopes the defect to multiple Qualcomm chipsets rather than one product, the enforcement has to enumerate the fixed build per affected device model and confirm zero devices remain below it past the due date; a single fleet-wide 'up to date' figure hides the models whose fixed release has not been taken. The control's second clause is the one that matters most here: account-privilege policy is not containment, because the packet's attacker is already an unprivileged local application, so restricting administrative rights changes nothing about the escalation path. The distinguishing test is a per-model build enumeration against the fixed release with a hard deadline, not a patch-compliance percentage.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet attack_vector: 'A local, already-present unprivileged application issues a crafted IOCTL to the Adreno GPU (kgsl) driver; an integer overflow during shared-virtual-memory assignment corrupts kernel memory and escalates privileges, typically as one stage of a mobile exploit chain.' Entry name 'Qualcomm Multiple Chipsets Integer Overflow Vulnerability'; CWE-190; CVSS 7.8; RWEP 53. cisa_kev true, kev_date 2023-12-05, active_exploitation 'confirmed'. patch_available true; live_patch_available false with live_patch_notes 'No vendor live-patch mechanism; remediation requires applying the fixed release and rebooting.'

new_control_requirements.name: MOBILE-OS-MINIMUM-PATCH-LEVEL-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: The packet's trigger is a locally installed unprivileged application issuing a crafted IOCTL, so on any device that has not yet taken the fixed release the operator's only remaining lever is constraining what code gets to run at all — restricting installation of untrusted or side-loaded applications, and denying the device access to organizational data rather than listing it on a patch-compliance report. For this CVE the fixed release for each affected chipset must be an access condition: a device below it is quarantined from mail, VPN and document access instead of being flagged for later. That is what the citing least-functionality gap actually demands on this vector, and it is the half of the control that does the work here, because the escalation path does not need network reachability or elevated rights — it needs an app on the device. The distinguishing test is to enrol a device pinned below the fixed release for its chipset and confirm the policy denies it access to protected resources; an estate that surfaces the stale build on a dashboard while the device keeps its access has recorded the exposure rather than removed it, and the packet describes this flaw as one stage of a chain, which means the device that keeps its access is the one that carries the rest of the chain inside the trust boundary.
