By injecting crafted HTML code, it is possible to remotely execute code in the Cobalt Strike UI.' live_patch_notes: 'No live-patch mechanism; Fortra released Cobalt Strike 4.7.2 as an out-of-band fix that properly escapes HTML in Swing components - remediation is upgrading the client and restarting it.' cisa_kev true, kev_date 2023-03-30, active_exploitation 'confirmed', poc_available true, cvss 9.8, rwep_score 62, patch_available true, live_patch_available false.

new_control_requirements.name: PEN-TEST-SCOPE-INCLUDES-SECURITY-PRODUCTS
new_control_requirements.description: This CVE runs the engagement's data flow backwards, and that is the part scoping documents do not anticipate. The packet has attacker-controlled implant data carrying an HTML <object> tag rendered by the Cobalt Strike client's Java Swing UI, which instantiates arbitrary Java objects and calls their setters, executing code in the operator's console -- so every host the team implants is an input source into the team's own console, and the console is reachable by whoever controls what that host returns. Scope and threat-model language must therefore name the engagement toolchain itself, the team server and each operator client, as attack surface with an untrusted input path, with the client's rendering of implant-returned data enumerated as the specific surface rather than left as instrumentation assumed to sit outside the tested boundary. Keep the scope to those components: the packet ties the defect to the Cobalt Strike client's Swing rendering and gives no basis for treating other consoles or agents in the estate as instances of it. Precondition, and it is the whole limit of this control: scoping and testing describe the surface, they do not remove it. On a team still running the affected client the only closure is the packet's fix -- Cobalt Strike 4.7.2, client upgraded and restarted, with no live-patch path -- and until that lands, any implant on a host the team does not fully control is a live path into the operator's console regardless of how the engagement is scoped.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet attack_vector: 'Attacker-controlled implant data containing an HTML <object> tag is rendered by the Cobalt Strike client's Java Swing UI, which instantiates arbitrary Java objects and calls their setters, executing code in the operator's console.' cwe_refs CWE-116. live_patch_notes gives the fix as Cobalt Strike 4.7.2 with the client upgraded and restarted; live_patch_available false. cisa_kev true, kev_date 2023-03-30, active_exploitation 'confirmed', poc_available true. Citing gaps include UK-CAF-B4 (System security).

CVE-2022-39197.name: Fortra Cobalt Strike Teamserver Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An attacker sets a malformed username in a Beacon payload's configuration; when the teamserver's Java Swing UI renders that username as HTML, the injected markup executes and, via the Java rendering path, can reach code execution on the teamserver.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none in the classic sense — the attacker supplies a crafted beacon; exploitation triggers when the teamserver processes/renders the malicious username
attack_vector.complexity: low — extracting and modifying a beacon username field is straightforward and publicly documented.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — reported by IBM X-Force Red researchers. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading past 4.7 to a fully-fixed Cobalt Strike release that output-encodes/validates beacon-derived fields.
prevention.adequacy: The corrected release closes the injection; note the first fix (4.7.1) was incomplete, so verifying the fully-patched version is essential.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Monitoring the teamserver host for unexpected process execution originating from the Java UI process and reviewing beacon metadata for markup.
detection.adequacy: Detects post-exploitation activity but not the rendering-time injection itself.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rebuilding the teamserver host, updating to a fully-patched release, and rotating any keys/config it held.
response.adequacy: Reactive; appropriate given RCE on the C2 host.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: SI-10 information input validation is the core failure: the teamserver did not validate/encode the attacker-controllable username field from beacon metadata before rendering it in the Swing UI, so a malformed username became executable markup — no perimeter control substitutes for the missing output encoding fixed in 4.7.1.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: NIS2 vulnerability management assumes a fix fully remediates, but Cobalt Strike's initial 4.7.1 patch for this XSS was incomplete, so teamservers considered 'patched' could still be exploitable until later fixes — a reminder that KEV-listed (2023-03-30) issues need verification that the fix actually closes the vector.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 system security presumes application input handling is safe, but the teamserver renders attacker-influenced beacon fields as HTML; only the vendor code fix removes the injection, since the malicious input arrives through normal beacon processing rather than a misconfiguration.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight patching would require upgrading past 4.7 promptly, but because the first fix (4.7.1) was incomplete and this is niche operator software, the window between the 2023-03-30 KEV date and a fully-remediated teamserver left the injection-to-RCE path exploitable.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.28.gap: A.8.28 secure coding is exactly what was missing — the username field parsed from a beacon should be treated as untrusted and output-encoded; its absence let a stored XSS in the teamserver UI reach code execution, which only the corrected Cobalt Strike release resolves.

CVE-2021-30900.name: Apple iOS, iPadOS, and macOS Out-of-Bounds Write Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A malicious application triggers an out-of-bounds write in Apple's GPU drivers to execute code with kernel privileges, elevating from an app foothold to full kernel control.
attack_vector.privileges_required: local user / running app context
attack_vector.complexity: high in isolation (kernel out-of-bounds-write exploitation) but usable as a reliable local-escalation stage in a chain
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — reported to Apple by human researchers. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the October 2021 Apple updates and enforce minimum-OS compliance across managed Apple devices via MDM.
prevention.adequacy: The update closes the out-of-bounds write; prevention is effective once deployed, but requires that devices actually be updated from older iOS branches.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Mobile threat-defense telemetry and crash-log review for GPU-driver anomalies indicative of kernel-exploit attempts.
detection.adequacy: iOS detection is constrained by platform opacity; it mainly aids post-hoc discovery rather than prevention.

response.what_would_have_worked: Update immediately and, for high-risk users, consider device re-imaging given kernel-level code execution.
response.adequacy: Response limits persistence but cannot reverse kernel compromise that already occurred.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 flaw remediation only helps after the October 2021 Apple updates (iOS/iPadOS 14.8.1 / 15.1); with the flaw later KEV-listed 2023-03-30, devices left on older iOS retained an app-to-kernel escalation the control never forced to be closed.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: NIS2 Art.21 patch management for managed Apple fleets must push OS updates promptly, but a GPU-driver kernel write exploited in the wild means any lag between the October 2021 fix and deployment left kernel-level compromise reachable from a malicious app.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 endpoint hardening does not prevent an out-of-bounds write in the GPU driver that crosses into the kernel; app sandboxing and platform hardening are bypassed until the October 2021 update is applied.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight allows up to a month for high-severity OS patches, but this kernel-privilege out-of-bounds write was exploited in the wild, so a compliant monthly mobile-patch cadence still left the escalation live on unpatched Apple devices.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 technical-vulnerability management depends on tracking OS versions across the Apple estate; unmanaged or slow-updating devices kept the KEV-listed GPU-driver kernel write exploitable well after Apple's October 2021 fix.

CVE-2022-38181.name: Arm Mali GPU Kernel Driver Use-After-Free Vulnerability (CVE-2022-38181)

attack_vector.description: Mishandled Mali GPU memory operations leave a use-after-free; an unprivileged app accesses and reclaims the freed kernel memory to corrupt kernel state and escalate to root, typically as the LPE stage after a browser/renderer foothold.
attack_vector.privileges_required: local user (unprivileged app on the device)
attack_vector.complexity: high — reliable use-after-free grooming of GPU kernel memory requires advanced exploitation skill
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — reported by human researchers and fixed by Arm. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Installing the OEM firmware/OS update carrying the fixed Arm Mali driver (r40p0 or later) as soon as it was available for the device.
prevention.adequacy: The driver fix is definitive but was gated on OEM delivery, so devices stayed exposed until their vendor shipped the update.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Mobile EDR/telemetry flagging anomalous Mali driver ioctl patterns and unexpected root escalation from sandboxed apps.
detection.adequacy: Detection on mobile is limited and largely post-hoc; it does not prevent the kernel use-after-free.

response.what_would_have_worked: Forensic review of targeted devices, removing implants, and updating to the fixed driver build.
response.adequacy: Response supports incident handling but cannot recover data exfiltrated by the spyware implant.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 flaw remediation stalls on the Android delivery chain: Arm fixed the Mali use-after-free upstream, but the fix had to flow through SoC vendors and device OEMs, so many phones ran the vulnerable driver long after the 2023-03-30 KEV listing while the bug was actively exploited.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: NIS2 Art.21 patch-management assumes the operator can apply a vendor fix, yet for a GPU kernel driver the patch is gated on OEM firmware releases; organizations with affected Mali-based devices could not directly remediate CVE-2022-38181 and depended on carrier/OEM update timelines.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 assumes the app sandbox and least-privilege model contain untrusted code, but a use-after-free in the Mali GPU kernel driver lets an unprivileged app reach root, breaking the sandbox boundary that mobile system-security baselines rely on.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight 'patch operating systems' expects timely OS patching, but the fragmented Android patch pipeline meant Mali driver revisions r38p1/r39p0 stayed deployed past the fix, leaving the root-escalation path open during the in-the-wild spyware campaign.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 technical-vulnerability management struggles because the vulnerable component is a hardware GPU driver whose fix ships on OEM schedules; risk-rated patching cannot close a CVSS 8.8 kernel UAF when the fixed r40p0 driver is not yet available for the device model.

attack_vector.description: A local user invokes SNDRV_CTL_IOCTL_ELEM_READ/WRITE32 on an ALSA control device; missing rwsem locking in snd_ctl_elem_read creates a use-after-free race that is groomed into a kernel read/write primitive, escalating from system user to ring0.
attack_vector.privileges_required: local user (already-authenticated low-privilege foothold)
attack_vector.complexity: high — winning the missing-lock race and turning the use-after-free into a reliable ring0 primitive requires kernel-exploitation skill (CVSS AC:H)
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — reported by a human researcher and fixed upstream. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying the fixed kernel (past commit 56b88b50565c) and rebooting; where reboot must wait, kernel live-patching or restricting access to /dev/snd via device permissions/seccomp reduces reach.
prevention.adequacy: Patch closes the race; access restrictions only narrow which local principals can reach the vulnerable ioctl.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Auditing for unexpected use of the ALSA control ioctls by non-audio processes and EDR alerting on local privilege-escalation behavior.
detection.adequacy: Kernel-race exploitation leaves faint signals; detection is a weak backstop to patching.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rebuilding hosts where ring0 compromise is suspected and rotating any keys or credentials exposed to the kernel.
response.adequacy: Response addresses post-escalation compromise; it does not prevent the LPE.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: AC-6 least-privilege assumes the OS enforces the user/kernel boundary, but this ALSA PCM use-after-free lets any local system user race to ring0, so least-privilege account design gives no protection once the vulnerable ioctl is reachable — only the fixed kernel restores the boundary.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: NIS2 Art. 21 patch-management for kernels is reboot-gated and slow; with exploitation confirmed at the 2023-03-30 KEV listing, hosts awaiting a maintenance window ran a kernel whose ELEM_READ/WRITE32 race escalated a local foothold to full root.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 system-security hardening (seccomp, reduced attack surface) can narrow reach to the ioctl but does not fix the missing rwsem lock; a local attacker or a browser-renderer foothold that can call the ALSA control ioctl still wins ring0 until the kernel is patched.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight patch-operating-systems targets prompt kernel updates, but kernel patching requires a reboot and is often deferred; that latency leaves the use-after-free LPE available to chain after any initial code execution.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 technical-vulnerability management flags the KEV entry, yet the practical exposure is the reboot-deferred kernel-update window during which a local use-after-free continues to grant ring0 escalation.

CVE-2022-3038.name: Google Chromium Network Service Use-After-Free Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A victim visits a crafted HTML page that triggers a use-after-free (CWE-416) in Chromium's Network Service process, causing heap corruption that a remote attacker can leverage toward code execution; the flaw affects the shared Chromium base used by Chrome, Edge, Opera and others.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated) — but requires the victim to load attacker-controlled content (UI:R)
attack_vector.complexity: low — AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R; a single malicious page reaches the vulnerable Network Service, though a full RCE chain requires additional work
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — reported by Sergei Glazunov of Google Project Zero. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Keeping Chromium-based browsers auto-updated to 105.0.5195.52 or later across the whole fleet, including Edge and Opera.
prevention.adequacy: The patched build removes the use-after-free; because the flaw lives in the browser's own process, no external control substitutes for the update.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Browser crash telemetry and web-proxy inspection for pages targeting known Chromium exploits.
detection.adequacy: Detection of browser-exploit pages is unreliable and post-delivery; timely browser updates are the dependable control.

response.what_would_have_worked: Forcing browser relaunch to apply staged updates and validating that Edge/Opera variants were also patched.
response.adequacy: Response ensures the fix actually takes effect (staged Chromium updates apply only on restart) but does not itself remove the bug.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 flaw remediation depends on browsers actually updating: this Network Service use-after-free was fixed on 2022-08-30 but only KEV-listed on 2023-03-30, so environments that suppressed or delayed Chromium auto-update ran an exploitable browser for months.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: NIS2 patch-management for endpoint browsers is undermined when Chromium-based products (Chrome, Edge, Opera) update on separate channels; a crafted HTML page could exploit any host whose browser lagged 105.0.5195.52 despite the fix being public.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 secure configuration cannot mitigate a use-after-free in the browser's own Network Service process reached by simply rendering a page; only shipping the patched Chromium build removes the heap-corruption path.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight 'Patch applications' targets 48 hours for actively-exploited browser flaws, but the ~7-month gap between the 2022-08-30 fix and the 2023-03-30 KEV listing shows how easily an unmanaged browser-update posture leaves this drive-by-capable bug exploitable.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 technical-vulnerability management must track fast-moving Chromium releases across every derived browser; a program that inventories only 'Chrome' can miss Edge/Opera instances still exposed to this crafted-HTML use-after-free.

CVE-2022-22706.name: Arm Mali GPU Kernel Driver Unspecified Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unprivileged local app abuses the Mali GPU kernel driver to obtain host-writable mappings of read-only imported pages, corrupting kernel memory to escalate privileges to root (used as the local-escalation stage of a spyware chain).
attack_vector.privileges_required: local user (any unprivileged app on the device)
attack_vector.complexity: high - reliable kernel exploitation of the Mali driver, consistent with mercenary-spyware tooling; technique publicly documented
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered - reported via GitHub Security Lab, in-the-wild use found by Google TAG. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Installing the OEM security update (June 2023 Android patch level or later) that ships the fixed Mali driver.
prevention.adequacy: Patch is the fix, but it was inadequate in practice for ~17 months because the OEM/carrier supply chain gated delivery of Arm's January 2022 fix.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Mobile threat-defense/EDR watching for anomalous GPU-driver ioctl abuse and spyware persistence.
detection.adequacy: Detecting kernel-LPE spyware on mobile is limited and largely post-compromise.

response.what_would_have_worked: For targeted users, device reset/replacement and credential rotation.
response.adequacy: Appropriate for confirmed targeting but reactive.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 flaw remediation was defeated by the mobile supply chain: Arm fixed the Mali driver in January 2022, but the fix did not reach devices until the June 2023 Android patch level, so even diligent SI-2 patching could not close the read-only-page write primitive during the ~17-month gap that spanned the 2023-03-30 KEV listing.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: NIS2 patch-management cannot compel Android OEM/carrier update pipelines, so the Mali kernel LPE remained exploitable on managed handsets long after Arm's upstream fix, undermining any mobile patch SLA.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 system-security hardening does not address a GPU-driver kernel bug reachable by any unprivileged app; on-device hardening leaves the local privilege-escalation primitive intact until the OEM ships the driver fix.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential 8 'patch operating systems' assumes vendor updates are available and deployable, but the fixed Mali driver was gated behind OEM firmware for over a year, so the local-to-root escalation stayed live regardless of patch diligence.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 technical vulnerability management could not remediate a driver whose fix was withheld by the device supply chain; the kernel write primitive persisted on inventoried mobile assets despite being a known, KEV-listed exposure.

new_control_requirements.name: MOBILE-OS-MINIMUM-PATCH-LEVEL-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: The packet's remediation is an OEM firmware/security update that ships the fixed Mali driver and reboots the device — the operator does not build that update and cannot accelerate it, so the only lever they actually hold is whether a device still carrying an affected driver keeps its access. For this CVE the enforced minimum has to be expressed as the OEM build that carries a Mali kernel driver outside the affected revision ranges (Midgard r26p0 through r31p0, Bifrost r0p0 through r35p0, Valhall r19p0 through r35p0), and it must function as an access condition — mail, VPN and document access denied to a device below it — not as a row on a patch-compliance dashboard. Distinguishing test: enrol a device whose Mali driver is still inside an affected range and confirm the policy actually denies it access to protected resources; an estate that surfaces the stale build on a report while the device keeps its access has recorded the exposure rather than removed it. Precondition, and this is where the control is usually over-claimed: the packet's path starts with an unprivileged local app, so restricting which applications may be installed raises the bar for getting that app onto the device but does not evict one already installed and does not cover one that arrived through the normal store channel — a device suspected of having run it belongs on the incident path, because the escalation ends at root and the packet records this as the local-escalation stage of a spyware chain. The update also reboots the device, so a device that has downloaded it but not restarted still runs the vulnerable driver and is not remediated.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet vector: 'Arm Mali GPU Kernel Driver allows a non-privileged user to achieve write access to read-only memory pages. This affects Midgard r26p0 through r31p0, Bifrost r0p0 through r35p0, and Valhall r19p0 through r35p0.' Attack vector: 'An unprivileged local app abuses the Mali GPU kernel driver to obtain host-writable mappings of read-only imported pages, corrupting kernel memory to escalate privileges to root (used as the local-escalation stage of a spyware chain).' CISA KEV listed 2023-03-30; active_exploitation confirmed; poc_available true; CVSS 7.8; RWEP 72. patch_available true, live_patch_available false, live_patch_notes: 'No live-patch mechanism for the Mali GPU kernel driver on affected devices; remediation requires the OEM firmware/security update that ships the fixed driver, which reboots the device.'

new_control_requirements.name: SCANNER-PAPER-COMPLIANCE-TEST
new_control_requirements.description: The packet scopes this vulnerability by Mali kernel driver revision — Midgard r26p0 through r31p0, Bifrost r0p0 through r35p0, Valhall r19p0 through r35p0 — and not by an OS version or a reported patch-level string, while the fixed driver arrives inside an OEM firmware/security update rather than as a package the operator installs. So a fleet report that reads a device's OS build or patch-level date and marks it compliant has tested nothing about this CVE: the driver revision is chosen by the OEM's build, so two devices reporting the same patch level from different vendors can ship different Mali revisions, and one of them can still be inside an affected range. The operational test is to read the Mali driver revision actually loaded on a representative device of each OEM and model in the estate, check it against the three affected ranges, and re-run that check after every OEM update — because the update that moves the patch-level string is not necessarily the one that moves the driver, and that mismatch is exactly what a version-only scan cannot see. Precondition: this establishes exposure or its absence, it does not remediate. The packet records no live-patch mechanism, so a device found inside an affected range stays exposed until the OEM update lands and the device reboots, and a device the check clears today can regress if a later OEM build ships a driver revision back inside the range.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet vector names the affected component by driver revision: 'This affects Midgard r26p0 through r31p0, Bifrost r0p0 through r35p0, and Valhall r19p0 through r35p0.' live_patch_available false with live_patch_notes: 'No live-patch mechanism for the Mali GPU kernel driver on affected devices; remediation requires the OEM firmware/security update that ships the fixed driver, which reboots the device.' CISA KEV listed 2023-03-30; active_exploitation confirmed; poc_available true; CVSS 7.8; RWEP 72; patch_available true. Citing gaps on this entry include ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.8.8 (Management of technical vulnerabilities) and UK CAF B4 (System security).

CVE-2023-26360.name: Adobe ColdFusion Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability (CVE-2023-26360)

attack_vector.description: An improper-access-control flaw exposes a ColdFusion code path that deserializes attacker-controlled data without authentication, yielding arbitrary code execution and file read in the service context.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated network access to the ColdFusion endpoint)
attack_vector.complexity: low — public PoCs and a Metasploit module reduce exploitation to a crafted request
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — reported to Adobe by a researcher. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying ColdFusion 2018 Update 16 / 2021 Update 6 and following Adobe's lockdown guide, plus placing the server behind a WAF and off direct internet exposure.
prevention.adequacy: Patch closes the deserialization path; lockdown and WAF reduce exposure during the pre-patch window.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Monitoring for new files in the ColdFusion web root and for anomalous child processes or outbound connections from the ColdFusion service.
detection.adequacy: Effective post-compromise but does not prevent the initial unauthenticated RCE.

response.what_would_have_worked: Hunt for and remove web shells, rebuild compromised servers, and rotate any datasource/service credentials the ColdFusion instance held.
response.adequacy: Necessary because RCE on ColdFusion typically yields persistent web shells that survive a naive patch.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 flaw remediation on a routine cadence was too slow for CVE-2023-26360: it was already exploited when Adobe shipped APSB23-25 and CISA added it to KEV on 2023-03-15, so any multi-week patch SLA left an internet-facing ColdFusion server open to unauthenticated RCE.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: NIS2 Art.21 patch management does not force emergency patching of legacy web-application servers, yet ColdFusion instances are frequently internet-exposed and this preauth RCE was under active exploitation, warranting out-of-band action the routine process omits.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 secure-configuration assumes ColdFusion component methods enforce access control, but the improper-access-control flaw let unauthenticated requests reach a deserialization sink; B4 hardening baselines rarely restrict the specific CFC/AJAX endpoints abused here.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight's 48-hour patch window for exploited internet-facing services was already breached on release: exploitation preceded the fix, so patch-timeliness alone could not protect exposed ColdFusion servers by the 2023-03-15 KEV date.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 technical-vulnerability management often leaves aging ColdFusion deployments off the actively-tracked inventory, so this known-exploited deserialization RCE could sit unpatched on a public server past the KEV due date.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For Adobe ColdFusion the two clocks a normal remediation process keeps apart collapsed onto one day: the packet records CISA adding this to KEV on 2023-03-15, the same day Adobe shipped the fix, and notes that this indicates exploitation was already underway. A response measured in hours from that day is the only patch-side clock that had any window at all, and it is precisely what the cited routine cadences do not carry. Bound to this product, completion means the fixed update is the code actually running: ColdFusion 2018 Update 16 for instances at or below 2018 Update 15, and ColdFusion 2021 Update 6 for instances at or below 2021 Update 5, with the ColdFusion service restarted afterwards. Read patch_required_reboot carefully here — it is false, which means no host reboot is needed, not that the fix is live on install. The packet's own remediation note requires restarting the ColdFusion service, and live_patch_available is false, so there is no path that avoids that restart; an instance that installed the update and left the service running is still executing the pre-fix code and must be counted exposed until the restart. Measure per ColdFusion installation rather than per site: a host serving several applications through one ColdFusion instance is one remediation, and an application inventory that tracks web properties rather than ColdFusion installations will miss instances on both the 2018 and 2021 tracks, which update independently. Scope from what the packet's affected and affected_versions name — ColdFusion 2018 at or below Update 15 and ColdFusion 2021 at or below Update 5 — and widen only where a verified source identifies another product carrying the same code path. Residual to state plainly rather than let the SLA imply otherwise: this compresses the post-patch window only. The packet records exploitation preceding the fix, so even a same-day clock from 2023-03-15 covers nothing before it, and an internet-facing instance that was reachable before that date is a compromise-assessment case rather than a clean patch record.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: CWE-284, vector 'Adobe ColdFusion versions 2018 Update 15 (and earlier) and 2021 Update 5 (and earlier) are affected by an Improper Access Control vulnerability that could result in arbitrary code execution in the context of the current user. Exploitation of this issue does not require user interaction.' affected_versions: 'Adobe ColdFusion 2018 <= Update 15 (fixed in Update 16)', 'Adobe ColdFusion 2021 <= Update 5 (fixed in Update 6)'. cisa_kev true, kev_date 2023-03-15; active_exploitation_notes state the entry was 'Added to CISA KEV 2023-03-15, the same day as the Adobe fix, indicating exploitation was already underway.' patch_available true, patch_required_reboot false, live_patch_available false, live_patch_notes 'No live-patch mechanism; remediation requires applying Adobe ColdFusion 2018 Update 16 or 2021 Update 6 and restarting the ColdFusion service.' CVSS 8.6, RWEP 72, poc_available true. The NIST-800-53-SI-2 gap records that a routine cadence 'was too slow' and that 'any multi-week patch SLA left an internet-facing ColdFusion server open to unauthenticated RCE'; the NIS2-Art21-patch-management gap records that routine patch management 'does not force emergency patching of legacy web-application servers... warranting out-of-band action the routine process omits'.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: The packet records that CISA documented a federal agency's public-facing ColdFusion servers compromised through this flaw, and it names both halves of the primitive: unauthenticated arbitrary code execution and arbitrary file read in the ColdFusion service context. Both halves determine what remediation has to mean. The execution half is what leaves a persistent artifact written through a path the application legitimately exposes; the read half hands over datasource credentials, configuration and any key material the ColdFusion service account can read, and nothing about applying an update reverses a read. Applying ColdFusion 2018 Update 16 or 2021 Update 6 and restarting the service closes the improper-access-control path to the deserialization sink, and removes nothing already written through it. So for an internet-facing ColdFusion instance that was reachable during the pre-patch window — which on this entry's own timeline is a broad population, since the KEV listing and the vendor fix landed together on 2023-03-15 with exploitation already underway — the default response is a compromise assessment and rebuild rather than patch-in-place: inventory the files under the web root and the ColdFusion installation against what a deployment accounts for, rebuild from a known-good image where one exists, and rotate every credential the service account could read, including datasource passwords. Preconditions and limits. This does not close the flaw; the update plus the service restart does, and the packet records no live-patch path, so an instance assessed but left on 2018 Update 15 or 2021 Update 5 is exploitable again immediately. It applies to instances that were internet-facing or otherwise reachable by an untrusted caller during the window, not to every ColdFusion installation in the estate. And the assessment has to be a file-inventory-against-deployment exercise rather than a scan: an artifact written through a legitimate application path is bespoke, so signature-based anti-malware and authentication logging have nothing to match, and an authentication log is silent by construction for a flaw whose whole point is that no authentication took place.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: affected records 'an improper-access-control flaw permits deserialization of untrusted data, allowing unauthenticated arbitrary code execution and arbitrary file read in the ColdFusion service context'; attack_vector repeats the unauthenticated deserialization path 'yielding arbitrary code execution and file read in the service context'. active_exploitation confirmed; active_exploitation_notes state 'CISA later documented (in a June 2023 advisory) that a federal agency's public-facing ColdFusion servers were compromised via this flaw' and that the KEV listing on 2023-03-15 landed the same day as the Adobe fix, indicating exploitation was already underway. poc_available true, CVSS 8.6, RWEP 72. patch_available true, live_patch_available false, live_patch_notes 'remediation requires applying Adobe ColdFusion 2018 Update 16 or 2021 Update 6 and restarting the ColdFusion service'. The AU-Essential-8-Patch gap records that the 48-hour window 'was already breached on release: exploitation preceded the fix, so patch-timeliness alone could not protect exposed ColdFusion servers by the 2023-03-15 KEV date.'

CVE-2023-23397.name: Microsoft Office Outlook Privilege Escalation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A crafted Outlook reminder with a UNC path in the PidLidReminderFileParameter property forces the client to send the user's Net-NTLMv2 hash to an attacker SMB server with no interaction; the hash is relayed to impersonate the victim.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none for the attacker; zero-click for the victim (the reminder processing triggers the leak)
attack_vector.complexity: low — set one MAPI property to a UNC path; public PoCs and Microsoft's scanning script document it fully
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — credited to CERT-UA and Microsoft. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Installing the March 2023 Outlook update and blocking outbound TCP 445, adding privileged users to the Protected Users group, and enforcing SMB signing.
prevention.adequacy: Patch stops new leaks, but because exploitation predated it by ~a year, egress blocking and NTLM hardening were needed to prevent leaks and relays in the interim.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Microsoft's PowerShell script to scan Exchange for messages with a UNC PidLidReminderFileParameter, plus alerting on Outlook-originated outbound SMB.
detection.adequacy: The scanning script is effective for hunting planted messages, but the leak fires before most endpoint detection would react.

response.what_would_have_worked: Remove malicious messages, reset credentials for affected users, and hunt for relayed authentications and lateral movement.
response.adequacy: Necessary because a leaked/relayed credential outlives the patch; only credential rotation and relay hunting evict the attacker.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: SC-7 boundary protection would have blocked outbound SMB (TCP 445) at the perimeter, which is Microsoft's primary mitigation, but default enterprise egress rules rarely deny 445; without that block the zero-click reminder leaks the Net-NTLMv2 hash to the attacker's SMB server the moment the message is processed.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: NIS2 Art.21 network-security controls seldom restrict SMB egress or enforce SMB signing, so the forced-authentication leak reaches attacker infrastructure and the relayed hash authenticates internally; a patch-only response around the KEV 2023-03-14 date misses the credentials already captured by APT28.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: CAF B2 identity and access control trusts Net-NTLMv2 as an authenticator, but this flaw coerces the victim's client into leaking it with no interaction, enabling relay-based impersonation; B2 cannot distinguish the relayed session from the legitimate user without disabling NTLM or enforcing MFA/signing.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight patch-applications expects prompt Office updates, yet CVE-2023-23397 was a zero-click zero-day exploited from 2022; even the March 2023 patch does not retroactively protect credentials leaked before it, and unpatched Outlook clients kept leaking hashes after the KEV listing.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.22.gap: A.8.22 network segregation would have isolated user endpoints so a coerced SMB connection could not exit to an attacker server, but flat networks allow the outbound authentication; without segregation and SMB egress control, A.8.8 patching alone left the forced-auth leak reachable on unpatched clients.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For this CVE the mitigation the clock runs against is not one artifact. The KEV listing and the Microsoft March 2023 Outlook security update arrived together, so the patch arm is available from hour zero — but the packet's remediation note pairs that update with three named mitigations (block outbound TCP 445, add users to the Protected Users group, enforce SMB signing), and this control is what makes those the deployable alternative for any client that cannot take the update inside the clock. Scope is the Outlook for Windows estate the packet's affected_versions name — Microsoft 365 Apps and Office 2013, 2016, 2019 and LTSC 2021 below the March 2023 build — not Microsoft 365 Apps alone, since an estate standardised on a perpetual Office release is affected at its own pre-update build. Completion must be measured on Outlook itself: patch_required_reboot false means no machine reboot, and the packet states the Office update requires restarting Outlook, so a workstation that installed it while Outlook stayed open is still running the vulnerable reminder-processing path and is not remediated. Preconditions on the compensating half, which is where this gets recorded as done while the path stays open: blocking outbound TCP 445 stops the coerced authentication reaching an SMB server on the internet, but the UNC path in the reminder can name any destination the client can route to, so an attacker with an interior foothold still collects the hash — that internal case is the segregation problem, not something the egress rule covers. Protected Users membership removes NTLM only for the accounts placed in it, so the general user population keeps leaking Net-NTLMv2 until the update lands or SMB signing is enforced on the services that would accept the relay. And none of the three, nor the update, recovers a hash captured before they were in place.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: cisa_kev true with kev_date 2023-03-14, active_exploitation confirmed, CVSS 9.8, RWEP 65, poc_available true. patch_available true, patch_required_reboot false, live_patch_available false, with live_patch_notes stating 'No live-patch mechanism; remediation requires the Microsoft March 2023 Outlook security update, plus recommended mitigations (block outbound TCP 445, add users to Protected Users group, enforce SMB signing). Applying the Office update requires restarting Outlook but not the host.' affected_versions: 'Microsoft Outlook for Windows (Microsoft 365 Apps, Office 2013/2016/2019/LTSC 2021) before the March 2023 security update'. attack_vector: a crafted reminder with a UNC path in PidLidReminderFileParameter forces the client to send the user's Net-NTLMv2 hash to an attacker SMB server with no interaction. The NIST-800-53-SC-7 gap records that blocking outbound SMB (TCP 445) is Microsoft's primary mitigation but that default enterprise egress rules rarely deny 445; the UK-CAF-B2 gap records that B2 cannot distinguish the relayed session from the legitimate user without disabling NTLM or enforcing MFA/signing.

new_control_requirements.name: NATION-STATE-INITIAL-ACCESS-IR-ESCALATION
new_control_requirements.description: The packet's attribution is the trigger this control names by actor: confirmed in-the-wild zero-day exploitation from as early as April 2022 by APT28 (Fancy Bear / Forest Blizzard) against government, military, energy and transportation targets in Europe — roughly eleven months of collection before the KEV listing on 2023-03-14. Bound to Outlook, that changes what remediation means: the flaw's output is the user's Net-NTLMv2 hash delivered to an attacker-controlled SMB server with no interaction and then relayed to impersonate the victim, so what survives the March 2023 update is authentication material already taken, not a code path still open. The runbook must therefore treat a mailbox that received a message whose reminder carried a UNC path in PidLidReminderFileParameter during the exposure window as an intrusion lead rather than a patch-compliance exception: rotate credentials for the affected accounts, and hunt for authentication that arrived by relay rather than from the user's own workstation. Escalating under the nation-state path rather than a commodity-malware path is the packet's own justification — a state-aligned espionage group operating against those sectors uses a relayed session to move, so the commodity path's expectation of a malware artifact to find produces a clean result on a compromised estate. Preconditions: this is the response half and it prevents nothing — further leaks stop only when the update and the packet's named mitigations land. It also depends on mail retention covering the exposure window and on authentication telemetry that was already being collected when the relay happened; where neither survives, the honest output is that the exposure cannot be bounded, which is the finding rather than an all-clear.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: active_exploitation confirmed, with active_exploitation_notes stating exploitation in the wild as a zero-day from as early as April 2022 by the Russia-aligned APT28 (Fancy Bear / Forest Blizzard) against government, military, energy and transportation targets in Europe, CISA KEV addition 2023-03-14, and PoCs released immediately (poc_available true). attack_vector: the hash is relayed to impersonate the victim. The AU-Essential-8-Patch gap states that even the March 2023 patch does not retroactively protect credentials leaked before it; the NIS2-Art21-network-security gap states that a patch-only response around the KEV 2023-03-14 date misses the credentials already captured by APT28.

CVE-2023-24880.name: Microsoft Windows SmartScreen Security Feature Bypass Vulnerability (CVE-2023-24880)

attack_vector.description: An attacker crafts an MSI/PE with a malformed Authenticode signature and delivers it via drive-by download; when the target opens it, SmartScreen errors while parsing the signature and skips the Mark-of-the-Web reputation check, so the file runs without the usual warning and installs Magniber ransomware.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none for the bypass itself; requires the target user to open a downloaded file (user interaction)
attack_vector.complexity: low — craft a file with a malformed Authenticode signature; the technique is public
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — found by Google TAG during Magniber tracking. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying the March 2023 Windows update so SmartScreen fails closed on malformed signatures.
prevention.adequacy: The patch restores fail-closed MOTW enforcement; SmartScreen alone was insufficient because the bypass defeats it, so application control is a stronger layer.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Hunting for downloaded MSI/PE that carry MOTW yet executed without a SmartScreen prompt, and for malformed Authenticode signatures.
detection.adequacy: Detection can flag the anomaly but usually only after execution has begun.

response.what_would_have_worked: Contain infected hosts and block the malformed-signed installers at the mail/web gateway.
response.adequacy: Response limits spread but cannot reverse ransomware encryption already triggered on a host.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: SI-3 malicious-code protection leans on SmartScreen/reputation as a malware gate, but this bypass makes SmartScreen fail open on malformed signatures, so the reputation control silently passes Magniber payloads until the March 2023 patch.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The fix is a Windows update; endpoints slow to patch keep executing MOTW-bypassing MSIs, and the Magniber campaign was already live when the CVE entered KEV on 2023-03-14.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 endpoint protection that treats the SmartScreen MOTW prompt as a control does not fail closed here; without application control or attachment policy, the malformed-signature file runs unwarned.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Essential Eight application hardening (block/limit MSI and untrusted executables) is the compensating control once the SmartScreen reputation layer is bypassed; organizations relying on MOTW warnings alone stay exposed.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: A.8.7 anti-malware posture that depends on OS reputation warnings is defeated by the fail-open MOTW bypass; the control passes the ransomware installer without an alert.

new_control_requirements.name: PROTECTION-MECHANISM-FAILURE-CLASS-REGRESSION
new_control_requirements.description: SmartScreen is exactly the protection-mechanism class this control governs, and the packet describes the mechanism failing open rather than an application being exploited: an MSI or PE carrying a malformed Authenticode signature is delivered by drive-by download, SmartScreen errors while parsing that signature, the Mark-of-the-Web reputation check is skipped, and the file runs with no warning and installs Magniber ransomware. Bound to this estate, the control means every layer credited with covering the MOTW/SmartScreen class — the detonation chamber, the EDR rules written against 'unknown executable downloaded from the internet', and any AppLocker or WDAC policy an attestation leans on — carries a regression battery containing this primitive and runs it on every patch deployment, not once at remediation. The distinguishing test keys on the behaviour the packet documents rather than on a malware sample or a policy read-back: put an MSI and a PE with a deliberately malformed Authenticode signature and a Mark-of-the-Web tag on a test host, open them the way a drive-by download would, and confirm the reputation check actually runs and the file is warned on or blocked. Confirming that SmartScreen is 'enabled' in policy proves nothing here — the setting was enabled on every host this CVE was exploited against; the bypass is the check being skipped, not turned off. Precondition: this is a test regime and not a mitigation. It tells the operator whether the class is genuinely covered on a given build; it does not close the bypass. The packet records the March 2023 Windows security update as what makes SmartScreen fail closed on malformed signatures, with no live-patch path and a reboot required, so on a host that has not restarted the battery will still show the file executing silently — which is the correct result, and means that host is exposed rather than that the test failed.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet fields for CVE-2023-24880 (Microsoft Windows SmartScreen Security Feature Bypass Vulnerability, CWE-863): CISA KEV listed 2023-03-14, active_exploitation confirmed, poc_available true, CVSS 4.4, rwep_score 66. The attack_vector states the attacker crafts an MSI/PE with a malformed Authenticode signature and delivers it via drive-by download; when the target opens it, SmartScreen errors while parsing the signature and skips the Mark-of-the-Web reputation check, so the file runs without the usual warning and installs Magniber ransomware. patch_available true, live_patch_available false, with live_patch_notes stating remediation requires the March 2023 Windows security update that makes SmartScreen fail closed on malformed signatures, followed by a reboot. The entry's citing gaps are the malicious-code-protection, anti-malware and user-application-hardening controls that credit SmartScreen as the covering mechanism.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: This entry is the case the control exists for, because its severity band and its real-world priority point in opposite directions: the packet records CVSS 4.4 — below the threshold at which most patch policies open an expedited clock — against confirmed in-the-wild exploitation, a public PoC, a KEV listing dated 2023-03-14 and an RWEP of 66, with the observed outcome being ransomware installation. A programme that schedules by CVSS band puts this update in the routine monthly stream while the exploitation it is listed for is already running. For this CVE the requirement is that the clock starts at the KEV listing and that completion is measured per host as the March 2023 Windows security update installed and the machine restarted, not as 'approved', 'downloaded' or 'pending reboot' in the management console — the packet registers no live-patch path and states the fix takes effect only after that reboot, so a host holding the update without a restart is still running the code that skips the reputation check. Precondition, stated rather than glossed: the packet names no interim vendor mitigation for this entry, so there is nothing to deploy in place of the update. During the window before each host restarts, the only cover is on the delivery and execution side — which is a different control, and it must not be recorded as though it satisfied this one. Nor does the SLA reach a host already compromised: the packet's outcome is ransomware installed by a file that ran silently, and installing the update afterwards does not undo an execution that already happened.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet fields for CVE-2023-24880: cisa_kev true with kev_date 2023-03-14, active_exploitation confirmed, poc_available true, cvss 4.4, rwep_score 66. patch_available true, live_patch_available false, live_patch_notes stating remediation requires the March 2023 Windows security update that makes SmartScreen fail closed on malformed signatures, followed by a reboot. The attack_vector records the exploitation outcome as the crafted MSI/PE running without the usual warning and installing Magniber ransomware. The entry's citing gaps include the EU NIS2 vulnerability-handling/patch-management control and the UK CAF system-security control, both of which an estate can attest while scheduling this CVE by its 4.4 severity band.

attack_vector.description: An attacker with privileged FortiOS CLI access issues crafted commands that traverse outside the intended directory to read and write files on the underlying Linux system, which UNC3886 used to plant persistent implants in the FortiGate firmware.
attack_vector.privileges_required: local privileged (super-admin) CLI access (AV:L, PR:L), typically obtained via a separate initial-access flaw
attack_vector.complexity: low per CVSS (AC:L) once privileged CLI access is held, but the overall intrusion required chaining and was highly targeted
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — surfaced via Fortinet/Mandiant incident response. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrade to FortiOS 7.2.4 / 7.0.10 / 6.4.12, restrict and monitor super-admin CLI access, and verify firmware integrity on previously-exposed appliances.
prevention.adequacy: Patching removes the write primitive but is insufficient alone: implants already written to firmware require integrity verification and, if found, device rebuild.

detection.what_would_have_worked: FortiOS filesystem-integrity checks and logging of anomalous CLI commands writing outside expected paths.
detection.adequacy: Firmware-integrity verification is the reliable detection for UNC3886's persistence; standard logging often missed the traversal.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat exposed FortiGate devices as compromised, rebuild from verified firmware, rotate credentials, and hunt for THINCRUST/CASTLETAP and passive traffic-redirection tooling.
response.adequacy: Full response is required given confirmed nation-state firmware persistence.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 patching assumes the appliance firmware is trusted, but CVE-2022-41328 let UNC3886 write to the FortiOS filesystem for persistence; applying the 7.2.4/7.0.10/6.4.12 fix closes the write primitive yet does not by itself detect or remove implants already planted in firmware.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: NIS2 supply-chain/security expectations for network hardware don't cover an OEM firmware path-traversal that an attacker abuses post-access to modify the device image, so the framework offers no control forcing firmware-integrity verification on FortiGate appliances.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 system-security hardening of a firewall cannot prevent a super-admin from writing arbitrary files via the flawed CLI path handling; the traversal turns legitimate privileged CLI access into filesystem write, which B4's configuration controls do not constrain.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential 8 patch cadence rarely tracks firewall firmware and cannot help against a 0-day used in targeted intrusions before the 2023-03 fix; even after patching, Essential 8 has no requirement to re-verify FortiGate firmware integrity for prior tampering.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 technical-vulnerability management would schedule the FortiOS patch, but because exploitation writes persistent implants into the device image, A.8.8's patch focus misses the firmware-integrity check needed to catch UNC3886's THINCRUST/CASTLETAP footholds.

attack_vector.description: An attacker sends a crafted XML stream to a service that uses XStream to deserialize input; on pre-1.4.18 defaults XStream instantiates a gadget chain from the XML that executes an OS command on the host.
attack_vector.privileges_required: depends on the embedding product's endpoint — network-reachable with low/no auth in the exploited VMware case (CVSS PR:L)
attack_vector.complexity: high — requires crafting a working gadget chain for the target's classpath (reflected in the CVSS AC:H)
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — reported to the XStream project. No AI involvement documented.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading XStream to 1.4.18+ / applying the embedding vendor's patch and enabling an explicit type whitelist
prevention.adequacy: The patch or whitelist stops the gadget instantiation; the harder problem is discovering every product that ships the vulnerable XStream.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Monitoring application hosts for XML-processing services spawning shell/child processes
detection.adequacy: Deserialization RCE surfaces as unexpected child processes under the app service, detectable with host process monitoring.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a successful deserialization as host compromise and rotating credentials on the affected server
response.adequacy: Because the flaw yields code execution, a confirmed hit requires full host containment and credential rotation.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 flaw remediation is complicated because XStream is an embedded dependency; patching required each product (e.g. VMware Cloud Foundation) to ship an updated XStream, so downstream remediation lagged the 2021 library fix and the flaw was still KEV-listed as exploited on 2023-03-10.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: The RCE lives in a third-party serialization library shipped inside many products; NIS2 supply-chain security requires tracking such transitive components, but organizations often did not know XStream < 1.4.18 was embedded in their VMware or other stack until exploitation.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 assumes services reject hostile input; XStream's pre-1.4.18 default converts untrusted XML straight into arbitrary object graphs, so a service that deserializes external XML executes attacker code despite perimeter controls.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Essential Eight application hardening advises disabling unneeded functionality; the safe posture (an XStream type whitelist) was off by default before 1.4.18, so hardening depended on developers configuring it, which most embedding products had not.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 technical vulnerability management must cover embedded libraries; this deserialization flaw was remediable only by upgrading XStream to 1.4.18 or applying the embedding vendor's patch, and inventories that tracked only top-level products missed the vulnerable component.

CVE-2022-47986.name: IBM Aspera Faspex Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated POST to /aspera/faspex/package_relay/relay_package carries a YAML document inside the JSON external_emails field. The obsolete PackageRelayController#relay_package route hands that value to an unsafe YAML.load, instantiating a Gem::Installer / Gem::SpecFetcher -> Gem::Package::TarReader -> Net::BufferedIO -> Net::WriteAdapter -> PrettyPrint gadget chain that terminates in Kernel eval, so attacker shell commands run as the Faspex service account before any authentication decision is reached.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N, fully unauthenticated; the obsolete relay_package route is registered and reachable pre-login on every build at or below 4.4.2 Patch Level 1
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, UI:N, one HTTP POST with no preconditions beyond the route being present; EPSS 0.99968 (99.977th percentile)
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Max Garrett and Shubham Shah of Assetnote found it by hand-auditing the Rails codebase for unsafe YAML.load sinks and reported it privately to IBM in October 2022. No AI system is credited in the Assetnote writeup, the IBM Security Bulletin, or NVD.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrade to IBM Aspera Faspex 4.4.2 Patch Level 2, which deletes the obsolete relay_package API rather than sanitising it, or migrate to Faspex 5.x which is not affected.
prevention.adequacy: The upgrade genuinely removes the route, but the KEV due date of 2023-03-14 sat behind the exploitation curve: Assetnote published working Python exploit code on 2023-02-02 and IceFire was encrypting Faspex hosts on 2023-03-09. Patching on the deadline was legitimately compliant and still late, so the upgrade only counts as remediation when paired with a compromise assessment of the host.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on PackageRelayController#relay_package entries in /opt/aspera/faspex/log, on HTTP 500 bodies containing uid=/gid= command output, and on the Faspex Ruby process spawning sh, curl or wget children.
detection.adequacy: Every one of these signals fires after Kernel eval has already run — the log line is the record of a successful deserialization, not a warning before it — so detection buys eviction speed rather than prevention on a single-request pre-auth RCE.

response.what_would_have_worked: Hunt /opt/aspera/faspex for second-stage payloads and IceFire artifacts (.ifire renames, SHA-1 b676c38d5c309b64ab98c2cd82044891134a9973), rebuild the appliance, and notify every counterparty whose files transited the transfer hub.
response.adequacy: Rebuild is the only reliable eviction path once code has executed as the service account, and the counterparty notification is the part organisations skip — a managed-file-transfer breach is simultaneously a breach of every partner whose data crossed the box.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality is the control that would have removed this exposure, but CM-7 inventories packages, services and listening ports — not the dormant Rails routes an application still answers. A site fully conformant with CM-7 was still publishing an unauthenticated relay_package endpoint in front of a YAML.load sink.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: The vulnerability-handling procedure had every input it needed and still mis-ranked the asset: a file-transfer hub rated as an ordinary internal application queues behind higher-classified hosts, which is exactly the scheduling lag IceFire monetised on 2023-03-09.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 is assessed on how the deployed system is hardened, and no operator-side configuration of 4.4.2 PL1 closed this path — the gadget chain fires inside the application's own parse of the external_emails field. A strong B4 rating and total exposure to this CVE were fully compatible.

AU-ISM-1546.gap: ISM 1546's 48-hour window for an internet-facing application with a working exploit cannot be met by an appliance upgrade that requires a scheduled file-transfer outage and partner coordination, so the control sets a timeframe that is unachievable on precisely the asset class it matters most on.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The signal was maximal on every axis A.8.8 uses to prioritise — CVSS 9.8, EPSS 0.99968, KEV with ransomware status Known — yet Faspex is typically owned by a business unit rather than the server estate, so the risk-rated schedule reaches it only after the recognised internet-facing list.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-47986 was KEV-listed on 2023-02-21 with ransomware status Known, but Assetnote's working exploit was public on 2023-02-02 and IceFire was encrypting Faspex hosts on 2023-03-09 — five days before the 2023-03-14 KEV due date — so a legitimately compliant schedule was still late. Binding the clock to the KEV listing instead of to the risk rating a business-unit-owned file-transfer hub receives is what reaches this asset before the exploitation curve does.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR runbook for any perimeter device that suffers a pre-auth RCE CVE in active exploitation MUST default to config-exfil + rebuild + credential rotation, not patch-in-place. Patch-in-place leaves attacker-installed implants intact.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-47986 reaches Kernel eval as the Faspex service account from one unauthenticated POST to /aspera/faspex/package_relay/relay_package, and the fix (4.4.2 PL2) only deletes the obsolete route — it evicts nothing already dropped into /opt/aspera/faspex, so an internet-facing transfer appliance upgraded after the exploit went public is patched and still owned. The lesson's own remediation is rebuild plus counterparty notification, which no patch record captures.

CVE-2022-41223.name: Mitel MiVoice Connect Code Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An attacker holding a MiVoice Connect Director administrator session, reachable from the adjacent voice or management network, writes crafted data into the Director database component. Because the component does not restrict the stored data type, the injected value is later handled as code and executes inside the Director application, turning routine PBX configuration access into arbitrary code execution.
attack_vector.privileges_required: high — PR:H, a Director administrator session is the entire precondition, and AV:A means the attacker must already sit on the adjacent voice or management network
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, UI:N; the injection itself is trivial once the session exists, though no public exploit code has ever surfaced (zero Exploit-DB records, no Metasploit module, no nuclei template)
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — privately reported to Mitel and credited by name to Patrick Bennett of CrowdStrike in Product Security Advisory 22-0008. No AI system appears in the advisory, in NVD, or in any secondary reporting.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the remediation Mitel delivers through customer-portal Security Bulletin 22-0008-001 for MiVoice Connect 19.3 (22.22.6100.0) and earlier, and remove the standing shared Director administrator credential in favour of named accounts with MFA.
prevention.adequacy: Patching is necessary but only half the answer, and it is hard to evidence: Mitel's public advisory names no fixed build number, so remediated state cannot be checked against a version string. Because the exploit's whole cost is holding an admin credential, a patched PBX still operated through a shared vendor/reseller/staff account leaves the identity precondition untouched.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting when Director administrative authentication arrives from a host or VLAN that has never administered the PBX, and when Director configuration records store code or script syntax where a scalar value is expected.
detection.adequacy: Both signals are practical, but UC platforms are rarely forwarded into the SIEM at all — the Director host is usually monitored for telephony availability, not for administrative anomaly, so the detection exists in principle and is unwired in practice.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rotate every MiVoice Connect administrator credential, review the Director host for unexpected child processes and new files after configuration changes, and plan migration to MiVoice Business ahead of End of Technical Support on 2029-12-31.
response.adequacy: Credential rotation is the response step that actually closes the path, since code execution here is downstream of a credential the attacker already held; the migration is the durable answer because the platform is in lifecycle wind-down.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: AC-6 is satisfied on paper by documented role definitions that are never enforced on the PBX itself, where a single shared 'admin' account is routinely used by the telephony vendor, the reseller and internal staff at once — and that shared credential is the whole exploitation cost.

NIS2-Art21-identity-management.gap: Identity and access management is typically federated and hardened for email, VPN and cloud while telephony keeps a legacy local account store, so the one unmanaged privileged identity in the estate is the one that converts straight into code execution on the voice system incident response depends on.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2 evidence is drawn from corporate IdP coverage and privileged-access workflows, but Director authenticates against its own account database and is commonly excluded from federation as vendor-managed facilities kit — so the exact credential this CVE needs sits outside the identity estate that was assessed.

AU-Essential-8-MFA.gap: The Essential Eight counts MFA on internet-facing services, remote access and privileged actions on important data repositories; an on-premises PBX administration interface reachable only from the internal network is outside that scope entirely, so the single control that would price this attack out is never asked about.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.15.gap: Access control is evidenced only against systems named in the ISMS scope statement, and enterprise telephony is frequently scoped out as facilities infrastructure — leaving the entire exploitation precondition ungoverned while the certificate reads clean.

new_control_requirements.name: FLEET-CONTROL-PLANE-ADMIN-PRIVILEGE-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: Administrators of fleet-control-plane systems (MDM/UEM, EDR consoles, identity providers, container orchestrators, configuration management) must be classified as a distinct privilege tier above application admins, with: PAM-jumphost-only access, FIDO2 step-up per session, just-in-time elevation with approval workflow, separate identity from any other admin role, and dedicated PAW (privileged access workstation) hardware. Compliance frameworks must enumerate this tier explicitly rather than collapsing it into 'admin'.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41223 costs the attacker nothing beyond holding a MiVoice Connect Director administrator session — the injection itself is trivial — and that session is routinely one shared 'admin' credential used by the telephony vendor, the reseller and internal staff at once, against Director's own local account store outside the corporate IdP. Mitel's fix ships through a portal bulletin with no published build number, so a patched PBX operated through the same shared credential leaves the entire exploitation precondition intact; only tiering the voice control plane with named identities, step-up authentication and brokered access removes it.

CVE-2022-40765.name: Mitel MiVoice Connect Command Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An authenticated attacker with adjacent-network access sends a request to the Mitel Edge Gateway whose URL parameters are not restricted, so shell metacharacters — semicolons, pipes, backticks, $( ) — pass into an OS command invocation. Mitel and CISA both describe execution 'within the context of the system', meaning OS-level command execution on the appliance that terminates remote phones and bridges them into the internal voice network.
attack_vector.privileges_required: high — PR:H, an authenticated high-privilege session, and AV:A adjacency to the Edge Gateway's management surface
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, UI:N; injecting into an unfiltered URL parameter is trivial once reachable, and no public exploit code exists (no Exploit-DB entry, no Metasploit module, no nuclei template)
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — reported through coordinated disclosure by Patrick Bennett and Brian Pitchford of CrowdStrike, credited in Mitel Product Security Advisory 22-0007. No AI tooling is credited in any primary source.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the remediation delivered through customer-portal Security Bulletin 22-0007-001 for MiVoice Connect 19.3 (22.22.6100.0) and earlier, and restrict the Edge Gateway management surface to a dedicated telephony management segment so the AV:A adjacency is not available from general user VLANs.
prevention.adequacy: The update restarts the gateway and drops remote-phone registrations, so it needs a maintenance window — and because Mitel published no fixed build number, applying it cannot be verified from any public version string. Segmentation is the half of prevention that survives the platform's End of Technical Support date of 2029-12-31.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on Edge Gateway request logs whose parameter values carry command separators instead of the expected identifiers, and on the gateway host creating unexpected processes or initiating outbound connections.
detection.adequacy: Useful, but it asks the boundary device to report its own compromise. Once command execution lands on the gateway the attacker controls the process that would generate the telemetry, so detection is only reliable where gateway logs are shipped off-box in real time.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat the Edge Gateway as fully compromised — rebuild it from vendor media, rotate PBX administrator credentials, and hunt for lateral movement from the gateway into the internal voice VLAN.
response.adequacy: Rebuild is the correct posture for a boundary appliance that reached OS-level execution; patch-in-place leaves any persistence the attacker planted while they held root-equivalent access on the device.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: SC-7 treats the Edge Gateway as an enforcement point, but this injection executes OS commands on that enforcement point — so every boundary assumption is being upheld by a host under attacker control, and SC-7 carries no requirement to monitor the boundary device for its own compromise.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Art.21 network-security assessment credits the presence of segmentation and presumes the segmenting devices are trustworthy; command execution on the gateway that bridges remote phones into the internal voice network collapses exactly the separation the assessment scored.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 evidence for a UC estate reduces to 'vendor-supported appliance, patched per vendor guidance', but with the fix living only in a login-gated bulletin there is no published version string an assessor can reconcile against — the control's evidence becomes the operator's own assertion.

AU-ISM-1546.gap: ISM 1546's verification model assumes a public fixed version to reconcile the patch register against, and Mitel disclosed the fixed build only through customer-portal bulletin 22-0007-001, so an ISM-aligned register for this platform cannot be closed out against anything verifiable.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.22.gap: Network segregation is the control this CVE really tests, and voice networks are commonly segregated in the design document while softphones, provisioning VLANs and management jump paths bridge them in practice — so the A.8.22 conformance statement describes a boundary that does not exist.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR runbook for any perimeter device that suffers a pre-auth RCE CVE in active exploitation MUST default to config-exfil + rebuild + credential rotation, not patch-in-place. Patch-in-place leaves attacker-installed implants intact.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-40765 executes OS commands on the Mitel Edge Gateway itself — the boundary device that terminates remote phones and bridges them into the internal voice network — and KEV records ransomware use against the entry. The vendor update merely restarts the gateway, so any persistence planted while the attacker held root-equivalent access on the appliance survives it; the only sound posture is rebuild from vendor media plus PBX credential rotation.

new_control_requirements.name: FIREWALL-EGRESS-TELEMETRY-SEPARATE-TRUST-ZONE
new_control_requirements.description: Firewall and other perimeter-trust-boundary devices must forward syslog, threat logs, and authentication logs to a SIEM hosted in a separate trust zone (different management plane, different credentials, different authentication path). Telemetry stored on the compromised device is destroyed by the attacker; telemetry on a separate-trust-zone collector survives.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-40765's only observable artifacts are Edge Gateway request logs showing command separators in URL parameters and unexpected gateway process/outbound activity — telemetry produced by the very host the injection runs on, which the attacker owns the moment execution lands. Shipping the gateway's logs in real time to a collector on a separate management plane is what makes the boundary device's own compromise detectable at all.

attack_vector.description: remote_agent.php is reachable without authentication and authorises callers by resolving the client IP to a hostname present in the poller table. get_client_addr() prefers attacker-controllable proxy headers over REMOTE_ADDR, so setting X-Forwarded-For to the Cacti server's own IP makes gethostbyaddr() return the hostname already sitting in the default poller row and the authorisation check passes. With that bypassed, action=polldata reaches poll_for_data(), which interpolates the unfiltered poller_id request variable into a proc_open() invocation — so poller_id=;id executes shell commands as the web-server user.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N, unauthenticated; the only extra practical condition is one poller_item with the POLLER_ACTION_SCRIPT_PHP action, which stock templates such as 'Device - Uptime' create on virtually every production instance
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, UI:N; host_id and local_data_id are small integers the public Metasploit module brute-forces automatically, and EPSS sits at 0.99826 (99.959th percentile)
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Stefan Schiller of Sonar found it through manual and static review of the remote_agent.php authorisation logic, with an independent discovery by Steven Seeley via ZDI. No AI system is credited in GHSA-6p93-p743-35gf, in Sonar's research, or in NVD.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrade to Cacti 1.2.23 or 1.3.0 (or the distribution backports shipped as Debian DSA-5298-1 and DLA-3252-1), and stop the web tier from honouring client-supplied X-Forwarded-For values that are not injected by a trusted reverse proxy.
prevention.adequacy: The fix shipped 2022-12-05, MooBot and ShellBot were mass-exploiting from January 2023, and the KEV due date was 2023-03-09 — so a compliant patch cadence still ran a two-month exposure. Upgrading also does not undo the disclosure: every SNMP community string and device credential in the Cacti database must be rotated because the exploit's value to the attacker was harvesting them.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on unauthenticated requests to remote_agent.php carrying an X-Forwarded-For header equal to the Cacti server's own address, on poller_id parameters containing shell metacharacters, and on www-data spawning curl, wget, perl or sh.
detection.adequacy: Strong signals with a real blind spot: a spoofed X-Forwarded-For is byte-identical to a legitimate reverse-proxy header, so the reliable trigger is the header value matching the server's own IP rather than the header's presence.

response.what_would_have_worked: Hunt for MooBot and ShellBot artifacts — perl bots masquerading as /usr/sbin/sshd or /usr/sbin/mysql, callbacks to troon[.]dns[.]army and the FortiGuard-documented C2 set — then rebuild the host and rotate every credential the Cacti database held.
response.adequacy: Credential rotation is the step that limits blast radius beyond the host, because a Cacti compromise hands over the monitoring credentials for the entire monitored estate, not just one server.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: Input validation failed twice in one request — an attacker-controlled HTTP header became the authoritative client identity for an authorisation decision, and poller_id reached proc_open() unfiltered — and neither failure is visible to the WAF or API gateway where SI-10 is normally evidenced.
