new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-4262's fix is V8 commit 27fa951ae4a3801126e84bc94d5c82dd2370d18b in Chrome 108.0.5359.94, but auto-update only stages it on disk — a browser process running for days keeps executing the vulnerable V8 build until it relaunches, and SI-2, NIS2 Art.21(2)(e) and the E8 application-patching control are all discharged at 'update installed'. A security-channel ring that cannot be deferred past 24h, paired with RelaunchNotification enforcement and extended to every Chromium-derived browser on the estate, is what actually retires the binary.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-4262 was KEV-listed 2022-12-05 as a live zero-day inside Variston's Heliconia framework — Google shipped 108.0.5359.94 only after TAG recovered a working exploit — yet a CVSS 8.8 discounted by UI:R and S:U reads as a routine renderer bug beneath a queue of unauthenticated 9.8s. The KEV entry is the only input that ranks it correctly, so it has to carry its own mitigation deadline instead of feeding the risk-ordered A.8.8 queue.

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated POST of Content-Type text/xml to /oam/server/opensso/sessionservice on the Access Manager managed server (default TCP 14100) carries a RequestSet/Request document whose CDATA authIdentifier holds a base64 requester attribute decoding to the literal prefix 'object:' followed by a serialized Java object graph. Access Manager deserializes it with no class allowlist, and a modified CVE-2020-2883 WebLogic gadget chain runs OS commands as the application-server account — after which the attacker owns the SSO broker and can mint accounts with arbitrary privileges.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N/UI:N; the deserialization endpoint sits in front of the login flow. Execution lands as the application-server account (the 'oracle' user on Linux), not as root
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, a single deterministic HTTP POST with no race and no memory-corruption reliability problem; Metasploit ships prebuilt gadget binaries for 12.2.1.3.0 and 12.2.1.4.0, leaving a hand-built chain for 11.1.2.3.0 as the sole remaining friction
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Jang (@testanull) and Peterjson found it while building a proof-of-concept for an unrelated bug, with Y4er credited for the modified WebLogic gadget chain. The manual gadget-chain construction described in their write-up is the opposite of automated discovery, and no AI tooling appears anywhere in the disclosure chain.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the January 2022 Critical Patch Update with OPatch to the Access Manager Oracle home and restart the WebLogic managed servers — the 12c patch removes /oam/server/opensso/sessionservice outright rather than filtering deserialized classes. Where the CPU cannot land immediately, block /oam/server/opensso/* at the reverse proxy and restrict TCP 14100.
prevention.adequacy: No hot-patch path exists, so remediation costs a maintenance window — and Access Manager 11.1.2.0.0 with WebLogic Server 10.3.6 has been end of life since 2022-01-01 and outside Critical Patch Update scope, so that population has no fix at all and must be migrated rather than patched.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on POSTs to the sessionservice endpoint whose base64 requester attribute decodes to the 'object:' prefix, on child processes spawned by the WebLogic JVM, on curl or wget staging into /tmp or %TEMP% immediately after, and on new Access Manager administrative accounts or altered authentication policies appearing without change control.
detection.adequacy: The pre-authentication fingerprint is public in a KEV-tagged Nuclei template and in published Shodan/FOFA queries, so attackers enumerate exposure faster than most operators inventory it — and post-exploitation account creation is indistinguishable from legitimate SSO administration without a baseline.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rebuild the OAM host from vendor media, invalidate every session and token it issued, audit the directory for accounts minted and policies altered during the intrusion, then re-federate the applications behind it.
response.adequacy: Host rebuild alone is not enough: the finders documented that takeover permits creating users with arbitrary privileges, so identities minted during the intrusion survive unless the directory is audited too, and the response scope is every application federated behind the broker.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: The endpoint base64-decodes the requester attribute, recognises the 'object:' prefix and hands the bytes straight to Java deserialization with no class allowlist. Length, type, format and encoding checks cannot reject an object graph whose danger lies in which classes it instantiates — Oracle conceded the point by deleting the 12c endpoint rather than validating what reaches it.

NIS2-Art21-identity-management.gap: Access Manager is what enforces session policy, step-up authentication and authorisation for every application behind it, and one unauthenticated POST puts the attacker beneath all of it as the application-server account. Identity measures are inherited wholesale from a compromised broker, and no obligation treats the IdP's own patch state as an identity-management control.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: The vulnerable deserialization path sits in front of the login flow, so MFA coverage, privileged-account separation and joiner-mover-leaver hygiene are all measured on a control plane an attacker can take without touching an account — and B2 has no outcome asking whether OAM carries the January 2022 CPU with /oam/server/opensso/* network-restricted.

AU-Essential-8-MFA.gap: Oracle Access Manager is the broker implementing MFA across most Fusion Middleware estates, and this exploit runs beside the enforcement point rather than through it, so Maturity Level 3 phishing-resistant MFA is fully deployed and entirely irrelevant. Takeover also permits minting users with arbitrary privileges, which produces identities that satisfy the control by construction.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.15.gap: Access control is audited as documented policy expressed through identity, role and entitlement management, which offers nothing against a code-level defect in the product implementing it — EPSS 0.963, an ExcellentRanking Metasploit module and a KEV-tagged Nuclei template. On 11.1.2.0.0 with WebLogic 10.3.6, outside CPU scope since 2022-01-01, no patch can ever realign the implementation with the policy.

new_control_requirements.name: ENTERPRISE-ERP-MANAGEMENT-FUNCTION-AUTHENTICATION
new_control_requirements.description: An enterprise ERP platform (Oracle PeopleSoft, Oracle E-Business Suite, SAP, and similar) must authenticate every management-plane and environment-management function before it can be invoked, and must not expose any takeover-capable function to an unauthenticated network caller. Segment the ERP management surface from untrusted networks and place it behind authenticated access control. The distinguishing test: send an unauthenticated network request to each environment-management / configuration endpoint on a staging instance and confirm it is refused before any privileged action runs - paper 'ERP access control' policies that attest user-login authentication while leaving a critical management function reachable without credentials still permit unauthenticated takeover.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2021-35587 lets one unauthenticated HTTP POST to /oam/server/opensso/sessionservice take over Oracle Access Manager — the broker enforcing session policy, step-up authentication and authorisation for every Fusion Middleware application behind it — and the finders documented that takeover also permits creating users with arbitrary privileges, minting identities that satisfy the MFA control by construction. NIS2 Art.21(2)(d), CAF B2 and E8 MFA all measure identity outcomes on that broker; none requires that no takeover-capable function on it be reachable without credentials.

new_control_requirements.name: APPSERVER-REMOTING-PROTOCOL-RESTRICTION
new_control_requirements.description: Application servers that expose binary remoting protocols (Oracle WebLogic T3/IIOP, and equivalents) must restrict those protocols to trusted hosts and apply vendor critical patch updates on an accelerated schedule when a remoting flaw is KEV-listed. Place T3/IIOP behind a connection filter (weblogic.security.net.ConnectionFilterImpl) or network ACLs so only known hosts can reach them, never expose the ports to untrusted networks, and apply the Oracle CPU bundle (with server restart) rather than deferring to the next quarterly window. The distinguishing test: from an untrusted network segment, attempt an unauthenticated T3/IIOP connection to a staging WebLogic instance and confirm it is refused at the connection filter before any data is served - a perimeter-firewall + quarterly-patch policy that still leaves T3/IIOP reachable from an internal untrusted segment leaves the unauthenticated data-access path open.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2021-35587 base64-decodes the requester attribute, recognises the 'object:' prefix and hands the bytes to Java deserialization of a WebLogic gadget chain with no class allowlist, so no SI-10 length, type, format or encoding check can reject it — Oracle conceded the point by deleting the 12c endpoint outright. The controls that do work are exactly this requirement's: restrict the WebLogic-hosted unauthenticated data path (/oam/server/opensso/*, TCP 14100) to known hosts, and apply the January 2022 Critical Patch Update with OPatch and a managed-server restart instead of waiting for the next quarterly window.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: Network-reachable end-of-life devices with no vendor patch path must be isolated and decommissioned within a bounded window; mandatory compensating segmentation applies until removal since no remediation exists.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2021-35587 has no fix for Access Manager 11.1.2.0.0 on WebLogic Server 10.3.6 — end of life since 2022-01-01 and, per Oracle's own advisory, not even tested for the vulnerabilities the Critical Patch Update addresses — while the endpoint is pre-auth fingerprintable by a KEV-tagged Nuclei template at EPSS 0.963 with an ExcellentRanking Metasploit module. No patch can ever realign that build with the documented A.5.15 access-control policy, so segmentation plus a bounded migration-and-decommission window is the only remediation that exists.

CVE-2022-4135.name: Google Chromium GPU Heap Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: From a renderer the attacker already controls, ordinary GLES2 traffic binds a texture created from a shared image and then references mipmap level 1 or higher — CreateGLES2TextureWithLightRef hardcodes max_levels to 1 while validation checks against the computed MaxLevelsForTarget, producing a non-linear heap overflow with a controlled offset inside the more-privileged GPU process. The in-the-wild path corrupted a command-buffer bucket to read GPU-process memory and defeat ASLR, then hijacked control flow with a ROP chain.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none in the vector (PR:N — the page is served to any visitor, UI:R to open it), but the real precondition is renderer compromise: Project Zero recorded the analysed chain as also incorporating CVE-2022-3723, so a separate bug must land first
attack_vector.complexity: low once inside the renderer — AC:L, reached through documented GLES2 calls with no race and no timing dependency. The cost is the prerequisite renderer bug, and only a crash reproducer was ever published; the weaponized sample was withheld
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — the Chrome stable-channel note credits Clement Lecigne of Google's Threat Analysis Group, who surfaced it by analysing a live exploit, and Project Zero's RCA by Sergei Glazunov lists no bug-introducing CL, consistent with a manually-found logic inconsistency. No AI tooling is credited.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Update to Chrome 107.0.5304.121 (107.0.5304.121/.122 on Windows) or Edge 107.0.1418.62 and force a relaunch so the GPU process picks up the fixed code, then sweep packaged desktop applications — CEF hosts and Electron apps pin a Chromium base and never follow the browser update channel.
prevention.adequacy: Browser patching leaves the largest exposed population untouched: embedded Chromium has no update channel to obey, and a machine that has staged the update on disk keeps a vulnerable GPU process alive until the browser restarts.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Correlate GPU-process crash telemetry and repeated WebGL context loss clustered on a single origin with a renderer compromise on the same host in the same session.
detection.adequacy: Weak by design: Chromium bug 1392715 stayed access-restricted and the exploit sample was explicitly withheld, so operators had no indicator or signature to hunt with during the exposure window.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat any renderer compromise in that period as potentially chained into a GPU-process escape, rebuild the host, and rotate the credentials the browser held.
response.adequacy: The S:C scope change means the blast radius is the machine rather than the tab, so host rebuild is the right call — but with no exploit sample published, retrospectively scoping which sessions were actually chained was guesswork.

NIST-800-53-SC-39.gap: The separate execution domain is the thing that breaks: ordinary GLES2 traffic from a compromised renderer binds a shared-image texture at a mipmap level level_infos was never sized for and writes out of bounds in the more-privileged GPU process. CVSS S:C records the crossed boundary, and SC-39 has no compensating requirement for the case where the isolation mechanism is itself the defect.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Handling presumes an actionable disclosure event, and entities received a version number and nothing more — Chromium bug 1392715 stayed access-restricted and the exploit sample was withheld — so there was no indicator or signature on which to judge whether renderer-compromise telemetry from that period had already been chained into a GPU-process escape.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Browser protection is evidenced through configuration — extension allow-lists, site isolation, disabled plugins, managed policy — and none of it reaches a path that rides WebGL2, enabled by default and disabled by no CAF-aligned baseline, after a separate renderer bug has already landed.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The control is scored on the browser settings surface, but the escape is reached with a webgl2 context and blendColor() from an already-compromised renderer, so a Maturity Level 3 endpoint is exactly as exposed as a Maturity Level 0 one — the defect lives beneath the settings, in the validating command decoder's level_infos bounds check.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Vulnerability management is inventory-driven and the inventory rarely lists the affected component: CEF hosts, Electron applications and Edge below 107.0.1418.62 all pin a Chromium base and never follow the browser update channel, so a register showing 'browsers patched' still carries vulnerable Chromium 107.0.5304.x inside packaged desktop apps with no ticket against it.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-4135's fix (Chromium commit 2bd6ab1a16090fd20d422c11d794edf5c0ff6b89, Chrome 107.0.5304.121, Edge 107.0.1418.62) only takes effect once the GPU process relaunches, and Google disclosed it with bug 1392715 access-restricted and the in-the-wild sample explicitly withheld — entities received a version number, no indicator and no signature. With nothing to hunt, an update ring that cannot defer the security channel past 24h plus a forced relaunch was the entire actionable response available under NIS2 vulnerability handling.

new_control_requirements.name: TIER-3-DEPENDENCY-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: Supply chain inventory must extend to tier-3 dependencies (dependencies of dependencies of direct dependencies). SBOM coverage for libsystemd-class transitive dependencies cannot be omitted under SR-3.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-4135's longest-exposed population is not browsers but embedded Chromium: CEF hosts and Electron applications pin a Chromium base and never follow the browser update channel, and Edge below 107.0.1418.62 carries base 107.0.5304.150. An A.8.8 register showing 'browsers patched' still holds vulnerable Chromium 107.0.5304.x inside packaged desktop applications with no remediation ticket, because the affected component is a bundled dependency the inventory never enumerates.

CVE-2022-41049.name: Microsoft Windows Mark of the Web (MOTW) Security Feature Bypass Vulnerability (CVE-2022-41049)

attack_vector.description: The attacker sets the low bit of the per-file ExternalAttributes field in a ZIP central directory (0x01 or 0x21) so extracted members carry the read-only attribute. When Explorer extracts them, zipfldr.dll's CheckUnZippedFile calls CAttachmentServices::SaveWithUI to write the Zone.Identifier alternate data stream, NtCreateFile fails with ACCESS_DENIED against the read-only file, and extraction completes with no Mark-of-the-Web and no error surfaced. SmartScreen, Smart App Control and Office internet-macro blocking all key off that stream, so every one of them stays silent when the victim opens the payload.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the victim only has to open a downloaded archive and double-click a file inside it (UI:R), which is exactly the action the missing warning makes routine
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, and the 'exploit' is one bit set in a ZIP central directory that any archiver can produce, with no race window, no heap grooming and no version-specific offsets across the whole affected Windows range
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Will Dormann of CERT/CC found the behaviour by hand in May 2022 while dragging files out of a mounted read-only ISO into a ZIP, and Kuba Gretzky's root-cause analysis was manual reverse engineering of zipfldr.dll. No AI tooling is credited by Microsoft, 0patch or either researcher.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Install the 2022-11-08 Windows security updates — KB5019980, KB5019961, KB5019959, KB5019966, KB5019964, KB5019970 and KB5019081/KB5019080 — and reboot. On Windows 7 and Server 2008 R2, which the November update never covered, 0patch's reboot-free micropatch is the only remediation that exists.
prevention.adequacy: The vendor fix arrived four months after Dormann's July 2022 report while MSRC's own record showed Exploitation Detected on both current and older releases — and for the end-of-life platforms it does not exist at all, so a third-party micropatch is the entire prevention story there.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Hunt archives that carry a Zone.Identifier stream while their extracted contents carry none, read-only attributes on files extracted from internet-sourced archives, and ZIP central directories that set the read-only bit on member files — anomalous for archives produced by normal packaging tooling.
detection.adequacy: The failure is silent — no error, no log entry, no SmartScreen verdict — so detection has to look for the absence of a marker rather than for an event, which no default Windows tooling does.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat any macro-enabled document or executable that ran without a prompt during the exposure window as executed malware: isolate the host, hunt follow-on staging, and re-scan Downloads and mail-attachment extraction paths for files missing the :Zone.Identifier:$DATA stream.
response.adequacy: Retrospective sweeps are possible because the missing stream persists on disk, but nothing links a given untagged file back to the archive that stripped the marker, so scoping the incident stays imprecise.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: On Windows every post-download malicious-code judgement — SmartScreen, Smart App Control, Office macro blocking — is downstream of the Zone.Identifier stream, and here that stream is never written because NtCreateFile is denied against the read-only extracted file. The controls fail open with no error, no log and no signature, and SI-3 never requires verifying the taint-marking mechanism itself.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: The flaw ran from Dormann's July 2022 report to the 2022-11-08 fix — more than 90 days — while MSRC recorded Exploited='Yes' with Exploitation Detected on both latest and older releases. With no advisory to act on and no notification trigger during that period, a fully compliant handling process produced zero protective action while exploitation was confirmed.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Mark-of-the-Web is a platform trust primitive rather than a configurable setting, so no B4 hardening item reads 'confirm the OS actually tags files extracted from a ZIP'. With no privilege, no memory corruption and no operator misconfiguration involved, a B4 assessment passes across a fleet where any downloaded archive can deliver its contents untagged.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The requirement to block internet-origin Office macros depends on Office reading Mark-of-the-Web to decide what 'internet-origin' means; a crafted ZIP makes a downloaded macro document look local, so a Maturity Level 3 macro control passes its audit with the GPO in place and still opens the attacker's document with macros enabled — configured and ineffective are indistinguishable to the assessor.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: Coverage percentages, signature currency, behavioural detection and quarantine workflow all presume the protection layer sees the file as untrusted, but stripping the trust signal in the central directory means SmartScreen and Smart App Control never engage and execution looks like an ordinary local launch. On Windows 7 and Server 2008 R2, never covered by the November 2022 update, no vendor fix exists to restore the marker at all.

new_control_requirements.name: ARCHIVE-CONTENT-TYPE-PROVENANCE
new_control_requirements.description: Archive and document handlers must dispatch rendering/execution on the content-verified file type rather than the displayed name or extension, and must propagate Mark-of-the-Web to every extracted file.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41049 is exactly a failure to propagate Mark-of-the-Web to extracted files: a ZIP central directory that sets the read-only bit on member files makes NtCreateFile fail with ACCESS_DENIED when the extracted file's :Zone.Identifier:$DATA stream is written, so the payload lands untagged and every MOTW-gated judgement — SmartScreen, Smart App Control, Office macro blocking — fails open with no error, no log and no signature. B4 has no hardening item that reads 'confirm the OS tags files extracted from a ZIP', and SI-3 never requires verifying the taint-marking mechanism itself.

new_control_requirements.name: DOWNLOAD-PROVENANCE-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Enforce Mark-of-the-Web / content-provenance on all internet-sourced files and block execution of provenance-stripped shortcuts, installers, and script hosts regardless of a reputation service verdict, which attackers bypass by design.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41049 makes a downloaded macro document look local, and Office decides 'internet-origin' by reading Mark-of-the-Web, so a Maturity Level 3 macro GPO passes its audit with the policy set and still opens the attacker's document with macros enabled — configured and ineffective are indistinguishable to the assessor. Provenance has to be enforced on the internet-sourced archive and its extracted contents, with execution blocked on provenance-stripped documents and script hosts, rather than trusting a marker the archive handler can be tricked into omitting.

new_control_requirements.name: PROTECTION-MECHANISM-FAILURE-CLASS-REGRESSION
new_control_requirements.description: Detonation chambers, EDR rules, and AppLocker/WDAC policies covering protection-mechanism classes (MOTW, SmartScreen, AMSI, ASR, WDAC, Driver Block Rules) must include class-level regression testing executed on every patch deployment, not just one-off bypass-CVE remediation. The test battery for class-X must include all historic class-X bypass primitives — incomplete patches re-introduce risk that one-off testing does not detect.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41049 sat live from Dormann's July 2022 report to the 2022-11-08 updates — more than 90 days with MSRC recording Exploited='Yes' and Exploitation Detected — and it is one of a run of MOTW-primitive bypasses that kept returning (CVE-2022-44698, then CVE-2023-24880). An operator-run battery that re-executes every historic MOTW bypass on each patch deployment surfaces the gap without waiting for an advisory, and is the only way to confirm the marker survives on hosts the November update never covered, such as Windows 7 and Server 2008 R2.

CVE-2017-5521.name: NETGEAR Multiple Devices Exposure of Sensitive Information Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An attacker who can reach the router's web management interface cancels the authentication prompt, is redirected to /unauth.cgi?id=<token>, scrapes that token and requests /passwordrecovered.cgi?id=<token> — the router replies with an HTML table carrying the admin username and password in cleartext, which is then used to log into the GUI and rewrite the device's DNS servers. A second variant needs no valid token at all: passwordrecovered.cgi answers the first request after a reboot regardless of the id value.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the credential-disclosure request is entirely unauthenticated. AV:N holds only where remote management is enabled (off by default); otherwise the attacker needs LAN/WLAN adjacency or a LAN-side browser coaxed into issuing the two requests.
attack_vector.complexity: high — AC:H, but the metric reflects preconditions rather than difficulty: password recovery must never have been enabled on the device, and the token-free variant only answers on the first request after a reboot. The working exploit is a forty-line Python script issuing one GET to scrape the token and one to retrieve the credential.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Simon Kenin of Trustwave SpiderLabs found it by hand-testing web interfaces across 31 device models and published it as TWSL2017-003 after a nine-month coordinated disclosure. No AI tooling in the discovery or weaponisation path.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Flash the fixed firmware NETGEAR published in KB 30632 for the 19 supported router models and for the C6300 (released through the subscriber's ISP), and on the twelve devices that never received a build apply the vendor workaround in full — enable the password-recovery feature so the exploit fails permanently, and confirm remote management is disabled.
prevention.adequacy: Firmware closes it on supported models, but eight routers and four DSL gateways never got a fix, so for those the configuration workaround is the entire remediation — and either half alone leaves the device exposed. CISA's required action adds that any affected unit now past end-of-life should be disconnected rather than kept in service.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on the /unauth.cgi to /passwordrecovered.cgi request pair from a single source, and on any router HTTP response body containing the strings 'Router Admin Username' and 'Router Admin Password'.
detection.adequacy: The signature is unambiguous, but branch and home-office CPE is almost never fronted by anything that inspects its own management traffic, and the exchange is two requests long — detection realistically fires after the credential has already left the device.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rotate the router admin password, re-verify the configured DNS servers (DNS rewrite is the documented post-exploitation move), turn remote management off and password recovery on, and replace any of the twelve models that never received fixed firmware.
response.adequacy: Rotation only holds once the disclosure path is closed: password recovery has to be enabled first, or the replacement credential is handed out by the same unauthenticated request.

NIST-800-53-IA-2.gap: IA-2 hardens the authentication exchange, but the router discloses its admin credential to a caller that never attempted authentication — there is no authenticator to strengthen, rotate or multi-factor because no IA-2 decision point is reached, and consumer-grade CPE of this class typically sits outside the authorization boundary the control is assessed against.

EU-CRA-Art13.gap: The Cyber Resilience Act's manufacturer vulnerability-handling and declared-support-period duties post-date this CVE by seven years, so nothing compelled NETGEAR to ship firmware for the twelve devices it left unfixed — their owners have a manual UI workaround and no manufacturer remedy to invoke.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2 governs entitlements against identities the operator administers, with joiner-mover-leaver process and credential-strength policy; here the device itself hands the credential over before any authorisation is evaluated, and CAF's identity scope stops at enterprise IdM rather than the router terminating the circuit.

AU-ISM-1546.gap: ISM-1546's patch clocks run from a vendor release date, and twelve of the affected models have no release to measure from — no maturity level is reachable by patching an AC1450 or a DGN2200v4, and the position that actually works (enable password recovery, disable remote management) has no expression the control can evidence.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: Configuration management works by detecting drift from a baseline, and the exploitable state is the as-shipped baseline: password recovery is disabled out of the box and the exploit only fails once an operator turns it on, so a device in perfect agreement with its build standard is fully exposed and drift monitoring raises nothing.

new_control_requirements.name: UNSUPPORTED-NETWORK-DEVICE-ENUMERATION-AND-RETIREMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Every network-attached embedded device (IP cameras, video servers, NVRs, routers, print/scan appliances) must carry an end-of-support date in the asset inventory, and any device past that date that exposes a remotely reachable management or media surface must be removed from untrusted networks and scheduled for replacement — patching is not an option once the vendor retires the model. The distinguishing test: query the asset inventory for devices whose firmware lifecycle has ended and whose management interface is reachable from an untrusted segment; any non-empty result that lacks a replace-or-formally-risk-accept decision is a finding. Paper patch-management policies that assume a fix always exists leave actively-exploited EOL devices (GeoVision IP cameras, recruited by Mirai-style botnets) on the network indefinitely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2017-5521 — NETGEAR published fixed firmware for 19 router models in KB 30632 but left eight routers and four DSL gateways (AC1450, WNR1000v3, WNDR4000, DGN2200v4 and others) with no build at all, and CISA's KEV required action adds that any affected unit past end-of-life should be disconnected rather than kept in service. Only an inventory that carries each router's end-of-support date and forces a replace-or-risk-accept decision produces an action for those twelve models, because there is no vendor release to patch to.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2017-5521 — two unauthenticated requests to /unauth.cgi then /passwordrecovered.cgi return the router admin username and password in cleartext, with the exploit shipped in Exploit-DB 41205, a Nuclei template and a RouterSploit module; on the twelve unfixed models the entire remediation is the vendor workaround (enable password recovery AND disable remote management, either alone insufficient). The KEV clock has to bind documented compensating controls, not only firmware, which a patch timeframe measured from a vendor release date cannot express.

CVE-2011-4723.name: D-Link DIR-300 Router Cleartext Storage of a Password Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: The DIR-300 stores its administrator password without hashing, so an attacker with LAN or WLAN adjacency and a low-privilege foothold reads the credential straight out of the device's management surface — NVD records the retrieval path only as 'unspecified vectors', so there is no request shape to block, just a value that should never have been stored in recoverable form. The recovered password unlocks the router's entire configuration, and because SOHO admin passwords are heavily reused the realised damage usually lands on systems other than the router.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L combined with AV:A: the attacker needs a low-privilege foothold and LAN or WLAN adjacency to the router, not internet reachability
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; there is no exploitation primitive to execute. The password is simply not hashed, so recovery is a deterministic read with no race, no memory corruption and no brute force.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Sergey Scherbel of the Positive Research Center found it during a 2011 firmware audit and reported it as PT-2011-30. Password hashing was never implemented in the DIR-300 management system; no AI tooling was involved and none was plausible for the era.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Retire the DIR-300. D-Link did ship a fixed build on 2011-09-19, but the model was phased out on 2013-05-15 with last date of support 2015-05-15, and CISA's required action for this entry is disconnection rather than patching — so the reliable prevention is replacing the device and rotating every credential it ever held.
prevention.adequacy: Even the 2011 fix is unverifiable in practice: neither the advisory nor NVD names a fixed version — the affected CPE is the unversioned dir-300_firmware:- — so an operator cannot confirm remediation from a version string and has to reason from firmware release date. Replacement is the only outcome that can actually be evidenced.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Watching for configuration-export or firmware-backup downloads from the router by any client that is not the management station, and for router credentials appearing verbatim inside files pulled off the device.
detection.adequacy: Weak by construction: reading a password the device already stores in cleartext generates no authentication event and no failed-login sequence, so the first observable is usually the reuse of that credential somewhere else, long after the window has closed.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat the router's admin password as public — rotate it and every account sharing it, replace the hardware, and review DNS and firewall settings on any DIR-300 still deployed.
response.adequacy: Rotating on the device itself is close to pointless while the device stays in service, because the replacement password is stored exactly the same way; the response only holds once the hardware is gone.

NIST-800-53-SC-28.gap: A stored authenticator is precisely the data SC-28 protects, but the unhashed storage lives inside third-party firmware with no operator-reachable setting — the control states a requirement and supplies no lever, and a consumer router acting as branch CPE typically sits below the authorization boundary the SSP describes.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: Supplier-security measures presume a relationship in which requirements can be asserted; a retail SOHO router bought off a shelf carries no such channel, and D-Link's support obligations ended in 2015 while CISA still listed the flaw as known-exploited in 2022.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: C1 monitoring is built on analysing events that indicate an incident, and reading a password the device already holds in cleartext produces no event at all — no authentication attempt, no anomalous command, nothing to alert on at the moment of compromise.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The patching maturity ladder measures against a vendor stream, and the DIR-300's ended on 2015-05-15, so no maturity level is achievable for those assets; the action that satisfies the control's intent — physically removing the devices — is not something the model scores or evidences.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.24.gap: A cryptography policy forbidding unhashed storage of an admin password can be written, audited and passed in full while the offending device stays deployed, because A.8.24 binds cryptography the organisation itself applies rather than a supplier's failure to apply any.

new_control_requirements.name: UNSUPPORTED-NETWORK-DEVICE-ENUMERATION-AND-RETIREMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Every network-attached embedded device (IP cameras, video servers, NVRs, routers, print/scan appliances) must carry an end-of-support date in the asset inventory, and any device past that date that exposes a remotely reachable management or media surface must be removed from untrusted networks and scheduled for replacement — patching is not an option once the vendor retires the model. The distinguishing test: query the asset inventory for devices whose firmware lifecycle has ended and whose management interface is reachable from an untrusted segment; any non-empty result that lacks a replace-or-formally-risk-accept decision is a finding. Paper patch-management policies that assume a fix always exists leave actively-exploited EOL devices (GeoVision IP cameras, recruited by Mirai-style botnets) on the network indefinitely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2011-4723 — the DIR-300 stores its admin password unhashed inside firmware the operator cannot alter, D-Link phased the model out on 2013-05-15 with last date of support 2015-05-15, and CISA's required action for this KEV entry is disconnection rather than patching. Rotating the credential on a device still in service is pointless because the replacement is stored the same way, so only an end-of-support date in the asset inventory that forces replacement removes the exposure.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2011-4723 — NVD's affected CPE is the unversioned dlink:dir-300_firmware:-, so even the 2011-09-19 fix cannot be confirmed from a version string and no patch state is evidenceable; the KEV listing on 2022-09-08 therefore has to be satisfied by documented compensating action — disconnect the unit and rotate every credential it held — which a patch-maturity ladder measuring against a dead vendor stream scores as nothing at all.

attack_vector.description: Any installed application opens a PF_NETLINK (NETLINK_KOBJECT_UEVENT) socket — no Android permission gated it on 2.3.x — and sends a forged uevent whose PARTN field is negative and whose MINOR field is the address of libc's system(). DirectVolume::handlePartitionAdded() validates only the upper bound on part_num, so the negative value indexes mPartMinors[part_num - 1] below the array and writes into vold's GOT; the next time root-running vold calls the overwritten function it executes system("/data/local/tmp/boomsh"), which chmods a shell setuid-root so root survives after the exploit exits.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L with AV:L: local execution as an ordinary application is required, but on Android 2.3.x that means any sideloaded app, including one declaring no permissions at all
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; a deterministic arbitrary write with attacker control of both the offset and the written value in a single message, no race and no memory grooming. The only unreliability is per-device offset calculation, which weaponised variants solved by shipping offset tables inside the malware.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Sebastian Krahmer published GingerBreak and its source in April 2011 after hand-auditing vold's uevent handling, and xorl published an independent analysis of the mPartMinors signedness defect a week later. No AI tooling in the discovery path.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Update the handset to Android 2.3.4 or later (3.1 or later on Honeycomb hardware), which carries the AOSP vold change enabling SO_PASSCRED so vold receives and verifies sender credentials on every netlink message instead of trusting uevents forged by unprivileged apps.
prevention.adequacy: The fix existed within days of the exploit, so availability was never the problem — delivery was. It reaches a handset only when its OEM and carrier ship a 2.3.4 OTA, and devices that never received one have no remediation path short of replacement.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Watching for an unprivileged app opening NETLINK_KOBJECT_UEVENT and emitting uevents with a negative PARTN and an address-shaped MINOR, for vold invoking system() immediately after processing a netlink message, and for files staged under /data/local/tmp such as boomsh.
detection.adequacy: All three are decisive signals, but they need host telemetry on a device that characteristically has none — the victim handset is unenrolled, outside MDM and installing repackaged apps carrying the exploit.

response.what_would_have_worked: Factory-reset or reimage the device rather than only removing the offending app, then re-enrol it; the setuid-root shell the exploit drops outlives the exploiting process.
response.adequacy: Reimaging is the only reliable eviction, but it returns the device to the same unpatched build unless an OTA exists — so on handsets the OEM abandoned, response and prevention fail together.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 presumes the organisation can install a fix that exists; the AOSP commits landed 2011-04-18 and shipped in 2.3.4, yet on a carrier-locked handset the operator cannot apply them, and the control has no vocabulary for 'fixed upstream, never delivered to the device'.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: The obligation attaches to the entity whose estate carries the handset, while the ability to remediate sits with the handset maker and the mobile operator — NIS2 provides no mechanism to compel the 2.3.4 OTA that carries the vold fix.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 hardening operates above the defect: vold ran as root and trusted unauthenticated PF_NETLINK input, and no permission gated opening that socket on 2.3.x, so no setting, policy or hardening profile available to the operator would have blocked the write.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The OS-patching control is written for systems the organisation administers, with a 48-hour ML3 target once a public exploit exists; GingerBreak was public within days while 2011-era Android OTAs took months or never arrived, and the model offers no compensating position for a device that will provably never be patched.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Remediation is scheduled from an asset and vulnerability register, and the characteristic victim — an unenrolled personal handset sideloading repackaged apps, exactly what GingerMaster and the Lotoor family targeted — was never registered, so no A.8.8 scheduling decision ever touched it.

new_control_requirements.name: MOBILE-OS-MINIMUM-PATCH-LEVEL-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Managed mobile fleets must enforce a minimum OS security-patch level as a condition of access to organizational data, not merely report it. For Android, the MDM/EMM must read the device security-patch level and block or quarantine devices below the patch level that fixes a KEV-listed Framework flaw (here, 2026-06-01), and constrain installation of untrusted/side-loaded apps on devices that cannot yet update - since the privilege escalation is driven by locally running code. The distinguishing test: enroll a device pinned below 2026-06-01 and confirm the MDM policy denies it access to protected resources (rather than only recording the stale patch level on a dashboard) - paper 'mobile patching' policies that surface patch level without enforcing it leave exploitable devices in production.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2011-1823 — the vold SO_PASSCRED fix landed in AOSP on 2011-04-18 and shipped in Android 2.3.4, but reached a handset only when its OEM and carrier pushed an OTA, and GingerBreak was delivered by locally-installed repackaged apps (GingerMaster, DroidKungFu) on unenrolled personal devices. Reading the device build level and denying access below the fixed release — plus constraining side-loaded installs on handsets that will never update — is the only lever available when the fix exists upstream and never arrives on the device.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2011-1823 — CISA added this Android LPE to KEV on 2022-09-08, eleven years after Krahmer published the working GingerBreak exploit, and on handsets that never received a 2.3.4 OTA there is no patch to deploy at any cadence. Binding the KEV clock to documented compensating controls (quarantine the handset, reimage rather than merely uninstall, since the setuid-root shell survives the exploit process) gives flaw remediation an executable action where 'fixed upstream, never delivered' otherwise leaves none.

CVE-2022-26352.name: dotCMS Unrestricted Upload of File Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A single unauthenticated POST to /api/content/ carries multipart/form-data whose Content-Disposition filename holds directory-traversal sequences. dotCMS writes the uploaded bytes to a temp file using that filename verbatim, so the traversal escapes the temp directory and lands a .jsp inside Tomcat's ROOT webapp — the public PoCs target /srv/dotserver/tomcat-9.0.41/webapps/ROOT/ directly while the Metasploit module traverses relatively with ../../. A follow-up GET to the planted .jsp executes it as the dotCMS service user, giving a webshell.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; /api/content/ accepts anonymous writes whenever CONTENT_APIS_ALLOW_ANONYMOUS is set to WRITE, which is the value dotCMS shipped, so the default deployment is the exploitable one
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; one request, no race, no memory corruption, no authentication and no user interaction. The only variable is the absolute path to the ROOT webapp, and the public tooling removes even that with either a hardcoded container path or a relative traversal from the temp directory.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Hussein Daher and Shubham Shah of Assetnote found it by whitebox source review of the ContentResource upload path during a bank engagement, then ran a coordinated disclosure with the vendor. No AI tooling credited.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrade to dotCMS 22.03, 5.3.8.10_lts or 21.06.7_lts per advisory SI-62, and where an upgrade cannot be scheduled immediately set CONTENT_APIS_ALLOW_ANONYMOUS to anything other than WRITE so /api/content/ stops accepting unauthenticated writes.
prevention.adequacy: Upgrading closes the write but does not undo one: the exploit's whole purpose is leaving a file behind, so the Tomcat ROOT webapp and its nested asset directories have to be swept for unexpected .jsp files before the host is treated as clean. CISA records ransomware campaign use for this CVE as Known.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on POSTs to /api/content/ whose multipart filename contains traversal sequences, on 200 responses for .jsp paths under the web root that did not exist before (frequently with a cmd= parameter), and on the dotCMS/Tomcat JVM spawning shell children as the service account.
detection.adequacy: The traversal in the filename header is a clean signature, but many WAFs normalise the URL path and never inspect multipart headers, and the webshell fetch that follows looks like an ordinary GET — process lineage on the JVM is the more reliable of the three.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat any planted .jsp as full compromise of the application host — remove it, rotate dotCMS and database credentials, review content and route objects for tampering, and hunt for the ransomware staging CISA associates with this CVE.
response.adequacy: Well-defined but reactive: it starts only after a file lands, and because the webshell converts to hands-on-keyboard access so cheaply, the deciding variable is how long the ROOT webapp goes unexamined.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: Input-validation evidence enumerates form fields, query parameters and request bodies, while the injection point was upload metadata — the multipart Content-Disposition filename, treated as a name and used verbatim as a filesystem path. The uploaded bytes were never the problem; the field describing them was, and it sits outside the input surface SI-10 assessments list.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Measuring the window from vendor fix to deployment presumes the pre-patch window is at least gated by authentication, and it was not — CONTENT_APIS_ALLOW_ANONYMOUS shipped as WRITE, so every internet-facing instance from 3.0 onward exposed a preauth 9.8 file-write. A compliant cadence still leaves that window open, and the change that closes it instantly is a configuration setting the directive does not name.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The vulnerable write happens inside dotCMS's own temp-file handling, before the upload becomes content and therefore before any of the CMS permission model or the operator's content-governance settings apply — there is no B4-visible configuration item covering how the application names files it has not yet accepted.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The 48-hour internet-facing timeframe is the right tempo for a preauth RCE, but the control is scoped to an enumerated hardened-application list built around browsers, office suites, PDF readers and runtimes; a self-hosted Java CMS is not on it, so an ML3 assessment coexists with an unpatched dotCMS 22.02 answering anonymous writes.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.28.gap: Canonicalising a path and taking the basename of an attacker-supplied filename is textbook secure coding, but A.8.28 binds the organisation's own development — it produces no finding at all for an operator deploying dotCMS, and for the vendor it is satisfied by having a programme that nevertheless missed a filename-as-path across every release from 3.0 to 22.02.

new_control_requirements.name: CONFIGURATION-SIDE-LIVE-PATCH-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: For any web-fabric vulnerability with a configuration-side mitigation path: that path must be inventoried, tested, and deployable independent of the vendor-patch path. Operators cannot wait for nginx 1.30.1+ if a named-capture refactor mitigates immediately.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-26352 — setting CONTENT_APIS_ALLOW_ANONYMOUS to anything other than WRITE stops /api/content/ accepting unauthenticated writes immediately and removes the preauth reachability that makes this a 9.8, without waiting for the 22.03 / 5.3.8.10_lts / 21.06.7_lts upgrade and its Tomcat restart. That configuration path has to be inventoried and pre-tested, because dotCMS shipped the anonymous-write default from 3.0 onward and the patch-cadence control the operator is measured against never names it.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-26352 — a single unauthenticated multipart POST whose Content-Disposition filename carries traversal plants a .jsp webshell inside Tomcat's ROOT webapp, the exploit ships in Metasploit and Nuclei, and CISA records ransomware campaign use for this CVE as Known. A KEV-triggered 4-hour clock is the only cadence matching that exposure, where a fix-to-deployment window leaves every internet-facing instance a live ransomware entry point until the next maintenance slot.

CVE-2022-24706.name: Apache CouchDB Insecure Default Initialization of Resource Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: The attacker queries epmd on the fixed port 4369/tcp, which advertises the random port CouchDB's Erlang distribution listener bound to on all interfaces, connects to that port and completes the distribution handshake using the cookie CouchDB's packaging set for every installation — 'monster' — then sends an rex control message invoking os:cmd/1 to run arbitrary shell commands as the couchdb service account. Two round trips and no exploitation primitive: the credential was published in the vendor's own packaging, and exposed nodes were enumerated wholesale with the Shodan query port:4369 "name couchdb at".
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; authentication to the distribution port is a single shared secret that the packaging set to a publicly known constant
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; a protocol conversation with no race and no memory corruption. The one genuine precondition is that the distribution port is externally reachable, which is what the default binary packages produced — the Apache advisory is explicit that installations which never exposed it were not vulnerable.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Alex Vandiver reported it to the CouchDB project as a packaging-and-defaults analysis rather than a memory-safety or fuzzing result, and the public exploits that followed were hand-written. No AI tooling credited in discovery or weaponisation.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrade to Apache CouchDB 3.2.2 or later, which refuses to start while the Erlang cookie is still 'monster' and whose binary packages bind epmd and the distribution port to loopback; where an upgrade cannot be scheduled, set a unique Erlang cookie and firewall the distribution port together with epmd on 4369/tcp so only the API port 5984/tcp is reachable.
prevention.adequacy: Either half works and the advisory says so, but neither undoes an exploited host: nodes were mass-enrolled into Kinsing cryptomining, so the per-minute crontab entry, /lib/systemd/system/bot.service, the kdevtmpfsi miner and the libsystem.so preload have to be cleared before the host returns to service.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on inbound connections to epmd on 4369/tcp followed immediately by a connection to the port it advertised, on a distribution handshake completing with the cookie 'monster' plus an rex os:cmd/1 call, and on shell commands whose parent process is erl_child_setup.
detection.adequacy: The process-lineage signal is decisive, but CounterCraft measured under half a second from first reconnaissance to command execution against exposed nodes — detection has no window to act in before the payload lands, only to scope the cleanup afterwards.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rebuild or fully clean exploited hosts — remove the Kinsing persistence set, restore the firewall and NMI watchdog the dropper disabled, rotate the Erlang cookie and every credential the couchdb account could reach, and re-verify database contents.
response.adequacy: Complete eviction requires treating the host as compromised rather than the service as misconfigured, because the dropper disables host hardening and installs a rootkit preload before the miner ever runs.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: The port-and-service baseline CM-7 is evidenced with cannot name a listener whose port is assigned at process start; CouchDB's packaging opened epmd on 4369 and an all-interfaces distribution port on a single-node install purely in anticipation of clustering, so 'only 5984 authorised' was accurate about intent and blind to the real listening surface.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: A segmentation review built from a static port inventory reported the database as API-on-5984-only, while the exploited listener's port was chosen at start-up, advertised by epmd, and authenticated by a cookie the packaging had set to a published string — assurance and actual exposure diverged with no operator error anywhere.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2 assumes authentication runs against managed identities subject to entitlement review and credential lifecycle; the distribution port authenticates peers with one shared secret set to 'monster' for every installation worldwide, a credential no joiner-mover-leaver or privileged-access review ever touched, while B2 assessments of CouchDB admin accounts and HTTP auth found nothing wrong.

AU-ISM-1546.gap: The 48-hour ML3 target is orders of magnitude slower than the sub-second reconnaissance-to-execution tempo observed against exposed nodes, and it is measured against an exposure the operator could not identify by port number — the honest control statement is that the distribution port needed firewalling before the advisory, not patching within two days after it.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.22.gap: Network segregation is exactly what CouchDB's own guidance asks for, and operators applied it to the documented registered API port 5984 because that is the only port the public interface documentation requires. A service whose port is assigned at start-up defeats a zone rule set written from a service inventory, so the segmentation was complete against the documented surface and open against the real one.

new_control_requirements.name: APPSERVER-REMOTING-PROTOCOL-RESTRICTION
new_control_requirements.description: Application servers that expose binary remoting protocols (Oracle WebLogic T3/IIOP, and equivalents) must restrict those protocols to trusted hosts and apply vendor critical patch updates on an accelerated schedule when a remoting flaw is KEV-listed. Place T3/IIOP behind a connection filter (weblogic.security.net.ConnectionFilterImpl) or network ACLs so only known hosts can reach them, never expose the ports to untrusted networks, and apply the Oracle CPU bundle (with server restart) rather than deferring to the next quarterly window. The distinguishing test: from an untrusted network segment, attempt an unauthenticated T3/IIOP connection to a staging WebLogic instance and confirm it is refused at the connection filter before any data is served - a perimeter-firewall + quarterly-patch policy that still leaves T3/IIOP reachable from an internal untrusted segment leaves the unauthenticated data-access path open.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-24706 — CouchDB's packaging opened epmd on 4369/tcp plus an Erlang distribution listener bound to all interfaces on a port assigned at process start, and exploitation is an ordinary distribution handshake followed by an rex os:cmd/1 call. Restricting that binary remoting protocol to known hosts by network ACL is exactly the vendor's own 'firewall in front of all CouchDB installations' guidance, and it is the control a port-list baseline and a 5984-only segmentation review both structurally missed because the port is not fixed in configuration.

new_control_requirements.name: FRAMEWORK-DEFAULT-SECRET-DETECTION
new_control_requirements.description: Deployment gating that fails any release shipping or running an unrotated framework default cryptographic secret (APP_KEY / SECRET_KEY and equivalents), which turn a leaked constant into unauthenticated deserialization RCE.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-24706 — the Erlang distribution port authenticates peers with one shared secret, and CouchDB's packaging set it to the constant 'monster' for every installation worldwide; the Metasploit module hardcodes COOKIE = 'monster'. A deployment gate that fails an unrotated shipped default secret is the only check that reaches a credential no joiner-mover-leaver process, entitlement review or rotation policy ever touches.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-24706 — the public exploit landed 2022-05-11 and CounterCraft observed under half a second from first reconnaissance to command execution against exposed nodes before Kinsing enrolment, so a two-day patch timeframe is orders of magnitude behind the tempo. A KEV-bound 4-hour clock that accepts the firewall-plus-unique-cookie mitigation as verified remediation is the only response window in the same order of magnitude.

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated POST to /apisix/batch-requests carries a JSON headers object setting X-Real-IP to 127.0.0.1; the batch-requests plugin copies that attacker-supplied header into the sub-request instead of the real remote address, so the ip-restriction plugin guarding the Admin API evaluates the call as local. The pipelined sub-request is a PUT to /apisix/admin/routes/<id> using the shipped default token edd1c9f034335f136f87ad84b625c8f1, registering a route whose filter_func or script field is Lua calling os.execute(); a follow-up GET to the new route URI runs the command as the OpenResty worker user.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the batch-requests endpoint is unauthenticated and the Admin API accepts the built-in default key
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; two deterministic requests, no race, no memory grooming, no user interaction. The nuance is that this CVE is the IP-restriction bypass rather than the code execution — reaching RCE additionally requires the Admin API to still accept its default token, and where the key was rotated or the Admin API moved to its own port the impact degrades to bypassing the data plane's IP restriction.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — reported to the Apache Software Foundation by the Sauercloud team and disclosed by the APISIX project in February 2022, with the chained default-token half credited separately to YuanSheng Wang. No AI tooling appears anywhere in the disclosure chain.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrade to APISIX 2.12.1 (current line) or 2.10.4 (LTS line), and independently rotate the shipped Admin key edd1c9f034335f136f87ad84b625c8f1 and bind the Admin API to a port and interface separate from the data plane. The vendor's interim mitigation is commenting batch-requests out of conf/config.yaml and conf/config-default.yaml and restarting.
prevention.adequacy: The upgrade removes the header-spoofing primitive, but the two configuration changes are what decide whether any future bypass reaches code execution — a patched gateway still answering on its default Admin token is one bug away from the same outcome.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on POSTs to /apisix/batch-requests whose body sets X-Real-IP or X-Forwarded-For to a loopback or allowlisted address, on Admin API calls carrying the default api_key, and on route objects whose filter_func or script value contains os.execute, io.popen, curl or bash.
detection.adequacy: The route-object indicator is strong and durable — Lua shelling out has no legitimate place in a routing rule — but it is a post-registration artifact, so detection lands after the control plane has already been written to.

response.what_would_have_worked: Delete attacker-registered routes from etcd and the Admin API, rotate the Admin key and every upstream credential the gateway held, and treat the host running the OpenResty worker as compromised given the public PoC's reverse shell.
response.adequacy: Adequate only if it extends past the gateway: APISIX sits in front of everything it proxies, so the response has to cover the upstreams whose traffic an attacker with route-write could silently rewrite.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality tells the operator to disable services that are not needed, but batch-requests ships inside APISIX's own default enabled-plugin list — the vendor mitigation is literally to comment it out of config-default.yaml — and CM-7 gives no way to know that this one bundled plugin, out of dozens, voids the Admin API's allowlist.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: The Admin API's IP allowlist reads as network segmentation on the architecture diagram, but it is header-trusting application logic evaluating a client address that batch-requests takes from the request body — the control existed everywhere except in the packet path.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2 checks that the admin interface sits behind authentication, and APISIX's did — with a static, publicly documented token that appears verbatim in the vendor's own config and as a Metasploit default option. No B2 outcome gates conformance on default-credential rotation, so an instance could be conformant on paper while its control plane accepted a globally known constant.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Application hardening is scoped to user-facing software — browser plugins, Office macros, PDF readers — and says nothing about an API gateway's own control plane; both changes that actually closed this path sit entirely outside the maturity model's hardening surface.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: The exploited state is the vendor baseline — default Admin token, batch-requests enabled, Admin API answering on the data-plane port — so a control demanding secure configurations gives the operator no signal about which shipped default is remotely fatal when the documentation presents all three as normal starting configuration.

new_control_requirements.name: FRAMEWORK-DEFAULT-SECRET-DETECTION
new_control_requirements.description: Deployment gating that fails any release shipping or running an unrotated framework default cryptographic secret (APP_KEY / SECRET_KEY and equivalents), which turn a leaked constant into unauthenticated deserialization RCE.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-24112 — the batch-requests X-Real-IP spoof only reaches route registration and Lua os.execute because APISIX ships the static Admin token edd1c9f034335f136f87ad84b625c8f1, which appears verbatim in the vendor's own config and as a Metasploit default option; the Apache advisory states impact drops sharply once that key is rotated. A release gate that fails an unrotated shipped default secret turns a documented-as-normal vendor baseline into a blocking finding.

new_control_requirements.name: CONFIGURATION-SIDE-LIVE-PATCH-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: For any web-fabric vulnerability with a configuration-side mitigation path: that path must be inventoried, tested, and deployable independent of the vendor-patch path. Operators cannot wait for nginx 1.30.1+ if a named-capture refactor mitigates immediately.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-24112 — commenting batch-requests out of conf/config.yaml and conf/config-default.yaml removes the header-spoofing primitive outright, and rebinding the Admin API to its own port and interface removes the reachability, both deployable before the 2.12.1 / 2.10.4 upgrade. Those paths must be inventoried and rehearsed in advance, because nothing in a least-functionality baseline tells an operator that this one plugin, out of dozens shipped enabled, voids the Admin API's IP allowlist.

CVE-2022-22963.name: VMware Tanzu Spring Cloud Function Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A single unauthenticated POST to the function-routing endpoint (commonly /functionRouter) carries the header spring.cloud.function.routing-expression. RoutingFunction hands that header value to a StandardEvaluationContext, which grants full type access, so a SpEL type reference such as T(java.lang.Runtime).getRuntime().exec(new String[]{'/bin/sh','-c','<cmd>'}) executes as the JVM's user. Exploitation is blind — patched and vulnerable servers both return HTTP 500 — so the mass-scanning campaigns confirmed hits out of band with T(java.net.InetAddress).getByName('<callback>') instead of reading the response.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the routing endpoint is unauthenticated and reachable by default once RoutingFunction is on the classpath
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; one request, one header, no authentication, no user interaction, no race and no memory grooming, with EPSS 0.99939 among the highest in the corpus
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — credited to the researcher m09u3r in Spring's own advisory after manual source review of the routing-expression handling. No AI-assisted discovery or triage is credited by the vendor or in the downstream Cisco, SonicWall or Oracle advisories.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrade spring-cloud-function-context and the spring-cloud-function BOM to 3.1.7 on the 3.1.x line or 3.2.3 on the 3.2.x line and redeploy; where the redeploy cannot happen immediately, stop publishing the routing endpoint and drop any request carrying the spring.cloud.function.routing-expression header at the reverse proxy or WAF, since the header has no legitimate external use.
prevention.adequacy: Sufficient for an application you build, unavailable for one you bought: embedded copies need the embedding vendor's release, and Oracle's fixes ran to the April and July 2022 Critical Patch Updates while Akamai observed mass exploitation attempts three days after the Spring fix shipped.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Logging and alerting on the literal header name spring.cloud.function.routing-expression, on POSTs to /functionRouter from unexpected sources, and on JVM HTTP worker threads spawning /bin/sh -c or cmd.exe children.
detection.adequacy: The header name is an unambiguous, cheap signature, but the HTTP 500 that follows is identical on patched and vulnerable servers — response-based detection cannot separate an attempt from a success, so only out-of-band callbacks and process lineage close the loop.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rebuild the affected application host, hunt for the cryptominers and reverse shells the campaigns dropped under the service account, and rotate every credential within the JVM's reach.
response.adequacy: Workable where the operator owns the deployment; where the library is buried inside a commercial banking, telecom or network-appliance stack, the operator can neither confirm the bundled version nor rebuild the product and has to wait on the vendor's release.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: The routing-expression header is not operator-handled application input — it is framework input the library is designed to evaluate as an expression, with full type access granted by default. No bean, filter or input-validation configuration on the operator's side sits between the request and the evaluation.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: Supplier-governance measures address relationships, contracts and assurance, not a preauth SpEL RCE arriving because a vendor bundled spring-cloud-function-context four layers down; most affected operators had no inventory naming the library at all, so the control could not locate the exposure it was supposed to manage.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: /functionRouter is a framework-provided endpoint that appears because the routing feature is on the classpath, not because a deployment team chose to publish it — no host hardening, service minimisation or network policy blocks a single unauthenticated POST to an endpoint nobody knew existed.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The 48-hour ML3 window is measured against the operator's own upgrade, but mass exploitation began three days after the fix shipped and the real exposure lived inside downstream vendor products whose Critical Patch Update cycles ran to April and July — the arithmetic defeats the control before the operator can act.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.28.gap: Evaluating an attacker-controlled string in an expression language is exactly the defect class A.8.28 targets, but it binds the organization's own developers — an exemplary secure-coding programme, code review and SAST across everything the operator wrote still deploys this untouched, because the flawed line is outside the scope A.8.28 defines.

new_control_requirements.name: TIER-3-DEPENDENCY-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: Supply chain inventory must extend to tier-3 dependencies (dependencies of dependencies of direct dependencies). SBOM coverage for libsystemd-class transitive dependencies cannot be omitted under SR-3.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-22963 — the vulnerable spring-cloud-function-context sat four layers down inside dozens of Oracle banking, communications and financial-services products plus Cisco and SonicWall appliances, and most affected operators had no inventory naming the library at all. Supplier governance cannot manage an exposure it cannot locate, so transitive-dependency inventory is the precondition for any supply-chain response to this class.

new_control_requirements.name: CONFIGURATION-SIDE-LIVE-PATCH-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: For any web-fabric vulnerability with a configuration-side mitigation path: that path must be inventoried, tested, and deployable independent of the vendor-patch path. Operators cannot wait for nginx 1.30.1+ if a named-capture refactor mitigates immediately.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-22963 — the spring.cloud.function.routing-expression header has no legitimate external use, so dropping it at the reverse proxy or WAF and unpublishing /functionRouter mitigates in minutes, while operators of embedded copies waited on Oracle's April and July 2022 Critical Patch Updates. That proxy-side path must be inventoried and testable independent of the vendor release, because Akamai observed mass exploitation attempts three days after the 3.1.7 / 3.2.3 fix shipped.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-22963 — one unauthenticated POST carrying a SpEL type reference executes as the JVM user, Metasploit and Nuclei both ship modules, and thousands of source IPs were scanning within 72 hours of the vendor fix. A 48-hour patch timeframe measured against the operator's own upgrade is already outside the exploitation window, so only a KEV-bound clock that also accepts the header-drop as documented mitigation lands inside it.

attack_vector.description: A page creates an RTCPeerConnection whose transceiver declares multiple sendEncodings, calls createOffer(), strips one encoding's a=rid and a=simulcast lines from the SDP, then passes the shortened SDP to setLocalDescription. WebRTC reconciles the original supported-encodings vector against the shorter current-encodings vector by copying properties positionally and writes past the end of the shorter vector on the heap. Candiru delivered this from a compromised Lebanese news-agency site, fingerprinting visitors across roughly 50 attributes and serving the exploit per-victim under an RSA-2048/AES-256-CBC layer nested inside TLS, then chaining a renderer-sandbox escape and a bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver kernel step to load DevilsTongue.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N, but UI:R: the victim must load attacker-controlled content, which the campaign supplied by compromising a legitimate news site rather than by phishing
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L for the memory-corruption trigger, which is deterministic (two vectors of mismatched length reconciled by positional copy) and only a few lines of JavaScript. Converting the out-of-bounds write into code execution required heap grooming plus a sandbox escape, economics consistent with a commercial spyware vendor rather than opportunistic crimeware.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered and not proactively researched — Jan Vojtesek of Avast caught the exploit being served to Avast's own users in the Middle East and reported it to Google. This was incident-response discovery of an already-deployed zero-day, with no AI-assisted fuzzing or triage in the path.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Update to Chrome 103.0.5060.114 or a Chromium build rebased on it, plus the parallel fixes in the shared WebRTC library — WebKitGTK and WPE WebKit 2.36.5, iOS/iPadOS 15.6, macOS Monterey 12.5, Big Sur 11.6.8, tvOS 15.6, watchOS 8.7 — and the corresponding distribution rebuilds.
prevention.adequacy: Nothing prevented this before 2022-07-04, because the fix did not exist while the exploit was in use. Afterwards the residual gap is embedded copies: Electron apps, conferencing SDKs and kiosk builds vendor their own WebRTC and stay vulnerable long after the browsers are updated.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Hunting the post-exploitation stage rather than the exploit — the abused signed driver at C:\Windows\System32\drivers\HW.sys and its physical-memory read/write IOCTLs, DevilsTongue DLLs staged under Windows\System32\migration\, hijacked COM CLSID persistence, and the stylishblock[.]com infrastructure.
detection.adequacy: The host artifacts are concrete, but delivery is engineered against detection: per-victim targeting, ~50-point browser fingerprinting before any exploit is served, and a per-session encryption layer inside TLS mean there is no repeatable payload and no recoverable exploit body in network capture.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rebuild targeted endpoints from known-good media, revoke and rotate everything the user held, and treat kernel-level tooling on the host as untrustworthy given the BYOVD step.
response.adequacy: Reimaging is the only defensible outcome once a signed vulnerable driver has been loaded for arbitrary physical-memory access — but targeting is highly selective, so the hard part is knowing which endpoints to rebuild at all.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation has no purchase on a flaw exploited before it is known: Candiru was already serving this WebRTC overflow to journalists and regional targets when Avast caught it, so every endpoint in the pre-patch window was exploitable at whatever remediation cadence the organization had documented.

NIS2-Art21-incident-handling.gap: Incident handling begins at detection, and this chain suppresses detection by design — selective per-target delivery, browser profiling before any exploit is served, and nested per-session encryption that leaves nothing recoverable from passive interception, so the telemetry the reporting clocks presume is deliberately absent.
