UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 treats browser security as a configuration outcome, but the vulnerable code is the WebRTC media stack reachable from ordinary page JavaScript via RTCPeerConnection; no enterprise policy or hardening baseline disables SDP handling, and because WebRTC is shared, standardising on a non-Chrome browser gained nothing.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The control enumerates specific browser reductions — block Flash, ads, Java, disable unneeded features — none of which touch WebRTC, and the mitigation that would have mattered (constraining the real-time media stack) is absent from the maturity model entirely.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: Malware protection depends on endpoint visibility that the chain removes before the payload lands: the BYOVD step loads a legitimately signed driver whose IOCTLs give arbitrary physical-memory read and write, disarming the kernel-level detection A.8.7 relies on to catch DevilsTongue.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-2294 — Candiru was already serving this WebRTC heap overflow to selected targets when Avast caught it, and the first fix in existence was Chrome 103.0.5060.114 on 2022-07-04 (with the shared-library parallels in WebKitGTK/WPE 2.36.5, iOS 15.6 and macOS 12.5). Because no browser policy or hardening baseline disables SDP handling, update latency is the entire defensive margin, and any deferral ring spends it on the hottest exploit window.

new_control_requirements.name: VULNERABLE-DRIVER-BLOCKLIST-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Enforce a kernel vulnerable/malicious-driver blocklist (HVCI plus the vendor recommended-driver blocklist) so a signed-but-vulnerable driver cannot be loaded for bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver privilege escalation.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-2294 — the documented in-the-wild chain's step after renderer compromise is BYOVD: loading the legitimately signed HW.sys driver whose IOCTLs give arbitrary physical-memory read and write, which is precisely what disarms the kernel-level visibility that would otherwise catch DevilsTongue. HVCI plus the vendor driver blocklist refuses that load, and it is the one control in the chain that still functions after the browser bug has already fired.

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated GET to /api/snapshots/:key or /dashboard/snapshot/:key — with the literal string ':key' sent verbatim, never substituted for a real key — returns the snapshot holding the lowest database id. Deleting that snapshot (unauthenticated via /api/snapshots-delete/:deleteKey when snapshot public_mode is on, and by any authenticated user of any role otherwise) makes the next-lowest snapshot reachable, so a read-then-delete loop walks the entire snapshot table while irreversibly destroying it.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none for the read half — PR:N. The delete half is unauthenticated only when snapshot public_mode is enabled (non-default); otherwise it needs any authenticated user, so a low-privilege dashboard viewer is sufficient.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; one GET with a literal placeholder in the path, no payload, no encoding trick, no race, and EPSS 0.99933. Target discovery is free because Grafana is routinely exposed to make dashboards reachable and login-page fingerprints ship inside the public tooling.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Tran Viet Tuan reported it to Grafana Labs after manual route and authorization review of the snapshot endpoints. Neither the GitHub Security Advisory nor the release notes credit any AI-assisted discovery or triage tooling.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrade Grafana to 8.1.6 on the 8.x line or 7.5.11 on the 7.5.x line, or block the literal paths /api/snapshots/:key, /api/snapshots-delete/:deleteKey and /dashboard/snapshot/:key at the reverse proxy — the vendor states these paths have no normal function and can be blocked with no side effects.
prevention.adequacy: Both work and the proxy block is immediate, but because deletion is irreversible, prevention has to be paired with checking for prior exploitation rather than treated as the end of the task. Repackaged copies — NetApp, distribution rebuilds, embedded dashboards — need their own fix path.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Reverse-proxy or load-balancer access logs showing HTTP 200 for the literal ':key' paths, alternating read-then-delete cycles from a single source, and unexplained disappearance of consecutive low-id snapshots.
detection.adequacy: Grafana's own guidance points at proxy logs precisely because Grafana OSS records nothing: snapshot reads and deletions produce no audit entry outside the Enterprise tier, so an instance not fronted by request-level logging has no evidence of the event at all.

response.what_would_have_worked: Restore snapshots from backup where they exist, treat every snapshot that ever lived in the instance as disclosed, and review what those dashboards embedded — query results, hostnames, metric labels and occasionally credentials in datasource URLs.
response.adequacy: Restoration is frequently impossible: the enumeration destroys each record in order to reach the next, and snapshots are rarely inside a backup scope, so response usually reduces to assessing what was exposed.

NIST-800-53-AC-3.gap: Access enforcement requires an enforcement point in the code path, and there was none — the snapshot routes accepted ':key' as though it were a real key and returned the lowest-id record without evaluating any authorization decision, so no policy, role definition or operator configuration could have changed the outcome.

NIS2-Art21-incident-handling.gap: The same requests exfiltrate and destroy, because deletion is the mechanism that advances the enumeration, so the confidentiality-versus-availability classification the reporting duty depends on has no clean answer — and Grafana OSS records neither event, leaving classification to whatever the reverse proxy happened to log.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: C1 assumes the monitored system produces its own evidence, but Grafana OSS emits no audit record for snapshot reads or deletions — that is an Enterprise-tier feature — which pushes detection onto an external reverse-proxy dependency C1 does not anticipate for an internally deployed observability tool.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch timeframes are driven by severity rating and the rating actively misleads here: CVSS 7.3 with C:L/I:L/A:L reads as partial impact, while the real primitive is unauthenticated enumeration plus irreversible destruction of every snapshot, and the KEV listing landed nearly a year after the October 2021 fix.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.15.gap: The organization's access rules were coherent — snapshots shared by an unguessable key — and were simply not enforced by the software implementing them, because a placeholder string resolved to a real record inside the product's routing layer.

new_control_requirements.name: CONFIGURATION-SIDE-LIVE-PATCH-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: For any web-fabric vulnerability with a configuration-side mitigation path: that path must be inventoried, tested, and deployable independent of the vendor-patch path. Operators cannot wait for nginx 1.30.1+ if a named-capture refactor mitigates immediately.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2021-39226 — Grafana states the three literal paths (/api/snapshots/:key, /api/snapshots-delete/:deleteKey, /dashboard/snapshot/:key) have no normal function and can be blocked at the reverse proxy with no side effects, which stops the read-then-delete enumeration instantly and also covers repackaged copies — NetApp, distribution rebuilds, embedded dashboards — that have no 8.1.6 / 7.5.11 upgrade of their own. Because each read destroys a snapshot to reach the next, that path has to be already inventoried, not devised after the first deletion.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2021-39226 — the CVSS 7.3 C:L/I:L/A:L rating schedules this as partial-impact while the actual primitive is unauthenticated enumeration plus irreversible destruction of every snapshot in the instance; EPSS is 0.99933 and the KEV listing arrived nearly a year after the October 2021 fix. A KEV-triggered clock replaces the severity-driven patch window that under-rated the exposure for that entire year.

CVE-2021-38406.name: Delta Electronics DOPSoft 2 Improper Input Validation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An engineer opens a crafted DOPSoft 2 project file — arriving as an email attachment, on removable media, or inside an integrator's project handoff — and the parser, which performs no bounds validation on user-supplied data, executes an out-of-bounds write and runs code in the context of the current process, meaning the engineer's own account on an OT engineering workstation. That host is by design trusted to program DOP-series HMIs and typically holds project archives, comms parameters and controller credentials, so the write is a foothold on the boundary between the corporate network and the plant floor.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker supplies a file rather than holding an account, but UI:R means an engineer must open it, so in OT practice this is spearphishing an engineering workstation or poisoning an integrator-supplied handoff
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the parser performs no bounds validation at all, so the write is deterministic with no race and no probabilistic step, and CISA groups this CVE with a stack-based overflow and a heap-based overflow in the same project-file parser — three memory-safety sinks reachable from one file format.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — reported by the researcher kimiya through Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative and credited by name in CISA's ICS advisory. This was manual file-format reverse engineering of the project parser, with no AI-assisted discovery credited by CISA, ZDI or Delta Electronics.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: There is no patch and there will not be one — CISA states DOPSoft 2 will not receive an update because it is an end-of-life product, and the KEV required action is disconnection rather than patching. The vendor's answer is migration: move HMI hardware to the DOP-100 family and replace the engineering software with DIAScreen, shipped in DIAStudio v1.1.2 or later. Until that completes the only controls available are procedural — open project files only from trusted sources, refuse unsolicited attachments, and run DOPSoft on an isolated engineering workstation kept off the plant and corporate networks.
prevention.adequacy: Inadequate by construction: the prescribed remediation is a capital hardware programme rather than a patch window, and every interim control depends on engineer behaviour instead of removing the defect. Unlike a patchable CVE the exposure does not decay — it persists for the remaining service life of the HMI fleet.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Watching engineering workstations for DOPSoft.exe crashing or spawning child processes while parsing a project file, for project files staged in DOPSoft working directories whose provenance cannot be traced to a controlled repository, and for lateral movement from the engineering host toward HMI and PLC networks after a file is opened.
detection.adequacy: Workable in principle but rarely instrumented: OT engineering workstations are frequently excluded from endpoint monitoring for vendor-support reasons, and CISA published no sample, hash or indicator set for this CVE, so there is nothing to match on beyond behaviour.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rebuild the engineering workstation, rotate the controller and HMI credentials it held, and verify the integrity of project archives and of any HMI programmed from that host since the file was opened.
response.adequacy: Rebuilding restores the host but returns it to the same unsupported toolchain, because the workstation has to keep running DOPSoft 2 to program HMIs still in production — the response closes an incident without reducing the exposure that produced it.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 presumes a fix exists to apply within some timeframe; Delta declared the product end-of-life and shipped nothing, so the control has no available action. The only response that removes the flaw is decommissioning, which SI-2 does not require and which cannot be executed on a maintenance timescale because it means replacing deployed HMI hardware.

EU-CRA-Art13.gap: The manufacturer's vulnerability-handling and declared-support-period duties did not exist when Delta ended DOPSoft 2's life in 2021, so the operator carries an unfixable out-of-bounds write in the software required to maintain equipment already running on the plant floor, with no vendor obligation to invoke. The Regulation changes incentives for products placed on the market from now on and offers nothing to the installed base.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 expects systems to be designed securely and kept secure across their operational life, but this is an end-of-life engineering tool with a memory-safety defect in its file parser and no vendor fix — the outcome cannot be met without an HMI replacement programme, so in practice the assessment is satisfied by a documented risk exception that leaves the exposure untouched.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The control is unusually explicit that applications no longer supported by vendors must be removed, and that is exactly what the operator cannot do, because removing DOPSoft 2 means abandoning the ability to program HMIs still in production service. It prescribes the one action that would work and offers no maturity path for the case where running the plant depends on the unsupported software.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: With no vendor fix every finding terminates in permanent risk acceptance on the first pass, and the compensating controls A.8.8 would point at — isolating the engineering workstation, controlling project-file provenance, restricting removable media — are procedural and depend on engineer behaviour, so the out-of-bounds write stays reachable by anyone who opens a supplied project file, indefinitely.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: Network-reachable end-of-life devices with no vendor patch path must be isolated and decommissioned within a bounded window; mandatory compensating segmentation applies until removal since no remediation exists.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2021-38406 — CISA ICSA-21-252-02 Update A states DOPSoft 2 will not receive an update because it is an end-of-life product, and Delta's answer is migration to DOP-100 hardware with DIAScreen in DIAStudio v1.1.2+. The only defensible posture is a bounded migration window with mandatory interim segmentation — DOPSoft confined to an isolated engineering workstation kept off the plant and corporate networks — because the out-of-bounds write in the project-file parser will never be fixed.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2021-38406 — the KEV required action for this CVE is not 'apply updates per vendor instructions' but that the end-of-life product be disconnected if still in use, so the only thing the KEV clock can bind is documented compensating controls: workstation isolation, project-file provenance control, and a dated migration plan. Without that, flaw remediation records an open defect with no permitted action and vulnerability management terminates in permanent risk acceptance on the first pass.

CVE-2022-37969.name: Microsoft Windows Common Log File System (CLFS) Driver Privilege Escalation Vulnerability (CVE-2022-37969)

attack_vector.description: A low-privileged local user writes a malformed CLFS base log file whose cbSymbolZone is altered from 0x000000F8 to 0x0001114B so the SignaturesOffset field escapes the missing bounds check, making CLFS.sys perform an out-of-bounds memset in the kernel pool. The overwrite corrupts the pContainer pointer inside _CLFS_CONTAINER_CONTEXT to reference heap-sprayed attacker memory, and a vtable call through that pointer is chained via ClfsEarlierLsn() and SeSetAccessStateGenericMapping() into an arbitrary kernel write. The final write copies the SYSTEM token located through NtQuerySystemInformation over the current process token, yielding a SYSTEM shell.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; MSRC's own FAQ states the attacker must already hold access and the ability to run code on the target, but no administrative rights are needed
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the trigger is a deterministic malformed base log file with no race, though it needs pool grooming (sprays at 0x10000 and 0x5000000, repeated file creation for constant Base Block offsets) and is build-sensitive, with Windows 11 21H2 requiring two triggers where Windows 10 needs one
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Zscaler ThreatLabz captured a live in-the-wild sample on 2022-09-02, eleven days before the fix. MSRC acknowledges four independent IR and threat-intel teams (Zscaler ThreatLabz, CrowdStrike, Mandiant FLARE OTF, DBAPPSecurity), the convergence pattern of a sample-driven find rather than fuzzing or code audit. No AI tooling credited by Microsoft or by any acknowledged party.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Install the September 2022 cumulative update matching the running branch — KB5017315 for Windows 11 21H2 (to 22000.978), KB5017308 for Windows 10 20H2/21H1/21H2 (to 19042/19043/19044.2006), or the matching Server 2016 / 2019 / 2022 rollup — and complete the restart, since CLFS.sys is boot-loaded and cannot be unloaded or replaced while running.
prevention.adequacy: The update closes the SignaturesOffset bounds gap, but it arrived after the exploit was already operating in the wild, and every affected KB is marked RestartRequired=Yes — a fleet that downloads on schedule and defers reboots to a monthly window keeps the vulnerable driver image live. Windows 7 SP1, 8.1, RT 8.1, Server 2008 SP2, 2008 R2 SP1, 2012 and 2012 R2 receive it only through the September 2022 monthly rollup or ESU, so an unenrolled host has no remediation short of leaving the platform.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on CLFS base log files created in user-writable paths followed by tight NtFsControlFile loops against the log handle with FsControlCode 0x11003C and 0x110038, on SystemBigPoolInformation (class 0x42) queries from non-diagnostic processes, and on a SYSTEM-integrity shell spawned from a medium- or low-integrity parent.
detection.adequacy: Detection was the only available lever during the pre-patch window and it works — Zscaler's Win32.GenExploit.LogFile and Win32.Exploit.CVE-2022-37969 signatures fire on the malformed .BLF artifact itself. It catches the escalation step, not the loader or phishing payload that supplied the code-execution precondition.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat any host where the token swap succeeded as fully compromised: rebuild rather than clean, rotate every credential cached on the machine, and hunt backwards for the delivery stage that gave the attacker local code execution in the first place.
response.adequacy: The outcome is a SYSTEM token, so nothing short of rebuild plus credential rotation reliably evicts the attacker; applying the September update after exploitation removes the vector but leaves the intruder and anything they installed in place.

NIST-800-53-SC-39.gap: SC-39 mandates a separate execution domain per process, and that is the boundary CLFS.sys dissolved: it trusted a SignaturesOffset value taken from a log file any standard user can author, wrote out of bounds in the kernel pool, and let user-mode code reach into _EPROCESS and take the SYSTEM token. No SC-39 parameter or setting exists that an operator can apply to a driver that loads at boot on every supported Windows build and is callable from any integrity level.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Art.21 vulnerability handling runs disclosure first, remediation second. Here the order was reversed — a working exploit was in the wild on 2022-09-02 and no advisory or update existed until 2022-09-13 — so for eleven days an essential entity's handling process had nothing to triage and nothing to deploy while its entire Windows 10 and 11 estate could be escalated to SYSTEM.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4's system-security outcome is written around networked and internet-exposed systems, and this vulnerability needs no network path at all: it is the internal step that converts an already-landed payload into SYSTEM through a logging driver present on every endpoint by default. A CAF assessment can find the exposed estate fully hardened and never look at the local privilege boundary this flaw crosses.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The 48-hour window for an exploited operating-system flaw assumes a patch exists to install; here weaponised use preceded the fix entirely. When the fix did ship it was inside cumulative updates that all require a restart, so the maturity model's evidence — updates approved and downloaded — can read green on hosts still executing the vulnerable CLFS.sys image in memory.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.28.gap: A.8.28 governs secure coding inside the organisation's own development lifecycle. The missing strict bounds check on the base-log-file SignaturesOffset field sits in Microsoft's closed-source CLFS.sys, where a certified organisation has no code review, static analysis or coding standard to apply and no option to remove the component, so conformance says nothing about whether its endpoints carry a low-privilege-to-SYSTEM out-of-bounds write.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-37969 was added to CISA KEV on 2022-09-14 with confirmed in-the-wild use captured by Zscaler ThreatLabz on 2022-09-02, eleven days before Microsoft had any advisory or update to ship, so the only defensible posture is a KEV-triggered clock that forces documented compensating controls (detection on malformed .BLF artifacts, restriction of local code execution) while no patch exists and forces the September 2022 cumulative update plus restart the moment it does.

new_control_requirements.name: LIVE-PATCH-CAPABILITY
new_control_requirements.description: For any system that processes production workloads and cannot tolerate unplanned reboots: live kernel patching capability (kpatch, livepatch, kGraft, or equivalent) must be deployed and tested quarterly.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-37969 has no live-patch path at all: CLFS.sys is boot-loaded and cannot be unloaded, disabled or replaced while running, and every fixed build (KB5017315, KB5017308, the Server 2016/2019/2022 rollups) is flagged RestartRequired=Yes, so a fleet that downloads updates on schedule but defers reboots to a monthly window keeps executing the vulnerable driver image in memory while its patch evidence reads green.

new_control_requirements.name: KERNEL-EXPLOITATION-DETECTION
new_control_requirements.description: Deploy auditd or eBPF-based monitoring rules for kernel privilege escalation indicators. Alert within 60 seconds of detection.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-37969 was weaponised before the patch existed, which left detection as the only lever during the pre-advisory window, and the escalation is observable at the kernel boundary — tight NtFsControlFile loops with FsControlCode 0x11003C/0x110038 against a user-authored base log file, SystemBigPoolInformation queries from non-diagnostic processes, and a SYSTEM-integrity shell spawned from a medium- or low-integrity parent — yet no framework required any of it.

CVE-2022-32917.name: Apple iOS, iPadOS, and macOS Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An application already executing inside Apple's normal app sandbox reaches an XNU kernel service path that performs an out-of-bounds write, escaping confinement to run arbitrary code with kernel privileges. Apple describes the correction only as 'improved bounds checks' and has never published the vulnerable subsystem, the syscall, the bug-report identifier or the in-the-wild sample. Operators should note the naming mismatch: CISA KEV titles this a remote code execution vulnerability while both Apple and NVD scope it as local kernel code execution from an installed application, with the remote element appearing only if it is chained behind a separate browser or messaging bug Apple never documented.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; the precondition is an application already running on the device, with no user interaction and no network path required at the moment of exploitation
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the 'improved bounds checks' wording places it in the deterministic out-of-bounds-write class rather than a race, but with no public analysis the kernel-heap grooming difficulty cannot be assessed independently and can only be inferred from Apple's own statement that it was already being exploited when the fix shipped
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Apple credits 'an anonymous researcher' in the Kernel entry of HT213443, HT213444, HT213445 and HT213446 (all 2022-09-12) and says it 'may have been actively exploited', the phrasing it uses for an externally supplied report carrying exploitation evidence rather than an internal audit find. No discovery method, tooling or AI involvement is credited by Apple or any third party.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Move every device onto macOS Big Sur 11.7, macOS Monterey 12.6, iOS 15.7 / iPadOS 15.7 or iOS 16 — all released 2022-09-12 — and complete the restart; hardware that cannot run iOS 16 (iPhone 6s and 7 families, iPad mini 4, iPad 5th generation, iPod touch 7th generation) must be taken onto the 15.7 branch instead.
prevention.adequacy: A full OS image was the only unit of remediation available — Apple's Rapid Security Response mechanism did not exist until 2023 — so there was no smaller change to push. The limit is enforcement rather than availability: update commands to unsupervised and personally-owned iPhones and iPads are advisory and user-deferrable, which makes the 2022-10-05 KEV due date unreachable for any BYO fleet.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Continuous version-state inventory against the 15.7 / 11.7 / 12.6 boundaries, plus review of kernel panic and crash-report telemetry on affected builds correlated with recently installed or side-loaded applications, and any sign of unsigned code executing outside the app container on a device with no jailbreak marker.
detection.adequacy: This is the entire detection surface. Apple published no hash, path, domain or network indicator and no third party has supplied one, so an operator can observe only version state and post-exploitation behaviour inconsistent with sandbox confinement — never the exploitation itself.

response.what_would_have_worked: Wipe and restore any device showing unsigned execution outside the container, modified system daemons or cross-application data access on an affected build, rotate the credentials and tokens it held, and pull the suspect application from the fleet.
response.adequacy: Kernel-level code execution invalidates every on-device integrity signal, so a wipe is the only trustworthy eviction. With no vendor indicator set there is no way to scope the incident from the device, meaning response has to assume the worst rather than confirm it.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 lets an organisation define an installation window but gives it no way to enforce one on the devices most at risk. The remediation is a full OS image with a mandatory restart, and MDM update commands on unsupervised or personally-owned Apple hardware are advisory and deferrable, so a 72-hour policy for an actively-exploited kernel flaw still cannot move a staff-owned iPhone 7 off iOS 15.6.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Art.21 patch management depends on being able to triage a disclosure into an emergency or routine track, and Apple's advisory supplied nothing to triage with — no severity, no CVSS, no affected component, only the hedged 'may have been actively exploited'. NVD's CWE-787 classification did not land until 2022-09-20, six days after the CVE was already in KEV.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 covers configuration and hardening the operator can actually apply, and nothing in that repertoire sits on this path: the precondition is simply an application running inside Apple's sandbox and the target is XNU kernel memory. No configuration profile, restriction payload, app allowlist or baseline interposes between an installed app and an out-of-bounds kernel write, so B4 conformance and exposure move independently.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: User application hardening is specified against Windows workstations — browser plugin removal, OLE disabled in Office, PDF reader hardening — and has no iOS, iPadOS or macOS control surface at any maturity level. The mechanism it relies on, stripping abusable features from named applications, has nothing to strip when the exploitation precondition is the mere presence of a running app.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 needs timely technical vulnerability information and a risk-based evaluation of exposure, and both inputs failed. Apple withheld severity and subsystem, NVD's record arrived after the KEV listing, and the 2022-10-05 due date passed before most fleets had even inventoried which devices were on the 15.x branch versus iOS 16 — leaving the process structurally behind both the attacker and the regulator.

new_control_requirements.name: MOBILE-ENDPOINT-MDM-ENFORCED-KEV-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: iOS / iPadOS / macOS estates must enforce KEV-class updates within 24h via DDM; user-deferral disallowed.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-32917 is an actively-exploited app-to-kernel code execution flaw whose only remediation unit is a full OS image with a mandatory restart (macOS 11.7 / 12.6, iOS and iPadOS 15.7, iOS 16), and the enforcement primitive is weakest where the risk is highest: MDM update commands on unsupervised and personally-owned iPhones and iPads are advisory and user-deferrable, so the 2022-10-05 KEV due date was unreachable for any BYO fleet without a deferral-disallowed update policy.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-32917 gave defenders nothing to triage on — no vendor severity, no CVSS, no affected component, only Apple’s hedged "may have been actively exploited", with the NVD CWE-787 classification arriving 2022-09-20, six days after the 2022-09-14 KEV listing — so the KEV entry itself was the only trigger available and had to drive remediation on its own clock rather than through severity-based triage.

CVE-2022-3075.name: Google Chromium Mojo Insufficient Data Validation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A crafted HTML page drives a renderer the attacker has already compromised through a separate V8 or Blink bug to emit malformed Mojo IPC messages at a browser-process interface that accepts them without sufficient validation. Crossing that renderer-to-browser trust boundary is the scope change (S:C) that carries the 9.6 score: sandboxed code execution becomes full browser-process control. Google never named the vulnerable Mojo interface, and Chromium issue 1358134 remains access-restricted, so the message shape has never been published.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N with UI:R for the page visit; in practice NVD's own description makes prior renderer compromise a precondition, so this is the second stage of a chain rather than an entry point
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; a page visit is the whole delivery mechanism, but because the in-the-wild exploit was never released and issue 1358134 is still restricted, no independent assessment of grooming difficulty or reliability is possible
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Google credits an external reporter identified only as 'Anonymous' reporting on 2022-08-30, with a single-fix stable release three days later and an acknowledged in-the-wild exploit. Chrome's automated stack (ASan, MSan, UBSan, CFI, libFuzzer, AFL) is thanked generically in the same post for bugs caught before stable, which this one explicitly was not. No AI tooling is credited by Google or any third party.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Move to Chrome 105.0.5195.102 on Windows, macOS and Linux and force a browser relaunch, and pick up the matching Chromium-derived respins — Microsoft's Edge advisory build, the updated Fedora chromium package, Gentoo GLSA 202209-23 — for every browser in the estate built on the same upstream.
prevention.adequacy: Downloading the fixed build is not applying it: Chrome's component updater can refresh sub-components in place but cannot replace browser-process binaries, so a long-lived session that has not relaunched keeps executing the vulnerable Mojo path against attacker-controlled HTML. There is no flag, policy or configuration that disables Mojo as an interim mitigation, and organisations pinning Chrome to a validated build have to move the pin.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Watch for the browser process — rather than a renderer child — writing outside the Chrome profile directory, spawning child processes or opening network connections unrelated to any loaded page, and for clusters of renderer crashes or Mojo message-validation failures traced back to a single site or ad network.
detection.adequacy: Thin by construction. Delivery is ordinary-looking HTML, the escape creates no process and writes no file, and Google published no hash, domain or payload indicator. The renderer-crash cluster is a signal for the stage that must precede this bug, not for the escape itself.

response.what_would_have_worked: Force-relaunch every browser on the fleet so the update actually takes effect, then treat any host showing browser-process anomalies as compromised at user level: rotate the session cookies and OAuth tokens the browser held and review history for the delivering site.
response.adequacy: Escaped code runs with the browser's own identity and privileges, so everything the browser could reach has to be assumed exposed. With no published indicator set, scoping depends entirely on endpoint telemetry the organisation was already collecting.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: SI-10 names exactly the failure — validity checking of information inputs — but the input is a Mojo IPC message crossing Chrome's internal renderer-to-browser boundary inside a third-party binary, not an interface an agency defines or can author a validity rule for. The scope change out of the sandbox happened below the layer at which any SI-10 implementation operates.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Art.21 measures whether the update was deployed, and Chrome separates deployment from effect. The fixed 105.0.5195.102 binary can be present on every endpoint while browser processes that have not relaunched keep running the pre-fix code, so an entity can report complete coverage from software inventory and still be exposed — the regulation's deployment-oriented wording never forces it to measure relaunch.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: C1 security monitoring has essentially nothing to collect here. The lure is indistinguishable from normal browsing, execution stays inside a process that is already running, the escape creates no process, writes no file and generates no distinctive traffic, and Google published no indicator. A monitoring capability that fully meets C1's outcomes had zero detection content for an actively-exploited CVSS 9.6 flaw.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Browser hardening works by removing separable, abusable features, and Mojo is Chrome's core inter-process channel with no policy switch, reached through plain HTML. Every hardening setting at every maturity level can be enforced and the renderer-to-browser escape path stays exactly as reachable, because the control assumes the dangerous capability can be detached from the browser.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: A.8.7 leans on malware detection and application allowlisting, and both are inert against this. The payload is HTML and JavaScript interpreted by an allowlisted, vendor-signed binary; nothing lands on disk for an engine to scan; and the escaped code inherits the browser's own identity. The control is bypassed by the exploit's design, not by any evasion technique.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-3075 separates deployment from effect: Chrome’s component updater cannot replace browser-process binaries, so the fixed 105.0.5195.102 build can be fully downloaded on every endpoint while long-lived sessions keep executing the vulnerable Mojo path, and there is no flag or policy that disables Mojo as an interim mitigation — the only control is an update ring that forces the relaunch instead of deferring the security channel.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-3075 was KEV-listed on 2022-09-08 as a CVSS 9.6 renderer-to-browser sandbox escape reached through ordinary HTML, with no published hash, domain or payload indicator to detect on and no configuration mitigation, so a KEV-triggered mitigation clock covering Chrome and every Chromium-derived respin (the Edge advisory build, the Fedora chromium package, Gentoo GLSA 202209-23) is the only lever that acts inside the exploitation window.

CVE-2022-27593.name: QNAP Photo Station Externally Controlled Reference Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A single unauthenticated HTTP request to Photo Station's /photo/combine.php carrying a traversing `g` value — the public Nuclei template uses g=core-r7rules/../../../hello.php. — makes the application resolve an attacker-named path instead of an entry in its intended combine list, which is the externally controlled reference itself. DeadBolt used the same primitive in the write direction: reaching internet-exposed Photo Station over Tor, replacing /home/httpd/index.html with the ransom page while preserving the original as index.html.bak, writing /mnt/HDA_ROOT/update_pkg/SDDPd.bin and .SDDPd_required for persistence, then encrypting user data with AES-128-CBC and appending a .deadbolt extension and a 128-byte trailer.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N/UI:N; one unauthenticated request, with internet exposure of Photo Station as the only genuine precondition
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; no race, no memory grooming and no credentials, which is why EPSS sits around 0.879 (99.7th percentile) and a one-request public Nuclei check exists. The C:N/I:H/A:H shape is the tell: the value of the bug is writing to the appliance, not reading from it
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — QNAP PSIRT detected the DeadBolt campaign on the morning of 2022-09-03, published QSA-22-24 the same day with fixed builds already available, and added the CVE identifier in revision V1.1 on 2022-09-08. The CVE exists because the campaign was observed; no external researcher and no tooling is credited.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Update Photo Station through App Center to the build matching the QTS branch — 6.1.2 or later on QTS 5.0.1, 6.0.22 or later on 5.0.0 and 4.5.x, 5.7.18 or later on 4.3.6, 5.4.15 or later on 4.3.3, 5.2.14 or later on 4.2.6 — and follow QSA-22-24 in removing the exposure: disable router port forwarding, disable UPnP port forwarding under myQNAPcloud Auto Router Configuration, clear every entry under Published Services, and reach the NAS only through a myQNAPcloud Link SmartURL with device access set to Private or Customized.
prevention.adequacy: The App Center update closes the reference, but the vendor pairs it with switching off the features that published the appliance in the first place — an admission that the patch alone does not address why the device was reachable. It also does nothing for an already-encrypted NAS: roughly 19,000 were encrypted in the campaign's first days, and DeadBolt releases its key only through a Bitcoin OP_RETURN transaction.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on unauthenticated GETs to /photo/combine.php whose `g` value traverses out of the combine list, on Photo Station access from Tor exit infrastructure, and on the on-device artifacts — /home/httpd/index.html replaced with index.html.bak alongside it, SDDPd.bin and .SDDPd_required under /mnt/HDA_ROOT/update_pkg, and the runtime markers /tmp/deadbolt.pid, /tmp/deadbolt.status and /tmp/deadbolt.finish.
detection.adequacy: The request indicator is precise and cheap to match, but the devices that were hit are home and small-business NAS that forward logs nowhere and run no agent, so in practice the first observable was the ransom page replacing the QTS login screen — by which point the administrative interface is already gone.

response.what_would_have_worked: Restore from a copy held off the appliance, rebuild the NAS from clean firmware rather than cleaning it, and re-check that Photo Station is no longer published outward before returning it to service.
response.adequacy: Recovery turns entirely on whether a copy exists outside the device. QTS snapshots sit on the same volume the ransomware walks, so an organisation with a documented and tested backup regime can still finish the incident with nothing to restore from.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: Boundary protection assumes an administrator decided what crosses the perimeter, and these appliances published themselves: myQNAPcloud Auto Router Configuration requests a UPnP port-forward and Published Services exposes Photo Station through the consumer router, so /photo/combine.php became internet-reachable without any rule an operator wrote. QNAP's remediation is to go and turn those features off, which inverts the control's premise.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: Vulnerability handling is keyed to versioned assets, and the flaw is not in the QTS firmware an entity tracks — it is in an App Center application with five different fixed builds depending on the QTS branch underneath. An entity with firmware fully current still ran the vulnerable component, and QNAP shipped the fix the same day it saw the campaign, faster than any Art.21 cycle can turn five branch-specific version targets into fleet action.

UK-CAF-D1.gap: D1 response-and-recovery planning assumes the responder can reach the system and reconstruct from a recovery point, and DeadBolt removes both: the QTS administrative interface is replaced at the moment of discovery, and the key is released only via a public-blockchain transaction the victim must watch. D1 never requires an operator to show that its recovery point survives the loss of the device holding it.

AU-Essential-8-Backup.gap: The backup strategy asks for regular, retained and restore-tested copies of important data, and QNAP's own advice is to snapshot and back up regularly — but for most victims the encrypted asset was the backup target and the snapshots lived on the same volume. Every maturity level can be satisfied, tested restores included, without the copy ever leaving the appliance that CVE-2022-27593 exposed.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.22.gap: Network segregation expressed as organisational policy is defeated by the device's own behaviour: myQNAPcloud negotiates its own ingress through UPnP, Published Services advertises Photo Station outward, and the application exists to share content over the internet. A.8.22 has no way to express 'this asset must not arrange its own inbound path', which is how an unauthenticated file-modification flaw reached tens of thousands of NAS behind nominally segregated networks.

new_control_requirements.name: BACKUP-TIER-NETWORK-ISOLATION
new_control_requirements.description: Backup-orchestration appliances and backup-data destinations must be network-isolated from the data-plane networks they protect. Management surfaces must be reachable only from operator subnets; backup-data paths must use unidirectional or pull-only patterns from the backup tier to the protected systems where possible.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-27593 turned the backup destination itself into the ransomware target: the NAS published its own inbound path through myQNAPcloud UPnP port-forwarding and Published Services, and QTS snapshots sit on the same volume DeadBolt walked, so roughly 19,000 appliances were encrypted along with the only copy of the data — isolating the backup tier from the data plane and from untrusted ingress is what keeps a recovery point alive when the appliance holding it is lost.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-27593 was KEV-listed on 2022-09-08 with an in-flight DeadBolt ransomware campaign, and the flaw sits in Photo Station — an App Center application with five branch-specific fixed builds (6.1.2 / 6.0.22 / 5.7.18 / 5.4.15 / 5.2.14) rather than in the QTS firmware an asset register tracks — so only a KEV-triggered clock that accepts documented compensating controls (disabling port forwarding, UPnP and Published Services per QSA-22-24) acts fast enough to matter.

CVE-2022-26258.name: D-Link DIR-820L Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated POST to /get_set.ccp — the backend handler behind the Device Name field on /lan.asp — with ccp_act=set and lanHostCfg_DeviceName_1.1.1.0=%0atelnetd -l /bin/sh%0a. The firmware's hasInjectionString filter never treats the newline as a metacharacter, so the payload breaks out of the assignment and starts a root telnet shell; sending the request directly to the handler makes the front-end JavaScript validation irrelevant. Unit 42 documented MooBot firing the same /lan.asp DeviceName injection in volume in September 2022, chaining wget to pull architecture-specific bot binaries.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N/UI:N; one unauthenticated HTTP POST with no session and no chaining, and the injected command runs as root on the router's embedded Linux
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the only obstacle in the path omits the newline from its blocklist, so the bypass is a literal %0a. EPSS sits around 0.798 (99.6th percentile), and Mirai-derived botnets fold it straight into scan-and-infect loops alongside CVE-2015-2051, CVE-2018-6530 and CVE-2022-28958
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — a hand-read of the CGI handler observing that hasInjectionString omits the newline, published as an independent GitHub write-up (skyedai910's Vuln repository) that NVD ingested as the sole exploit reference. D-Link's SAP10295 describes it as a documented 0-day with no coordinated-disclosure timeline and no researcher acknowledgement, and no AI tooling is credited by anyone.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: There is no vendor fix and there will not be one: SAP10295 declares the DIR-820L end of life and end of service life across all hardware revisions with firmware development ceased, and CISA's required action is to disconnect the device rather than update it. Prevention means decommissioning the router and replacing it with supported hardware.
prevention.adequacy: Only removal remediates. For a unit that must stay in service pending replacement, the available measures are removing every inbound WAN path to the HTTP administration interface (no port-forward, no UPnP, remote management disabled), placing the router behind a supported firewall, and blocking its outbound access so the wget stage of the botnet chain fails — none of which repair the /get_set.ccp injection, which stays reachable from the LAN side on every affected unit.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on POSTs to /get_set.ccp whose lanHostCfg_DeviceName_1.1.1.0 value carries an encoded newline followed by a shell command, on an unexpected telnet listener appearing on the router, and on the device fetching per-architecture ELF payloads — Unit 42 recorded MooBot staging from 159.203.15[.]179 (wget.sh, wget.sh3, and mips/mipsel/arm/arm5/arm6/arm7/sh4/arc/sparc/x86_64/i686/i586 binaries) with command and control at vpn.komaru[.]today.
detection.adequacy: The indicators are concrete but the device forwards no logs and runs no agent, so detection has to happen on the network around it — the outbound fetch to the staging host, or DDoS traffic sourced from the router — rather than on the router itself. A stored Device Name containing newlines or shell metacharacters is the one on-device tell an operator can check by hand.

response.what_would_have_worked: Disconnect the unit, replace it, and treat everything that traversed it as exposed; a compromised DIR-820L is running attacker code as root between an internal network and the internet.
response.adequacy: There is no clean state to return the device to. No firmware exists that closes the injection, so a factory reset restores the vulnerability along with the defaults — replacement is the only terminal state for the incident.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation tells an organisation to identify, report and correct flaws by installing security-relevant updates, and no update exists — every DIR-820L hardware revision is end of life with firmware development ceased. The only action that closes an unauthenticated root command injection is physical replacement, which SI-2 neither names as remediation nor triggers, so full conformance is compatible with running the vulnerable router indefinitely.

EU-CRA-Art13.gap: Art.13's manufacturer duties — vulnerability handling and security updates across a declared support period — describe precisely the failure here, but they bind products placed on the EU market from the regulation's application date. A router sold years earlier sits outside their reach, so the installed base keeps a one-request root shell with a published payload while the manufacturer owes nothing and CISA's advice is to unplug it.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 is scoped to the estate supporting the essential function, and a consumer DIR-820L rarely appears in that inventory — it fronts a home-worker broadband line or an unmanaged branch connection. An operator can hold every in-scope asset supported and patched and still have an end-of-life router carrying an unauthenticated root shell between an essential-function user and the internet, with no CAF mechanism to reach equipment it neither owns nor can enumerate.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Both arms of the strategy fail on this CVE: the exploited-vulnerability window has nothing to apply because D-Link shipped no patch, and the requirement to remove vendor-unsupported products presumes the organisation has authority to decommission the device. For a router owned by a remote worker or bundled with a leased line, the mandated action lies outside the organisation's control even at Maturity Level Three.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 assumes timely vendor information leading to treatment by patch, mitigation or acceptance. The vendor channel answered with an end-of-life notice rather than a fix, and once the only remaining treatment is CISA's literal instruction to disconnect, no A.8.8 path keeps the asset in service. The residual risk recorded against the router is permanent, and the control offers the risk owner no re-evaluation trigger that will ever change it.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: Network-reachable end-of-life devices with no vendor patch path must be isolated and decommissioned within a bounded window; mandatory compensating segmentation applies until removal since no remediation exists.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-26258 has no fix and never will: D-Link’s SAP10295 declares every DIR-820L hardware revision end of life with firmware development ceased, and CISA’s KEV required action is to disconnect the device rather than update it, so the only terminal remediation for an unauthenticated CVSS 9.8 root command injection on /get_set.ccp is a bounded decommission window with mandatory segmentation until the unit is gone.

new_control_requirements.name: UNSUPPORTED-NETWORK-DEVICE-ENUMERATION-AND-RETIREMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Every network-attached embedded device (IP cameras, video servers, NVRs, routers, print/scan appliances) must carry an end-of-support date in the asset inventory, and any device past that date that exposes a remotely reachable management or media surface must be removed from untrusted networks and scheduled for replacement — patching is not an option once the vendor retires the model. The distinguishing test: query the asset inventory for devices whose firmware lifecycle has ended and whose management interface is reachable from an untrusted segment; any non-empty result that lacks a replace-or-formally-risk-accept decision is a finding. Paper patch-management policies that assume a fix always exists leave actively-exploited EOL devices (GeoVision IP cameras, recruited by Mirai-style botnets) on the network indefinitely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-26258 sits on consumer routers that front home-worker broadband lines and unmanaged branch connections and therefore never appear in any scoped asset register, so the exposure is invisible until the device is enumerated: an inventory that carries an end-of-support date for every network-attached embedded device is what surfaces an EOL DIR-820L whose HTTP admin surface is reachable and forces the replace-or-formally-risk-accept decision.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-26258 was KEV-listed on 2022-09-08 while MooBot was actively recruiting these routers, and because no patch exists the KEV clock is the only mechanism that forces the alternative within hours — removing every inbound WAN path to the HTTP admin interface, placing the unit behind a supported firewall, and blocking its outbound access so the wget staging step of the botnet chain fails.

CVE-2020-9934.name: Apple iOS, iPadOS, and macOS Input Validation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: tccd builds the path to its consent database by expanding $HOME, and launchd lets a logged-in user set that variable in their own domain. Four commands do the whole job: create a fake 'Library/Application Support/com.apple.TCC' tree under an attacker-owned path, run launchctl setenv HOME /tmp/tccbypass, stop and start com.apple.tccd so it re-reads its database path, then sqlite3 INSERT rows into the attacker-owned TCC.db. The consent daemon then enforces a policy the attacker wrote, granting kTCCServiceCamera, kTCCServiceMicrophone, kTCCServiceScreenCapture and kTCCServiceSystemPolicyAllFiles to a client bundle id such as com.apple.Terminal.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; an existing interactive session as an ordinary, non-administrative user, with no escalation needed anywhere in the chain
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; no race, no memory corruption, no user interaction and no exploit code — four shell commands, with a maintained Metasploit post module (post/osx/escalate/tccbypass) automating them. The demonstrated path is macOS; Apple also fixed iOS/iPadOS in 13.6, but launchctl setenv is not reachable to a normal iOS app, so field exploitation is a macOS story
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Matt Shockley found it by reading how tccd constructs its database path and noticing the $HOME expansion, reported it to Apple on 2020-02-26, and is credited by name in HT211289 under CoreFoundation. No fuzzer, static-analysis engine or AI tooling appears anywhere in the disclosure timeline or the vendor credit.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Move endpoints to macOS Catalina 10.15.6 (released 2020-07-15) or later, and iOS / iPadOS 13.6 or later; the fix stops tccd expanding $HOME and resolves the user's home directory through a getpwuid() lookup instead, so a launchd environment override no longer moves the consent database.
prevention.adequacy: The vendor fix is complete and addresses the mechanism rather than an instance of it. What failed was the signal to apply it: Apple shipped on 2020-07-15 and the KEV listing did not arrive until 2022-09-08, so for two years nothing but routine OS currency drove the upgrade — and on an unpatched Catalina host there is no supported switch that disables the behaviour.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on launchctl setenv HOME in a user's launchd domain, on a stop immediately followed by a start of com.apple.tccd, on any process opening a com.apple.TCC/TCC.db outside the real home directory and INSERTing into its access table, and on an application holding camera, microphone, screen-recording or Full Disk Access entitlements the user was never prompted to approve.
detection.adequacy: High fidelity — a legitimate macOS session never overrides HOME for the whole launchd domain — but it has to be collected live. launchctl unsetenv HOME plus a tccd restart reverses the bypass completely, so a host examined afterwards shows a consistent consent database and no evidence the grant ever existed.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat everything the account could read as exposed — Documents, Desktop, Mail, the Photos library — assume camera, microphone and screen capture were available, rotate any credentials reachable from those files, and check whether the recording entitlements were actually exercised.
response.adequacy: Because the bypass leaves no durable trace once reversed, scoping depends entirely on telemetry captured at the time; without it, response has to assume the full protected-data set plus the recording devices were reached.

NIST-800-53-AC-3.gap: Access enforcement assumes the reference monitor's policy store is out of the subject's reach. On affected macOS the monitor is tccd and its store is a SQLite file whose path tccd derives from a variable any non-administrative user can set in their own launchd domain, so a standard account rewrites the policy the enforcement point consults. AC-3 is satisfied by a mechanism faithfully enforcing attacker-authored rules.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Vulnerability handling is driven by severity signal and threat feeds, and both were silent for two years: Apple fixed this on 2020-07-15, CISA did not list it until 2022-09-08, and NVD scores it 5.5 with no CWE assigned. Nothing in the process would have forced macOS endpoints off 10.15.x, while a maintained Metasploit post module turned any low-privilege foothold into camera, microphone, screen and full-disk access.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2 asks whether sensitive data is reachable only by authorised identities and whether privileged access is minimised, but the attacker needs no privilege: the identity performing the bypass is the ordinary interactive user, and the boundary crossed is macOS consent, which is not an identity or directory construct a B2 assessment enumerates. An estate scoring well through MDM-enforced non-admin accounts is exactly the estate this works on.

AU-ISM-1546.gap: ISM-1546's patch windows are driven by vendor-assessed severity and internet exposure, and a local confidentiality-only macOS flaw lands in the slowest band under any reading, with the operating-system guidance written around a Windows SOE rather than a Catalina fleet. The one action that closes it therefore never receives an accelerated window, despite the exploit being four shell commands with a maintained module behind them.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Every input to A.8.8's risk rating understates this: CVSS 5.5, AV:L, no NVD CWE, no ransomware association. The rating cannot express that the flaw's value is post-exploitation reach — a foothold becomes the user's entire protected-data set plus their camera and microphone — nor that a single launchctl unsetenv erases the evidence, so the programme both deprioritises it and loses the proof it was used.

new_control_requirements.name: MOBILE-ENDPOINT-MDM-ENFORCED-KEV-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: iOS / iPadOS / macOS estates must enforce KEV-class updates within 24h via DDM; user-deferral disallowed.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2020-9934 was fixed by Apple on 2020-07-15 in macOS Catalina 10.15.6 and iOS/iPadOS 13.6 but not KEV-listed until 2022-09-08, and as a local confidentiality-only flaw scored CVSS 5.5 with no CWE it lands in the slowest band of every severity-driven patch window — only a KEV-deadline-bound, deferral-disallowed Apple update policy moves an estate off 10.15.x while a maintained Metasploit post module is turning any low-privilege foothold into camera, microphone and Full Disk Access.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2020-9934 spent two years with a complete vendor fix available and no signal to apply it — no CISA listing until 2022-09-08, no NVD CWE, no ransomware association — and there is no supported switch that disables the tccd $HOME expansion on an unpatched host, so the KEV listing is the single trigger that must convert into a bounded mitigation clock.

CVE-2018-7445.name: MikroTik RouterOS Stack-Based Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: NetBIOS session-request messages of type 0x81 sent to TCP/445 stage shellcode at a predictable heap address, then a request whose name-length byte exceeds the destination buffer overflows the stack in the SMB binary's name-parsing routine, which reads a length byte and copies that many bytes with no bounds check. A ROP chain loads EBX with the heap base (0x8072000 on x86 Cloud Hosted Router), ECX=0x14000 and EDX=7 and enters __kernel_vsyscall through INT 0x80 to call mprotect and mark the heap RWX; execution jumps to the staged shellcode, which locates the SMB socket file descriptor, dup2s it over stdin, stdout and stderr and execs /bin/sh — returning an interactive root-equivalent shell over the same connection, all before authentication.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N/UI:N; the overflow occurs before authentication takes place, so a single unauthenticated connection to the SMB listener is the entire precondition
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; deterministic, with no race and no delicate grooming because the RouterOS heap base is not randomised. Two qualifiers on the 9.8: SMB is off by default so only boards where an operator ran /ip smb set enabled=yes are exposed, and the published exploit's gadgets and hardcoded heap base target x86 Cloud Hosted Router, so MIPS, ARM and tile boards need the gadgets re-derived
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Juan Caillava and Maximiliano Vidal of Core Security Consulting Services found it with 2018-era mutation fuzzing (a Mutiny Fuzzer template built from captured SMB traffic) followed by manual root-cause analysis of the name-parsing routine, with Leandro Cuozzo coordinating publication. No AI-assisted discovery or crash triage is claimed in the advisory or the vendor exchange.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrade RouterOS to 6.41.3 or later on the stable channel, or 6.42rc27 or later on the release-candidate channel, and reboot the board — every architecture and every board below those versions is affected, so branch and CPE devices need the same upgrade as core routers. Where the reboot cannot be scheduled, /ip smb set enabled=no (also the factory default) or a firewall rule on TCP/445 removes the exposure outright.
prevention.adequacy: Unusually complete for a network appliance: the vendor-sanctioned mitigation is as effective as the patch, because the overflow is reachable only through the SMB listener and that listener is an optional service a router does not need. The failure mode is inventory rather than remediation — MikroTik confirmed the fix to Core Security on 2018-03-12, and boards installed as branch CPE or lab kit are still running pre-6.41.3 firmware because nobody has them on a list.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on inbound TCP/445 NetBIOS session requests carrying a name-length byte larger than the destination buffer, on several large session requests immediately preceding a malformed one (the staging pattern), on the RouterOS SMB process crashing and respawning when 445 is swept, and on segmentation-fault entries for the SMB binary in /rw/logs/backtrace.log.
detection.adequacy: The packet shape is distinctive and the crash artifact sits on the device, but the successful exploit serves /bin/sh back over the existing SMB socket rather than opening an outbound callback, so there is no egress signal to catch. Detection has to be watching inbound 445 or reading the router's own logs — and post-exploitation changes such as an ACCEPT input policy or a new scheduler entry are the later tell.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rebuild the board from a clean RouterOS image rather than upgrading in place, re-apply configuration from a pre-incident export, rotate every credential and key the device held, and audit for attacker-added firewall rules, admin users and scheduler or script entries.
response.adequacy: A shell on the router means the device enforcing segmentation was itself controlled, so every policy it applied and every secret it stored has to be treated as attacker-visible. An in-place upgrade closes the overflow but leaves attacker-authored configuration intact.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality is the control that actually closes this, and it is the one least likely to be applied to a router. RouterOS bundles an optional SMB file server unrelated to routing, off by default, and the pre-authentication overflow is reachable only once an operator enables it. CM-7 baselines for network gear are written against the management plane, so a hardening review can close Winbox, SSH, the API and the web UI and still leave /ip smb listening on 445.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Network security measures rest on segmenting networks and protecting what sits inside them, and this flaw inverts that: the vulnerable listener runs on the device that enforces the segmentation, and one unauthenticated session request yields a shell on it. Every downstream measure that depends on that router — VLAN separation, firewall policy, VPN termination, logging — is then administered by a process the attacker owns.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 expects systems supporting essential functions to be inventoried, hardened and current, and it is assessed against the asset register rather than what is actually reachable. MikroTik boards are the classic un-registered asset — cheap branch CPE, lab kit, a spare edge router a site team installed. B4 also gives no weight to the fact that the fix requires rebooting a live edge device, which is why these boards still run pre-6.41.3 firmware years on.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The strictest window applies from day one here — a working exploit shipped with the advisory on 2018-03-15 — so the timeframe is not the problem. Scope is: the strategy has no discovery requirement, so an organisation is assessed against the internet-facing devices it has listed, and it carries no obligation to audit whether an optional file-sharing service should ever have been enabled on a routing appliance.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.21.gap: A.8.21 governs network services whose security mechanisms, service levels and management requirements are identified and set out in agreements. A file-sharing daemon compiled into a router's firmware is not a network service in that sense — no supplier agreement, no service level, no named owner — so nothing in the A.8.21 process would ever surface /ip smb enabled=yes on a branch router, which is the entire precondition for a pre-authentication overflow returning a root-equivalent shell.

new_control_requirements.name: KERNEL-MODULE-INVENTORY-AND-DISABLE
new_control_requirements.description: Maintain an inventory of loaded kernel modules. For modules not required for business function (RxRPC, unused crypto modules), disable via modprobe blacklist as a least-functionality control. Review quarterly.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2018-7445 is reachable only through an optional SMB file server RouterOS bundles into a routing appliance and that is off by default, so the pre-authentication overflow exists purely because someone enabled a component the device does not need for its business function — an enumerate-what-is-loaded-and-disable-what-is-unnecessary discipline, reviewed on a schedule, removes the listener outright and is as effective as the 6.41.3 upgrade that requires rebooting a live edge board.

new_control_requirements.name: UNSUPPORTED-NETWORK-DEVICE-ENUMERATION-AND-RETIREMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Every network-attached embedded device (IP cameras, video servers, NVRs, routers, print/scan appliances) must carry an end-of-support date in the asset inventory, and any device past that date that exposes a remotely reachable management or media surface must be removed from untrusted networks and scheduled for replacement — patching is not an option once the vendor retires the model. The distinguishing test: query the asset inventory for devices whose firmware lifecycle has ended and whose management interface is reachable from an untrusted segment; any non-empty result that lacks a replace-or-formally-risk-accept decision is a finding. Paper patch-management policies that assume a fix always exists leave actively-exploited EOL devices (GeoVision IP cameras, recruited by Mirai-style botnets) on the network indefinitely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2018-7445 persists on MikroTik boards years after MikroTik confirmed the fix to Core Security on 2018-03-12, because the affected units are cheap branch CPE, lab kit and spare edge routers that no asset register lists — an organisation is only ever assessed against the internet-facing devices it has enumerated, so an inventory obligation covering every network-attached embedded device is the precondition for this CVE being remediated at all.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2018-7445 shipped with a working exploit alongside the 2018-03-15 advisory and was KEV-listed on 2022-09-08, four years later, on boards still running pre-6.41.3 firmware; the KEV clock is what forces the choice within hours between the reboot-requiring upgrade and the vendor-sanctioned compensating control (/ip smb set enabled=no, or a firewall rule on TCP/445) rather than leaving an unauthenticated root-equivalent shell reachable.

CVE-2018-6530.name: D-Link Multiple Routers OS Command Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: soapcgi_main in cgibin takes the `service` query parameter from a request to /soap.cgi and interpolates it into a shell script filename that is then executed, so shell metacharacters in that parameter run as commands on the router. The finder's published request is a single unauthenticated POST — /soap.cgi?service=whatever-control;iptables -P INPUT ACCEPT;telnetd -p 9999;whatever-invalid-shell — which flushes the inbound firewall policy to ACCEPT and starts a telnet daemon on TCP/9999, converting one HTTP request into a persistent shell that outlives the request. D-Link's own SAP10105 later records that the fix was bypassable using an `&&` substring, tracked separately as CVE-2018-20114.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N/UI:N; one unauthenticated request, with no memory corruption, no race and no information leak needed to chain
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; a `;` or `&&` plus the desired command is the entire exploit and weaponisation cost is effectively zero, consistent with KEV recording ransomware campaign use as Known. The one real variable is exposure: SAP10105 asserts the soap.cgi path is LAN-side only while NVD scores it AV:N, and the difference between those positions is whether remote administration is enabled
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — D-Link's SAP10080 credits Kaixiang Zhang of the Qihoo 360 Gear Team, logging the report on 2018-01-14 after firmware extraction and CGI reverse engineering, and the researcher published the reproducer himself; the follow-on `&&` bypass is credited by SAP10105 to MinGeun Kim of KAIST. Neither vendor advisory nor either researcher claims automated discovery tooling or AI involvement.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the last available firmware for the model — DIR-880L v1.08B06, DIR-868L v1.20B01, DIR-865L v1.10B01 and DIR-860L v1.11B01 from SAP10080, released 2018-02-28 — disable remote and WAN administration so /soap.cgi is not internet-reachable, and plan replacement, because SAP10189 (DIR-868L, DIR-880L; 2020-08-07) and SAP10190 (DIR-860L, DIR-865L) put all of these models out of support.
prevention.adequacy: The first fix was incomplete: the same handler stayed reachable through an `&&` substring, tracked as CVE-2018-20114, and the corrected build reached only DIR-818LW v2.06B01Beta and DIR-860L v2.04B04Beta01 in January 2019. CISA's required action names that later fix as what properly patches this entry, which means the DIR-880L, DIR-868L and DIR-865L never received a complete one — for those models the only remediation left is replacement.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on requests to /soap.cgi whose `service` parameter carries `;`, `&&`, backticks or `$(`; on the router flushing its inbound policy with iptables -P INPUT ACCEPT; on a telnetd listener appearing on TCP/9999; and on the device fetching a MIPS or ARM ELF over HTTP or TFTP immediately after a /soap.cgi request.
detection.adequacy: The `&&` form specifically distinguishes a bypass of the first fix from a pre-patch attempt, which is the detail that tells an operator whether their firmware update helped at all. As with any consumer router the device ships no telemetry, so detection has to happen on the surrounding network or not at all.

response.what_would_have_worked: Assume root on the router: replace the unit rather than reflashing, rotate any credentials that transited or were stored on it, and check every same-model device in the estate for attacker persistence — an open INPUT policy, an extra listener, router-originated scanning.
response.adequacy: For the three models that never received the complete fix there is no firmware to return to, so reflashing reinstalls the exposure. Replacement is the only end state, and until it happens the device stays enrollable as attack infrastructure.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 assumes identifying a flaw leads to an available fix, and here the sequence terminates: the 2018-02-28 firmware was bypassable with `&&`, the corrected build reached only two of the models in January 2019, and the rest went out of support in 2020 with no complete fix ever issued. A programme executing perfectly installs a patch CISA's own required action says does not close the CVE, then has nothing further to install.

EU-CRA-Art13.gap: Art.13 — security by design, a declared support period, free updates throughout it, vulnerability handling across the product lifetime — describes exactly what failed: an incomplete first fix, a second fix delivered to two of the affected models, end of support declared while the devices stayed in service. But the CRA binds products placed on the market from its application date, and these routers shipped in 2014-2015, so the installed base still answering /soap.cgi is outside its reach entirely.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 is assessed against systems the organisation knows it operates. These are consumer routers at homeworker premises and small branch sites, bought and installed outside procurement and absent from the CAF-scoped register, so corporate-estate outcomes can be scored as achieved while a homeworker's VPN terminates on an end-of-support DIR-880L executing shell commands taken straight from an unauthenticated query parameter.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Both triggers fire on paper — an internet-facing device with a working public exploit, and an operating system no longer vendor-supported — and neither produces a finding, because assessment is bounded to the organisation's own systems and a homeworker's or small-branch router is not one of them. Maturity Level Three on the managed fleet is compatible with routing that fleet's traffic through this device.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: A.8.9 wants configurations established, documented and monitored against a baseline, and the setting that decides everything here — whether remote/WAN administration is on, and therefore whether /soap.cgi faces the internet — is a consumer toggle set by whoever unboxed the router. The gap between D-Link's LAN-side claim and NVD's AV:N score is entirely that toggle, and it sits in a configuration register that never included the device.

new_control_requirements.name: SCANNER-PAPER-COMPLIANCE-TEST
new_control_requirements.description: A vulnerability scanner that reports 'patched' based on kernel package version alone is paper compliance. The operational test: does the scan account for the module-unload mitigation surface, AND does it verify the kernel is on a build that includes the specific Fragnesia patch (not just any version newer than the Dirty Frag patch that introduced Fragnesia)?
